It's not enough to cut their heads off, since they hold back progress. Would you believe it, Ivan, that all this really tears at my feelings? No, I can see you don't believe it, from your eyes. You believe what people say -- that I'm nothing but a buffoon. Alyosha, do you believe I'm nothing but a buffoon?"
"No, I don't believe it."

"And I believe that you don't, and that you're speaking the truth. You look sincere, and you speak sincerely. But not Ivan. Ivan's supercilious.... I'd still put an end to your monks, all the same. I'd take that whole mystical business and stamp it out, once and for all, everywhere in Russia, to bring all the fools to their senses. And think of the gold and silver that would come pouring into the mint!"
"But why suppress it?" asked Ivan.
"So that Truth may prevail. That's why."
"Well, if Truth were to prevail, you know, you'd be the very first one robbed and suppressed."

"Ah! I daresay you're right. Ah, what an ass I am!" Fyodor Pavlovitch burst out, striking himself lightly on the forehead. "Well, your monastery can stand then, Alyosha, if that's how it is. And we clever people will sit snug and enjoy our brandy. You know, Ivan, it must have been ordained that way by the Almighty himself. Ivan, tell me -- is there a God, or isn't there? Wait, tell me the truth, tell me seriously. Why are you laughing again?"
"I'm laughing because you made such a clever remark just now, about Smerdyakov's belief in the existence of two saints who could move mountains."
"Why, am I like him now, then?"
"Very much so."

"Well, that just shows I'm a Russian too, and I've got a Russian characteristic in me. And you might get caught the same way, philosopher though you are. Want to bet I'll catch you at it tomorrow? Tell me anyway -- is there a God, or isn't there? Only be serious. I want you to be serious now."
"No, there is no God."
"Alyosha, is there a God?"
"There is."
"Ivan, and is there any kind of immortality -- just a little, just a tiny bit?"
"There's no immortality either."
"None at all?"
"None at all."
"So it's absolute nothingness, then. Or maybe there's just something? Anything's better than nothing!"
"Absolute nothingness."
"Alyosha, is there immortality?"
"There is."
"God and immortality?"
"God and immortality. Immortality is in God."

"Hm! It's more likely Ivan's right. Good Lord, to think how much faith, how much strength of every kind, mankind has poured out for nothing, on that dream, and for how many thousand years. Who's it who's laughing at man? Ivan! For the last time, once and for all -- is there a God, or isn't there? I'm asking you for the last time!"
"And for the last time -- there isn't."
"Who's laughing at mankind, Ivan?"
"It must be the devil," said Ivan, smiling.
"And the devil? Does he exist?"
"No, there's no devil either."
"That's a pity. Damn it all, what wouldn't I do to the man who first invented God! Hanging on a bitter aspen tree would be too good for him."
"There'd have been no civilization at all if they hadn't invented God."
"Wouldn't there have been? Without God?"
"No. And there'd have been no brandy either. But I really must take your brandy away from you now."
"Stop, stop, stop, dear boy, just one more little glass. I've hurt Alyosha's feelings. You're not angry with me, Alyosha? My dear little Alexey!"
"No, I'm not angry. I know your thoughts. Your heart is better than your head."
"My heart better than my head, is it? Oh, Lord! And that, from you. Ivan, do you love Alyosha?"
"Yes."

"You must love him" (Fyodor Pavlovitch was very drunk by this point). "Listen, Alyosha, I was rude to your elder this morning. But I was worked up. Still, there's something witty about that elder, don't you think, Ivan?"
"Very likely."

"There is, there is. Il y a du Piron là-dedans. He's a Jesuit, a Russian one, mind you. Being an honorable man, he's got some hidden indignation boiling inside him at having to keep up the pretense of holiness."
"But he believes in God, of course."

"Not a bit of it. Didn't you know? Why, he tells everyone so himself. That is, not everyone -- just the clever people who come to see him. He said straight out to Governor Schultz not long ago: 'Credo, but I don't know in what.'"
"Really?"

"He really did say that. But I respect him. There's something of Mephistopheles about him, or rather of 'The Hero of Our Time' -- Arbenin, or whatever his name is.... You see, he's a sensualist. Such a sensualist, in fact, that I'd be afraid for my daughter or my wife if she went to confess to him. You know, when he starts telling stories.... The year before last he invited us to tea, tea with liqueur -- the ladies send him liqueur -- and started telling us about the old days until we nearly split our sides laughing.... Especially about the time he cured a paralyzed woman. 'If my legs weren't so bad, I know a dance I could show you,' he said. What do you make of that? 'I've had plenty of tricks up my sleeve in my time,' he said. He swindled Demidov, the merchant, out of sixty thousand."
"What, he stole it?"

"He brought him the money like a man he trusted, saying, 'Take care of this for me, friend, there'll be a police search at my place tomorrow.' And he kept it. 'You gave it to the Church,' he told him. I said to him: 'You're a scoundrel,' I said. 'No,' he said, 'I'm not a scoundrel, I'm just broad-minded.' But that wasn't him -- that was someone else. I've mixed him up with someone else... without even noticing. Come, one more glass and that's enough. Take the bottle away, Ivan. I've been telling lies. Why didn't you stop me, Ivan, and tell me I was lying?"
"I knew you'd stop on your own."
"That's a lie. You did it out of spite, out of plain spite against me. You despise me. You've come here and despised me in my own house."
"Well, I'm leaving. You've had too much brandy."
"I've begged you, for Christ's sake, to go to Tchermashnya for a day or two, and you won't go."
"I'll go tomorrow if you're so set on it."
"You won't go. You want to keep an eye on me. That's what you want, spiteful fellow. That's exactly why you won't go."
The old man kept at it. He'd reached that stage of drunkenness where a normally inoffensive drunk starts trying to pick a quarrel and assert himself.

"Why are you looking at me like that? Why do you look at me that way? Your eyes say, 'You ugly drunkard!' Your eyes are full of mistrust. They're contemptuous.... You've come here with some scheme in mind. Alyosha, here, looks at me and his eyes shine. Alyosha doesn't despise me. Alexey, you mustn't love Ivan."
"Don't be so hard on my brother. Leave off attacking him," Alyosha said firmly.
"Oh, all right. Ugh, my head aches. Take the brandy away, Ivan. That's the third time I've told you."
He fell into thought, and suddenly a slow, cunning grin spread across his face.

"Don't be angry with a feeble old man, Ivan. I know you don't love me, but don't be angry all the same. You've got nothing to love me for. You go to Tchermashnya. I'll come and visit you myself and bring you a present. I'll show you a little wench there. I've had my eye on her a long while. She still runs around barefoot. Don't be put off by barefoot wenches -- don't despise them -- they're pearls!"
And he kissed his own hand with a smack.

"To my mind," he revived at once, seeming to grow sober the instant he touched on his favorite topic, "to my mind... Ah, you boys! You children, little sucking pigs, to my mind... I've never thought a woman ugly in my whole life -- that's been my rule! Can you understand that? How could you possibly understand it? You've got milk in your veins, not blood. You haven't even hatched yet. My rule has always been that you can find something devilishly interesting in every single woman, something you won't find in any other. Only you have to know how to find it -- that's the whole trick! That's a real talent! To my mind there's no such thing as an ugly woman. The simple fact that she's a woman is half the battle right there... but how could you understand that? Even in old maids, even in them you can discover something that makes you wonder how men could have been such fools as to let them grow old without ever noticing them. Barefoot girls, or plain ones -- you have to catch them off guard. Didn't you know that? You have to astonish them until they're dazzled, thrown off balance, ashamed that a gentleman like you could possibly fall for a little nobody like her. It's a fine thing that there always have been, and always will be, masters and servants in this world, so there'll always be some little maid-of-all-work and her master, and you know, that's really all a man needs for happiness. Wait... listen, Alyosha, I always used to surprise your mother, but in a different way. I'd pay her no attention at all, and then, all at once, when the moment came, I'd turn into pure devotion, crawl on my knees, kiss her feet, and I always, always -- I remember it like it was yesterday -- reduced her to that tinkling, quiet, nervous, odd little laugh of hers. It was peculiar to her. I knew her attacks always started that way. The next day she'd start shrieking hysterically, and that little laugh wasn't a sign of pleasure at all, though it made a very convincing imitation of one. That's the great trick -- knowing how to handle every single person. Once a man named Belyavsky -- handsome fellow, and rich -- used to like coming round here and hanging about her -- suddenly gave me a slap across the face, right in front of her. And she -- meek as a lamb -- why, I thought she'd have knocked me flat for that blow. How she went at me! 'You've been struck, struck!' she said. 'You've taken a blow from him. You were trying to sell me to him,' she said.... 'And how dare he strike you in front of me! Never come near me again, never, never! Go at once, challenge him to a duel!' I took her to the monastery after that, to bring her back to her senses. The holy Fathers prayed her back to reason. But I swear to God, Alyosha, I never once insulted the poor crazy girl! Except once, maybe, that first year. She was very fond of praying back then. She used to observe the feasts of Our Lady especially, and would turn me out of her room on those days. I'll knock that mysticism right out of her, I thought! 'Here,' I said, 'you see this holy image of yours. Here it is. I'm taking it down. You believe it's miraculous, but here, I'll spit on it right now and nothing will happen to me for it!'... When she saw that, good Lord! I thought she'd kill me. But she just jumped up, wrung her hands, then suddenly buried her face in them, started shaking all over, and collapsed to the floor... fell in a heap. Alyosha, Alyosha, what's the matter?"

The old man jumped up in alarm. From the moment he'd started speaking about his mother, Alyosha's face had gradually changed. He'd flushed crimson, his eyes were glowing, his lips trembling. The old sot had gone rambling on, oblivious to all of it, until the moment when something very strange happened to Alyosha. What he was describing in the crazy woman was suddenly repeated in Alyosha, exactly. He jumped up from his seat exactly as his mother was said to have done, wrung his hands, buried his face in them, and fell back into his chair, shaking all over in a hysterical fit of sudden, silent, violent weeping. His startling resemblance to his mother struck the old man forcefully.

"Ivan, Ivan! Water, quick! It's exactly like her, exactly like her, his mother. Spit some water on him, that's what I used to do for her. He's upset about his mother, his mother," he muttered to Ivan.

"But she was my mother too, I believe -- his mother. Wasn't she?" said Ivan, with unrestrained anger and contempt. The old man shrank back before his blazing eyes. But something very strange had happened, though only for a second; it seemed to have genuinely slipped the old man's mind that Alyosha's mother was Ivan's mother too.

"Your mother?" he muttered, not understanding. "What do you mean? What mother are you talking about? Was she?... Why, damn it! Of course she was yours too! Damn it! My mind's never gone dark like that before. Forgive me, why, I was thinking, Ivan.... He he he!" He stopped. A broad, drunken, half-senseless grin spread across his face.
At that moment a fearful noise and uproar came from the hall -- violent shouting, the door was flung open, and Dmitri burst into the room. The old man rushed to Ivan in terror.
"He'll kill me! He'll kill me! Don't let him near me!" he screamed, clutching at the skirt of Ivan's coat.

chapters.title: IX. The Sensualists
paragraphs: Grigory and Smerdyakov ran into the room right after Dmitri. They'd been struggling with him in the passage, trying to keep him out, following instructions Fyodor Pavlovitch had given them some days before. Taking advantage of the moment Dmitri paused to look around the room after entering, Grigory ran around the table, shut the double doors on the far side leading to the inner rooms, and planted himself in front of them, arms spread wide, ready to defend the entrance, as it were, with the last drop of his blood. Seeing this, Dmitri let out something more like a scream than a shout and lunged at Grigory.
"So she's there! She's hiding in there! Out of my way, you scoundrel!"

He tried to drag Grigory aside, but the old servant shoved him back. Beside himself with fury, Dmitri struck out and hit Grigory with all his strength. The old man dropped like a log, and Dmitri, leaping right over him, broke through the door. Smerdyakov stood pale and trembling at the far end of the room, pressed close against Fyodor Pavlovitch.
"She's here!" Dmitri shouted. "I saw her turn toward the house just now, but I couldn't catch her. Where is she? Where is she?"
That single cry, "She's here!" had an indescribable effect on Fyodor Pavlovitch. Every trace of his terror vanished.

"Hold him! Hold him!" he cried, and dashed after Dmitri. Meanwhile Grigory had gotten up off the floor, but still seemed dazed. Ivan and Alyosha ran after their father. In the third room, something fell to the floor with a ringing crash -- a large glass vase, not an expensive one, on a marble pedestal, which Dmitri had knocked over as he ran past.
"After him!" shouted the old man. "Help!"
Ivan and Alyosha caught the old man and forcibly hauled him back.
"Why are you running after him? He'll murder you outright," Ivan cried furiously at his father.
"Ivan! Alyosha! She has to be here. Grushenka's here. He said he saw her himself, running."
He was choking. He hadn't been expecting Grushenka at all, and the sudden news that she was here had made him beside himself. He was shaking all over. He seemed frantic.
"But you've seen for yourself that she hasn't come," cried Ivan.
"But she might have come in by that other entrance."
"You know that entrance is locked, and you have the key."

Dmitri suddenly reappeared in the drawing room. He had, of course, found the other entrance locked, and the key was indeed in Fyodor Pavlovitch's pocket. The windows of every room were shut too, so Grushenka couldn't have come in anywhere, and couldn't have run out anywhere either.

"Hold him!" shrieked Fyodor Pavlovitch, the moment he saw him again. "He's been stealing money out of my bedroom." And, tearing himself free of Ivan, he rushed at Dmitri again. But Dmitri threw up both hands and suddenly seized the old man by the two tufts of hair left on his temples, yanked at them, and flung him crashing to the floor. He kicked him two or three times in the face with his heel. The old man let out a shrill moan. Ivan, though not as strong as Dmitri, threw his arms around him and pulled him away with all his might. Alyosha helped too, with his slender strength, holding Dmitri back from the front.
"Madman! You've killed him!" cried Ivan.
"Serves him right!" shouted Dmitri, breathless. "If I haven't killed him, I'll come back and finish the job. You can't protect him forever!"
"Dmitri! Leave, right now!" Alyosha cried, commanding.
"Alexey! Tell me. You're the only one I can believe; was she here just now, or not? I saw her myself, creeping this way along the fence from the lane. I shouted, and she ran."
"I swear she hasn't been here, and no one was expecting her."

"But I saw her.... So she must... I'll find out right now where she is.... Goodbye, Alexey! Not a word to Aesop about the money now. But go to Katerina Ivanovna at once, and be sure to tell her: 'He sends his compliments to you!' His compliments, his compliments! Just compliments, and farewell! Describe the whole scene to her."

Meanwhile Ivan and Grigory had lifted the old man and settled him into an armchair. His face was covered in blood, but he was conscious, and listened greedily to Dmitri's shouting. He was still convinced that Grushenka really was somewhere in the house. Dmitri looked at him with hatred as he went out.
"I don't regret spilling your blood!" he cried. "Beware, old man, beware of your dream, because I have a dream of my own too. I curse you, and I disown you completely."
He ran out of the room.
"She's here. She must be here. Smerdyakov! Smerdyakov!" the old man wheezed, barely audible, beckoning with his finger.
"No, she's not here, you old lunatic!" Ivan shouted at him angrily. "Look, he's fainting! Water! A towel! Hurry, Smerdyakov!"

Smerdyakov ran for water. They finally got the old man undressed and put him to bed. They wrapped a wet towel around his head. Worn out from the brandy, the violent emotion, and the blows he'd taken, he closed his eyes and fell asleep the moment his head touched the pillow. Ivan and Alyosha went back to the drawing room. Smerdyakov cleared away the pieces of the broken vase, while Grigory stood by the table, staring gloomily at the floor.
"Shouldn't you put a wet bandage on your own head and go to bed too?" Alyosha said to him. "We'll look after him. My brother gave you a terrible blow -- on the head."
"He's insulted me!" Grigory pronounced, gloomy and distinct.
"He's insulted his father, not just you," Ivan observed, with a forced smile.
"I used to wash him in his own tub. And he's insulted me," Grigory repeated.
"Damn it all, if I hadn't pulled him off, he might have killed him. It wouldn't take much to finish off Aesop, would it?" Ivan whispered to Alyosha.
"God forbid!" cried Alyosha.
"Why should he forbid it?" Ivan went on, still in a whisper, with a malicious twist to his mouth. "One reptile will devour the other. And serve them both right, too."
Alyosha shuddered.
"Of course I won't let him be murdered, any more than I did just now. Stay here, Alyosha, I'm going to take a turn in the yard. My head's started aching."

Alyosha went to his father's bedroom and sat beside the bed, behind the screen, for about an hour. The old man suddenly opened his eyes and stared at Alyosha for a long while, clearly remembering, clearly thinking things over. All at once his face showed extraordinary agitation.
"Alyosha," he whispered anxiously, "where's Ivan?"
"In the yard. He's got a headache. He's keeping watch."
"Give me that hand mirror. It's over there. Give it to me."

Alyosha handed him the little round folding mirror that stood on the chest of drawers. The old man looked at himself in it; his nose was considerably swollen, and on the left side of his forehead there was a large crimson bruise.
"What does Ivan say? Alyosha, my dear, my only son, I'm afraid of Ivan. I'm more afraid of Ivan than of the other one. You're the only one I'm not afraid of...."
"Don't be afraid of Ivan either. He's angry, but he'll defend you."
"Alyosha, and what about the other one? He's run off to Grushenka. My angel, tell me the truth -- was she here just now, or not?"
"No one saw her. It was a mistake. She hasn't been here at all."
"You know Mitya wants to marry her -- marry her."
"She won't marry him."
"She won't. She won't. She won't. She won't, no matter what!"

The old man positively fluttered with joy, as though nothing more comforting could have been said to him. In his delight he seized Alyosha's hand and pressed it warmly to his heart. Tears actually glistened in his eyes.

"That image of the Mother of God I was telling you about just now," he said. "Take it home and keep it for yourself. And I'll let you go back to the monastery.... I was only joking this morning, don't be angry with me. My head hurts, Alyosha.... Alyosha, comfort my heart. Be an angel and tell me the truth!"
"You're still asking whether she's been here or not?" Alyosha asked, sorrowfully.

"No, no, no. I believe you. Here's what I want: you go to Grushenka yourself, or find some way to see her; hurry, ask her; find out for yourself which of us she means to choose, him or me. Eh? What? Can you do that?"
"If I see her, I'll ask her," Alyosha muttered, embarrassed.
"No, she won't tell you," the old man broke in. "She's a rogue. She'll start kissing you and say it's you she wants. She's a deceitful, shameless hussy. You mustn't go near her, you mustn't!"
"No, father, and it wouldn't be suitable anyway, it wouldn't be right at all."
"Where was he sending you just now? He shouted 'Go' as he ran off."
"To Katerina Ivanovna's."
"For money? To ask her for money?"
"No. Not for money."

"He hasn't got a farthing. I'll settle in for the night now, and think things over, and you can go. Maybe you'll run into her.... Only be sure to come to me tomorrow morning. Be sure to. I've got something to tell you tomorrow. Will you come?"
"Yes."
"When you come, pretend you've come of your own accord, just to ask how I am. Don't tell anyone I asked you to. Not a word to Ivan."
"Very well."
"Goodbye, my angel. You stood up for me just now. I'll never forget it. I've got something to tell you tomorrow -- but I have to think it over first."
"And how are you feeling now?"
"I'll get up tomorrow and go out, perfectly well, perfectly well!"

Crossing the yard, Alyosha found Ivan sitting on the bench by the gate. He was sitting there, writing something in pencil in his notebook. Alyosha told Ivan that their father had woken up, was conscious, and had sent him back to sleep at the monastery.
"Alyosha, I'd be very glad to meet you tomorrow morning," said Ivan cordially, standing up. His warmth caught Alyosha completely off guard.
"I'll be at the Hohlakovs' tomorrow," Alyosha answered, "and I may go to Katerina Ivanovna's too, if I don't manage to find her now."
"But you're going to see her now, anyway? For that 'compliments and farewell'?" Ivan said, smiling. Alyosha looked flustered.
"I think I understand his outburst just now, and part of what led up to it, well enough. Dmitri's asked you to go to her and tell her that he -- well, in short -- is taking his leave of her?"
"Brother, how will all this horror end, between father and Dmitri?" Alyosha exclaimed.
"There's no telling for certain. Maybe it'll come to nothing: it might all fizzle out. That woman's a beast. In any case, we have to keep the old man indoors and not let Dmitri into the house."
"Brother, let me ask you one more thing: does any man have the right to look at other men and decide who deserves to live?"
"Why bring worth into it at all? The matter's usually settled in men's hearts on much more ordinary grounds than that. And as for rights -- who doesn't have the right to wish for something?"
"Not for another man's death?"

"What if it were for another man's death? Why lie to ourselves, since everyone lives this way, and perhaps can't help living this way. Are you referring to what I said just now -- that one reptile will devour the other? In that case let me ask you: do you think I'm capable, like Dmitri, of spilling Aesop's blood -- of murdering him, eh?"
"What are you saying, Ivan? A thought like that never crossed my mind. I don't think Dmitri's capable of it either."

"Thanks, if only for that," Ivan smiled. "Rest assured, I'd always defend him. But when it comes to my own wishes, I reserve myself full latitude in this case. Goodbye till tomorrow. Don't condemn me, and don't think of me as a villain," he added, with a smile.
They shook hands warmly, as they'd never done before. Alyosha felt that his brother had taken the first step toward him, and that he'd certainly done it with some particular purpose in mind.

chapters.title: X. Both Together
paragraphs: Alyosha left his father's house feeling even more exhausted and downcast in spirit than when he'd entered it. His mind, too, felt shattered and unhinged, while he sensed he was afraid to piece together the disjointed fragments and form any general picture out of all the agonizing, conflicting experiences of the day. He felt something close to despair, which he'd never known before that day. Towering like a mountain over everything else stood the fatal, unanswerable question: how would things end between his father and his brother Dmitri, with this terrible woman between them? He'd now witnessed it himself, had been there, had seen them face to face. And yet it might only be his brother Dmitri who ended up unhappy, terribly, completely unhappy: trouble was waiting for him. It seemed, too, that other people were caught up in it, far more than Alyosha could have imagined before. There was something downright mysterious in it too. Ivan had taken a step toward him, which was exactly what Alyosha had long been hoping for. And yet now, for some reason, he felt frightened by it. And these women? Strange to say, that morning he'd set out for Katerina Ivanovna's in an agony of embarrassment; now he felt nothing of the kind. On the contrary, he was hurrying there as though expecting to find guidance from her. And yet delivering this message to her was obviously harder now than it had been before. The matter of the three thousand roubles was irrevocably settled, and Dmitri, feeling himself dishonored, his last hope gone, might sink to any depth. He had, besides, told him to describe to Katerina Ivanovna the scene that had just taken place with his father.

It was by now seven o'clock, and growing dark, as Alyosha entered the large, comfortable house on the High Street where Katerina Ivanovna lived. Alyosha knew she lived with two aunts. One of them, a woman of little education, was the aunt of her half sister Agafya Ivanovna, who had looked after her in her father's house when she came home from boarding school. The other aunt was a fashionable Moscow lady, though her circumstances were straitened. It was said that both of them deferred to Katerina Ivanovna in everything, and that she kept them with her only as chaperones. Katerina Ivanovna herself deferred to no one but her benefactress, the general's widow, who'd been confined to Moscow by illness, and to whom she was obliged to write twice a week, a full account of everything she did.

When Alyosha entered the hall and asked the maid who answered the door to announce him, it was clear they already knew he'd arrived. Perhaps he'd been noticed from the window. At any rate, Alyosha heard a commotion, caught the sound of hurrying footsteps and rustling skirts. Two or three women, perhaps, had just run out of the room.

Alyosha found it strange that his arrival should cause such a stir. He was shown into the drawing room at once, though. It was a large room, elegantly and lavishly furnished, nothing like the usual provincial style. There were sofas, couches, settees everywhere, big and small tables. There were paintings on the walls, vases and lamps on the tables, masses of flowers, even an aquarium in the window. It was dusk, and rather dark. Alyosha made out a silk mantle thrown down on the sofa, where people had evidently just been sitting; and on a table in front of the sofa were two half-finished cups of chocolate, some cakes, a glass dish of blue raisins, and another of sweets. Alyosha saw he'd interrupted visitors, and frowned. But at that instant the curtain was drawn back, and Katerina Ivanovna came in with quick, hurrying steps, holding out both hands to Alyosha with a radiant, delighted smile. At the same moment a servant brought in two lit candles and set them on the table.
"Thank God! You've finally come too! I've been praying for you all day, simply praying! Sit down."

Alyosha had been struck by Katerina Ivanovna's beauty three weeks earlier, when Dmitri had first brought him, at her particular request, to be introduced to her. There had been no real conversation between them at that meeting, though. Assuming Alyosha was very shy, Katerina Ivanovna had talked the whole time to Dmitri, to spare him. Alyosha had stayed silent, but he'd seen a great deal, quite clearly. He'd been struck by the imperiousness, the proud ease, the self-assurance of the haughty girl. And he was certain of all that -- Alyosha felt he wasn't exaggerating it in the least. He thought her great glowing black eyes were very fine, especially set against her pale, rather sallow, longish face. But in those eyes, and in the line of her exquisite lips, there was something his brother might well fall passionately in love with, but which, perhaps, couldn't be loved for very long. He'd said almost exactly that to Dmitri afterward, when his brother pressed and insisted that he not hide his impressions of his betrothed.
"You'll be happy with her, but perhaps -- not peacefully happy."
"Quite right, brother. People like that never change. They don't bend to fate. So you think I won't love her forever."
"No -- perhaps you will love her forever. But perhaps you won't always be happy with her."

Alyosha had given his opinion at the time, blushing, and angry with himself for having given in to his brother's pleading and put such "foolish" ideas into words at all. His opinion had struck him as unbelievably foolish the moment he'd said it out loud. He'd felt ashamed, too, at having pronounced such a confident judgment about a woman. It was with all the more astonishment, then, that he now realized, at his very first glance at Katerina Ivanovna as she ran in to greet him, that he might have been utterly mistaken. This time her face glowed with spontaneous, good-natured warmth, with direct, wholehearted sincerity. The "pride and haughtiness" that had struck Alyosha so forcibly before showed itself now only as a frank, generous energy, and a kind of bright, powerful faith in herself. Alyosha understood at the first glance, at the very first word, that all the tragedy of her position with the man she loved so dearly was no secret to her; that she probably already knew everything, absolutely everything. And yet, in spite of that, there was such brightness in her face, such faith in the future. Alyosha felt at once that he'd badly wronged her in his thoughts. He was won over, captivated, immediately. Beyond all this, he noticed right away, from her very first words, that she was in a state of great excitement -- an excitement that seemed quite exceptional, almost bordering on ecstasy.
"I was so eager to see you, because you're the only one who can tell me the whole truth."
"I've come," Alyosha muttered, flustered, "I -- he sent me."

"Ah, he sent you! I knew he would. Now I know everything -- everything!" cried Katerina Ivanovna, her eyes flashing. "Wait a moment, Alexey Fyodorovitch, I'll tell you why I've been so desperate to see you. You see, I probably know a great deal more than you do yourself, and there's no need for you to tell me anything at all. I'll tell you what I want from you. I want to know your own last impression of him. I want you to tell me directly, plainly, even crudely if you have to -- oh, as crudely as you like -- what you thought of him just now, of his state of mind, after your meeting with him today. That would be better, maybe, than if I had it out with him in person, since he doesn't want to come to me. Do you understand what I'm asking of you? Now, tell me simply, tell me every word of the message he sent with you -- I knew he'd send you."
"He told me to give you his compliments -- and to say he'd never come again -- but to give you his compliments."
"His compliments? Was that the exact word he used?"
"Yes."
"Maybe he made a mistake in the word by accident, maybe he didn't use the right one?"
"No; he specifically told me to repeat that exact word. He begged me two or three times not to forget to say it."
Katerina Ivanovna flushed hotly.

"Help me now, Alexey Fyodorovitch. I really need your help now. I'll tell you what I think, and you just tell me whether it's right or not. Listen! If he'd sent me his compliments in passing, without insisting you repeat the exact words, without stressing them, that would be the end of everything! But if he particularly insisted on those exact words, if he particularly told you not to forget to repeat them to me -- then maybe he was in a state of excitement, beside himself. He'd made his decision and it frightened him. He wasn't walking away from me with a firm, steady step, he was leaping headlong. The emphasis on that phrase might have been nothing but bravado."
"Yes, yes!" Alyosha cried warmly. "I believe that's exactly it."
"And if that's so, he isn't altogether lost. I can still save him. Wait! Did he say anything to you about money -- about three thousand roubles?"

"He did mention it, and it's that, more than anything, that's crushing him. He said he'd lost his honor and that nothing matters now," Alyosha answered warmly, feeling a surge of hope in his heart, and beginning to believe there really might be some way out, some path to salvation for his brother. "But do you know about the money?" he added, and suddenly broke off.

"I've known about it for a long time; I telegraphed Moscow to ask, and learned long ago that the money never arrived. He never sent it, but I said nothing. Last week I found out he was still in need of money. My only aim in all of this was that he should know who to turn to, who his true friend was. No, he won't admit that I'm his truest friend; he won't know me, he only sees me as a woman. I've been tormented all week, trying to think how to keep him from feeling ashamed to face me over spending that three thousand. Let him be ashamed of himself, let him be ashamed that other people know -- but not that I know. He can tell God everything without shame. Why can't he understand how much I'm ready to bear for his sake? Why, why doesn't he know me? How dare he not know me, after everything that's happened? I want to save him forever. Let him forget me as his betrothed. And here he is, afraid he's dishonored in my eyes. Why -- he wasn't afraid to be open with you, Alexey Fyodorovitch. How is it I don't deserve the same?"
She spoke the last words in tears. Tears streamed from her eyes.
"I have to tell you," Alyosha began, his own voice trembling now, "what happened just now, between him and my father."

And he described the whole scene: how Dmitri had sent him to get the money, how he'd broken in, knocked his father down, and afterward had again, urgently and specifically, begged him to deliver his compliments and farewell. "He went to that woman," Alyosha added, softly.

"And do you suppose I can't put up with that woman? Does he think I can't? But he won't marry her," she suddenly laughed, a nervous laugh. "Could a passion like that really last forever, in a Karamazov? It's passion, not love. He won't marry her, because she won't marry him." Katerina Ivanovna laughed strangely again.
"He may marry her," Alyosha said mournfully, looking down.

"He won't marry her, I tell you. That girl's an angel. Do you know that? Do you know that?" Katerina Ivanovna exclaimed, suddenly, with extraordinary warmth. "She's one of the most fantastic of fantastic creatures alive. I know how bewitching she is, but I also know she's kind, firm, and noble. Why are you looking at me like that, Alexey Fyodorovitch? Are you wondering at my words, maybe? You don't believe me? Agrafena Alexandrovna, my angel!" she suddenly cried out, peering into the next room, "come in to us. This is a friend. This is Alyosha. He knows everything about our affairs. Show yourself to him."
"I've just been waiting behind the curtain for you to call me," said a soft, one might even say sugary, feminine voice.

The curtain lifted and Grushenka herself came up to the table, smiling and beaming. A violent revulsion swept over Alyosha. He fixed his eyes on her and couldn't look away. Here she was, then, that awful woman, that "beast," as Ivan had called her half an hour before. And yet you'd have thought the creature standing in front of him the simplest, most ordinary woman alive -- good-natured, kind, handsome certainly, but so like plenty of other good-looking ordinary women! It's true she was very, very good-looking, with that particular Russian beauty so passionately loved by so many men. She was a fairly tall woman, though a little shorter than Katerina Ivanovna, who was exceptionally tall. She had a full figure, with soft, almost noiseless movements, her voice as softened, as oversweetened, as her step. She moved, not like Katerina Ivanovna, with a vigorous, confident stride, but noiselessly. Her feet made absolutely no sound on the floor. She sank softly into a low chair, her sumptuous black silk dress rustling softly, and settled her milk-white neck and broad shoulders delicately into an expensive cashmere shawl. She was twenty-two, and her face looked exactly that age. She was very fair-skinned, with a pale pink flush on her cheeks. Her face could be called somewhat too broad in its modeling, and her lower jaw jutted forward slightly. Her upper lip was thin, but the slightly protruding lower one was at least twice as full, and had a pouting look. But her magnificent, abundant dark brown hair, her sable eyebrows, and her charming gray-blue eyes with their long lashes would have made even the most indifferent passerby, meeting her by chance in a crowd on the street, stop and remember her face long afterward. What struck Alyosha most about that face was its expression of childlike good nature. There was something childlike in her eyes, a look of childish delight. She came up to the table, glowing with delight, as though expecting something, with a childish, impatient, trusting curiosity. The light in her eyes gladdened the soul -- Alyosha felt that at once. There was something else about her, too, that he couldn't quite grasp or put a name to, and which nevertheless, perhaps unconsciously, affected him all the same. It was a certain softness, a voluptuousness to her physical movements, a catlike noiselessness. And yet it was a vigorous, ample body underneath. Beneath the shawl one could make out full, broad shoulders, a high, still girlish bosom. Her figure suggested the lines of the Venus de Milo, though already somewhat exaggerated in proportion. That much could be told already. Connoisseurs of Russian beauty could have predicted, with real confidence, that this fresh, still-youthful beauty would lose its harmony by the time she was thirty, would "spread"; that the face would grow puffy, that wrinkles would appear before long on the forehead and around the eyes; that the complexion would coarsen, might even redden -- in short, that this was the beauty of a moment, the fleeting beauty so often found among Russian women. Alyosha, of course, wasn't thinking any of this; but fascinated as he was, he still felt an unpleasant twinge, a kind of regret, wondering why she drawled her words that way and couldn't speak naturally. She did it, clearly, because she felt there was some charm in the exaggerated, honeyed way she drew out her syllables. It was, of course, nothing but a bad, underbred habit, betraying poor upbringing and a false notion of good manners. And yet this way of talking struck Alyosha as almost unbelievably at odds with the childishly simple, happy expression on her face, the soft, babyish joy in her eyes. Katerina Ivanovna sat her down at once in an armchair facing Alyosha, and kissed her rapturously, again and again, on her smiling lips. She seemed positively in love with her.

"This is the first time we've met, Alexey Fyodorovitch," she said, rapturously. "I wanted to know her, to see her. I wanted to go to her, and no sooner had I said so than she came to me. I knew we'd settle everything together -- everything. My heart told me so -- people begged me not to take this step, but I could tell it would be the way out of the whole difficulty, and I wasn't wrong. Grushenka's explained everything to me, told me everything she intends to do. She flew here like an angel of goodness, and brought us peace and joy."
"You didn't disdain me, sweet, excellent young lady," Grushenka drawled, in her singsong voice, still with that same charming, delighted smile.

"Don't you dare talk to me like that, you sorceress, you witch! Disdain you! Here, I have to kiss that lower lip of yours again. It looks like it's swelling, and now it'll swell even more, more and more. Look how she laughs, Alexey Fyodorovitch! It does the heart good just to look at the angel."
Alyosha flushed, and faint, barely perceptible shivers kept running through him.
"You make far too much of me, dear young lady, and maybe I'm not worthy of your kindness at all."

"Not worthy! She says she's not worthy of it!" Katerina Ivanovna cried again, with the same warmth. "You know, Alexey Fyodorovitch, we're fanciful, we're willful, but the proudest of the proud, deep in our little heart. We're noble, we're generous, Alexey Fyodorovitch, let me tell you that. We've only ever been unfortunate. We were too ready to sacrifice everything for a man who was, perhaps, unworthy of it, or fickle. There was a man once -- one, an officer too -- we loved him, we sacrificed everything for him. That was long ago, five years back, and he's forgotten us, he's married since. Now he's a widower, he's written to say he's coming, and, do you know, we've loved him, only him, this whole time, and we'll love him our whole lives! He'll come, and Grushenka will be happy again. For the last five years she's been wretched. But who can blame her for that, who can hold her past against her? Only that bedridden old merchant, and he's more like a father to her, a friend, a protector. He found her back then, in despair, in agony, abandoned by the man she loved. She was ready to drown herself then, but the old merchant saved her -- saved her!"
"You're being very kind to defend me, dear young lady. You're in a great hurry about everything," Grushenka drawled again.

"Defend you! Is it for me to defend you? Should I even dare to defend you? Grushenka, angel, give me your hand. Look at that charming, soft little hand, Alexey Fyodorovitch! Look at it! It's brought me happiness, it's lifted me up, and I'm going to kiss it, outside and in, here, here, here!"

And three times, in a kind of rapture, she kissed Grushenka's hand -- charming, certainly, though rather plump. Grushenka held it out with a musical, charming little nervous laugh, watching the "sweet young lady," plainly enjoying having her hand kissed.
"Maybe there's a bit too much rapture in all this," thought Alyosha. He blushed. He'd felt a peculiar unease in his heart the whole time.
"You won't make me blush, dear young lady, kissing my hand like that in front of Alexey Fyodorovitch."
"Do you think I meant to make you blush?" said Katerina Ivanovna, a little surprised. "Ah, my dear, how little you understand me!"

"Well, maybe you don't understand me either, dear young lady. Maybe I'm not as good as I seem to you. I've got a bad heart; I'll always have my own way. I charmed poor Dmitri Fyodorovitch that day simply for the fun of it."
"But now you'll save him. You've given me your word. You'll explain everything to him. You'll tell him you've long loved another man, who's now offering you his hand."
"Oh, no! I never gave you my word to do any such thing. It was you who kept talking about all that. I never gave you my word."
"Then I misunderstood you," Katerina Ivanovna said slowly, going a little pale. "You promised --"

"Oh, no, angel lady, I never promised anything," Grushenka interrupted, soft and even, still with that same gay, simple expression. "You see at once, dear young lady, what a willful wretch I am, next to you. If I want to do a thing, I do it. I might have promised you something just now. But now I'm thinking again: maybe I'll go back to Mitya after all. I liked him a great deal once -- liked him for almost a whole hour. Maybe I'll go now and tell him to stay with me from this day on. You see how changeable I am."
"Just now you said -- something quite different," Katerina Ivanovna whispered, faintly.
"Ah, just now! But you know, I'm such a soft-hearted, silly creature. Just think what he's gone through, on my account! What if, when I get home, I feel sorry for him? What then?"
"I never expected --"

"Ah, young lady, how good and generous you are, compared to me! Maybe now you won't care for a silly creature like me, now that you know what I'm really like. Give me your sweet little hand, angel lady," she said tenderly, and took Katerina Ivanovna's hand with something like reverence.

"Here, dear young lady, I'll take your hand and kiss it, the way you kissed mine. You kissed mine three times, but I ought to kiss yours three hundred to be even with you. Well, let that be. And then it'll be as God wills. Maybe I'll end up your slave entirely, wanting to do your bidding like a slave. Let it be as God wills, without any agreements or promises. What a sweet hand -- what a sweet hand you have! You sweet young lady, you unbelievable beauty!"
She slowly raised the hand to her lips, with what really did seem the odd aim of "getting even" with her in kisses.

Katerina Ivanovna didn't pull her hand away. She listened with a timid hope to these last words, though Grushenka's promise to do her bidding like a slave was strangely put. She looked intently into her eyes; she still saw in them the same simple-hearted, trusting expression, the same bright cheerfulness.
"She's perhaps too naive," thought Katerina Ivanovna, with a flicker of hope.

Grushenka, meanwhile, seemed positively enthralled by the "sweet hand." She raised it deliberately to her lips. But she held it there, near her mouth, for two or three minutes, as though reconsidering something.
"Do you know, angel lady," she suddenly drawled, her voice even softer and more sugary than before, "do you know, after all, I don't think I'll kiss your hand?" And she gave a little merry laugh.
"As you please. What's the matter with you?" said Katerina Ivanovna, starting suddenly.
"So that you'll have something to remember -- that you kissed my hand, but I didn't kiss yours."
There was a sudden gleam in her eyes. She looked at Katerina Ivanovna with a terrible intensity.
"Insolent creature!" cried Katerina Ivanovna, as though suddenly grasping something. She flushed all over and leapt up from her seat.
Grushenka got up too, but without any hurry.
"So I'll tell Mitya how you kissed my hand, but I didn't kiss yours at all. And how he'll laugh!"
"Vile slut! Get out!"
"Ah, for shame, young lady! Ah, for shame! That's not becoming of you at all, dear young lady, a word like that."
"Get out! You're a woman for sale!" screamed Katerina Ivanovna. Every feature of her face was twisted, utterly distorted.
"For sale, indeed! You used to visit gentlemen after dark for money once, didn't you -- putting your beauty up for sale. You see, I know all about it."
Katerina Ivanovna shrieked, and would have flown at her, but Alyosha held her back with all his strength.
"Not one step, not a word! Don't speak, don't answer her. She'll go -- she'll go this instant."
At that same moment Katerina Ivanovna's two aunts ran in at her cry, along with a maidservant. Everyone rushed to her side.
"I'll go," said Grushenka, taking her mantle up from the sofa. "Alyosha, darling, see me home!"
"Go away -- go away, hurry!" cried Alyosha, clasping his hands, pleading.
"Dear little Alyosha, see me home! I've got a lovely little story to tell you on the way. I put on this whole scene for your benefit, Alyosha. See me home, dear, you'll be glad of it afterward."
Alyosha turned away, wringing his hands. Grushenka ran out of the house, laughing musically.
Katerina Ivanovna fell into hysterics. She sobbed, shaken with convulsions. Everyone fussed around her.

"I warned you," said the elder of her two aunts. "I tried to stop you doing this. You're too impulsive. How could you do such a thing? You don't know creatures like that, and they say she's worse than any of them. You're much too willful."
"She's a tigress!" Katerina Ivanovna shrieked. "Why did you hold me back, Alexey Fyodorovitch? I'd have beaten her -- beaten her!"
She couldn't control herself in front of Alyosha; perhaps, indeed, she didn't even try to.
"She ought to be whipped in public, on a scaffold!"
Alyosha edged back toward the door.

"But, my God!" cried Katerina Ivanovna, clasping her hands. "He! He! How could he be so dishonorable, so inhuman! Why, he told that creature what happened on that terrible, cursed day! 'You brought your beauty for sale, dear young lady.' She knows it! Your brother's a scoundrel, Alexey Fyodorovitch."
Alyosha wanted to say something, but couldn't find the words. His heart ached.
"Go, Alexey Fyodorovitch! It's shameful, it's dreadful for me! Come tomorrow, I beg you, on my knees, come tomorrow. Don't judge me. Forgive me. I don't know what I'm going to do with myself now!"
Alyosha walked out into the street reeling. He could have wept, just as she had. Suddenly the maid caught up with him.
"The young lady forgot to give you this letter from Madame Hohlakov; it's been here since dinnertime."
Alyosha took the little pink envelope mechanically and, almost without noticing, put it in his pocket.

chapters.title: XI. Another Reputation Ruined
paragraphs: It wasn't much more than three-quarters of a mile from town to the monastery. Alyosha walked quickly along the road, deserted at that hour. It was almost night now, too dark to make anything out clearly thirty paces ahead. There was a crossroads halfway there. A figure appeared under a solitary willow at the crossroads. The moment Alyosha reached it, the figure stepped out and rushed at him, shouting savagely:
"Your money or your life!"
"So it's you, Mitya," Alyosha cried, startled, genuinely shaken despite his surprise.

"Ha ha ha! You didn't expect me? I couldn't decide where to wait for you. By her house? There are three roads from there, and I might have missed you. Finally I thought of waiting here, since you had to pass this way -- there's no other road to the monastery. Come on, tell me the truth. Crush me like a beetle. But what's wrong?"

"Nothing, brother -- it's just the fright you gave me. Oh, Dmitri! Father's blood, just now." (Alyosha started to cry; he'd been on the verge of tears for a while now, and something seemed to snap inside him at last.) "You nearly killed him -- cursed him -- and now -- here you are -- cracking jokes -- 'Your money or your life!'"
"Well, what of it? It's not proper -- is that it? Not suitable, given my situation?"
"No -- I only --"

"Wait. Look at the night. Look how dark it is, what clouds, what a wind's come up. I hid here under the willow, waiting for you. And, as God's my witness, I suddenly thought, why keep on suffering, what's there left to wait for? Here's a willow, a handkerchief, a shirt -- I could twist them into a rope in a minute, and braces besides, and why go on burdening the earth, dishonoring it with my vile presence? And then I heard you coming -- Heavens, it was as though something flew down and struck me right then. So there is a man, after all, whom I love. Here he is, that man, my dear little brother, whom I love more than anyone in the world, the only one I love in the whole world. And I loved you so much, so much, right at that moment, that I thought, 'I'll throw myself on his neck this instant.' Then a stupid idea struck me, to play a joke on you, give you a scare. I shouted like a fool, 'Your money!' Forgive my foolishness -- it was just nonsense, and there's nothing unseemly in my soul.... Damn it all, tell me what happened. What did she say? Strike me, crush me, don't spare me! Was she furious?"
"No, not that.... There was nothing like that, Mitya. There -- I found them both there."
"Both? Who?"
"Grushenka, at Katerina Ivanovna's."
Dmitri was struck dumb.
"Impossible!" he cried. "You're raving! Grushenka, with her?"

Alyosha described everything that had happened from the moment he'd gone in to see Katerina Ivanovna. It took him about ten minutes to tell the whole story. He couldn't exactly be said to have told it smoothly or in order, but he seemed to make it clear enough, leaving out no word or gesture of any importance, and vividly describing, often in a single word, his own feelings as they happened. Dmitri listened in silence, staring at him with a terrible, fixed gaze, but it was clear to Alyosha that he understood it all, had grasped every point. But as the story went on, his face grew not just gloomy but menacing. He scowled, clenched his teeth, and his fixed stare grew even more rigid, more concentrated, more terrible -- when suddenly, with astonishing speed, his wrathful, savage expression changed, his tightly compressed lips parted, and Dmitri Fyodorovitch broke into helpless, spontaneous laughter. He literally shook with it. For a long time he couldn't speak.

"So she wouldn't kiss her hand! So she didn't kiss it -- so she ran off!" he kept exclaiming, with a kind of hysterical delight -- insolent delight, you might even call it, if it hadn't been so completely genuine. "So the other one called her a tigress! And a tigress she is! So she ought to be flogged on a scaffold? Yes, yes, exactly what I think; she ought to have been, long ago. It's like this, brother -- let her be punished, but I have to get better first. I understand her, that queen of insolence. That's her all over! You saw the whole of her in that hand-kissing business, the she-devil! She's magnificent, in her own way! So she ran home? I'll go -- ah -- I'll run to her! Alyosha, don't blame me, I agree that hanging's too good for her."
"But Katerina Ivanovna!" Alyosha exclaimed, sorrowfully.

"I see her too! I see right through her, like never before! It's practically a discovery of the four continents of the world -- or five, rather! What a thing to do! That's just like Katya, wasn't it, not afraid to face down a coarse, ill-mannered officer, risking a deadly insult, out of pure generosity, to save her father! But the pride, the recklessness, the sheer defiance of fate, the unbounded defiance of it! You say that aunt tried to stop her? That aunt, you know, is overbearing in her own right. She's the sister of the general's widow in Moscow, and even more high and mighty than she is. But her husband was caught stealing government money. He lost everything -- his estate, all of it -- and the proud wife had to lower her colors, and hasn't raised them since. So she tried to stop Katya, but Katya wouldn't listen to her! She thinks she can overcome anything, that everything will bend to her will. She thought she could bewitch Grushenka if she wanted to, and she believed it herself -- she's playing a part for her own benefit, and whose fault is that? Do you think she kissed Grushenka's hand first on purpose, with some scheme in mind? No, she really was captivated by Grushenka -- or rather, not by Grushenka, but by her own dream, her own delusion -- because it was her dream, her delusion! Alyosha, darling, how did you get away from those women, from the pair of them? Did you hitch up your cassock and run? Ha ha ha!"

"Brother, you don't seem to have noticed how badly you insulted Katerina Ivanovna, telling Grushenka about that day. And she flung it right back in her face just now -- that she'd gone to gentlemen in secret to sell her beauty! Brother, what could be worse than that insult?"
What troubled Alyosha more than anything was that, incredible as it seemed, his brother appeared actually pleased by Katerina Ivanovna's humiliation.

"Bah!" Dmitri scowled fiercely and struck his forehead with his hand. He was only just realizing it now, though Alyosha had already told him of the insult, and of Katerina Ivanovna's cry: "Your brother's a scoundrel!"

"Yes, maybe I really did tell Grushenka about that 'fatal day,' as Katya calls it. Yes, I did tell her, I remember! It was that time at Mokroe. I was drunk, the gypsies were singing.... But I was sobbing. I was sobbing then, kneeling and praying before Katya's image, and Grushenka understood it. She understood everything, even then. I remember -- she cried herself.... Damn it all! But it was bound to end this way, all the same.... Then she cried, but now it's 'the dagger in the heart'! That's how women are."
He looked down and sank into thought.

"Yes, I'm a scoundrel, a thorough scoundrel!" he said suddenly, gloomily. "It doesn't matter whether I cried or not, I'm still a scoundrel! Tell her I accept the name, if that's any comfort to her. Come, that's enough. Goodbye. There's no point talking about it! It's not amusing. You go your way, and I'll go mine. And I don't want to see you again, except as a last resort. Goodbye, Alexey!"
He pressed Alyosha's hand warmly, and, still looking down, without raising his head, as though tearing himself away, turned quickly back toward town.
Alyosha watched him go, unable to believe he'd leave so abruptly.

"Wait, Alexey, one more confession, to you alone!" Dmitri suddenly cried, turning back. "Look at me. Look at me carefully. You see here, here -- there's terrible disgrace in store for me." (As he said "here," Dmitri struck his chest with his fist, in a strange way, as though the dishonor lay precisely at that spot, on his chest, in a pocket, perhaps, or hung round his neck.) "You know me now, a scoundrel, an open scoundrel, but let me tell you that I've never done anything before, and never will again, that could compare in baseness with the dishonor I'm carrying right now, at this very minute, on my chest, here, here -- which is going to happen, even though I'm perfectly free to stop it. I can stop it, or carry it through -- mark that. Well, let me tell you, I'm going to carry it through. I won't stop it. I told you everything just now, but I didn't tell you this, because even I didn't have the nerve for it. I could still pull back; if I do, I could give back the full half of my lost honor tomorrow. But I won't pull back. I'll carry out my vile plan, and you can bear witness that I told you so beforehand. Darkness and ruin! No need to explain further. You'll find out in due time. The filthy back alley, and the she-devil. Goodbye. Don't pray for me, I'm not worth it. And there's no need, no need at all.... I don't need it! Away!"
And he suddenly pulled away, this time for good. Alyosha went on toward the monastery.
"What? I'll never see him again! What does he mean?" he wondered wildly. "Why, I'll certainly see him tomorrow. I'll go look for him. I'll make a point of it. What did he mean?"

He walked around the monastery and crossed the pine wood to the hermitage. The door was opened to him, though no one was normally admitted at that hour. There was a tremor in his heart as he stepped into Father Zossima's cell.

"Why, why had he sent him out into the world? Why had he sent him forth? Here was peace. Here was holiness. But out there was confusion, darkness in which a man lost his way and went astray at once...."

In the cell he found the novice Porfiry, along with Father Païssy, who came every hour to check on Father Zossima. Alyosha learned, with alarm, that he was growing steadily worse. Even the elder's usual talk with the brothers couldn't take place that day. As a rule, every evening after the service, the monks would gather in Father Zossima's cell, and all would confess their sins of the day aloud, their sinful thoughts and temptations, even any quarrels they'd had. Some confessed on their knees. The elder absolved them, reconciled them, counseled, imposed penance, blessed, and dismissed them. It was against this general "confession" that the opponents of the eldership protested, insisting it was a profanation of the sacrament of confession, close to sacrilege, though this was really something quite different. They'd even reported to the diocesan authorities that such confessions accomplished no real good, but actually led, to a considerable degree, to sin and temptation. Many of the brothers disliked going to the elder, and went only against their own will, since everyone went, and out of fear they'd be accused of pride and rebellious thinking. It was said some of the monks agreed among themselves beforehand: "I'll confess I lost my temper with you this morning, and you back me up on it," just so as to have something to say. Alyosha knew this actually happened sometimes. He also knew that some among the monks deeply resented the fact that letters from relatives were routinely brought to the elder first, to be opened and read by him before they reached the people they were addressed to.

It was assumed, of course, that all this was done freely, in good faith, as an act of voluntary submission and beneficial guidance. But, in truth, there was often no small amount of insincerity in it, a good deal that was false and strained in the practice. And yet the older, more experienced monks held to their view, arguing that "for those who've come within these walls sincerely seeking salvation, this kind of obedience and sacrifice will certainly prove beneficial, of real value; while those who find it irksome, and grumble against it, aren't true monks at all, and made a mistake ever entering the monastery -- their proper place is out in the world. Even inside the temple, no one's safe from sin and the devil. So there's no point dwelling on it too much."

"He's weaker, a drowsiness has come over him," Father Païssy whispered to Alyosha, as he blessed him. "It's hard to rouse him. And he mustn't be roused. He woke for five minutes, sent his blessing to the brothers, and asked for their prayers for him tonight. He means to take the sacrament again in the morning. He remembered you, Alexey. He asked whether you'd gone away, and was told you were in town. 'I blessed him for that work,' he said, 'his place is there, not here, for a while.' Those were his exact words about you. He remembered you with love, with anxiety; do you understand how highly he honors you? But how has he decided that you should spend some time out in the world? He must have foreseen something in your fate! Understand, Alexey, that if you go back into the world, it must be to do the duty laid on you by your elder, and not for frivolous vanity or worldly pleasures."

Father Païssy went out. Alyosha had no doubt now that Father Zossima was dying, though he might live another day or two yet. Alyosha resolved firmly and fervently that, in spite of all his promises to his father, the Hohlakovs, and Katerina Ivanovna, he wouldn't leave the monastery the next day, but would stay with his elder to the end. His heart glowed with love, and he reproached himself bitterly for having been able, even for one instant, to forget the man he'd left in the monastery on his deathbed, the man he honored above anyone else in the world. He went into Father Zossima's bedroom, knelt down, and bowed to the ground before the elder, who slept quietly, without stirring, his breathing regular, barely audible, his face peaceful.

Alyosha went back to the other room, where Father Zossima had received his guests that morning. Taking off his boots, he lay down on the hard, narrow leather sofa he'd long used as a bed, bringing nothing but a pillow. He'd long since forgotten about the mattress his father had shouted about that morning. He took off his cassock and used it as a blanket. But before going to sleep, he knelt and prayed for a long time. In his fervent prayer he didn't ask God to lighten his darkness, but only thirsted for that joyful emotion which always came over his soul after praise and adoration, the way his evening prayers usually ended. That joy always brought him a light, untroubled sleep. As he was praying, he suddenly felt, in his pocket, the little pink note the servant had handed him as he left Katerina Ivanovna's. He was disturbed by it, but finished his prayer first. Then, after some hesitation, he opened the envelope. Inside was a letter addressed to him, signed by Lise, the young daughter of Madame Hohlakov, who had laughed at him in front of the elder that very morning.

"Alexey Fyodorovitch," she wrote, "I'm writing to you without anyone knowing, even mamma, and I know how wrong that is. But I can't go on living without telling you what's sprung up in my heart, and for now no one but the two of us must know it. But how am I supposed to say what I want so badly to tell you? Paper, they say, doesn't blush, but I promise you that's not true, and that it's blushing right now, just like I am, all over. Dear Alyosha, I love you, I've loved you since I was a child, since our Moscow days, when you were very different from how you are now, and I'll love you my whole life. My heart has chosen you, to join our lives together and carry them on to old age. Of course, on the condition that you leave the monastery. As for our age, we'll wait for whatever the law requires. By then I'll certainly be quite strong, I'll be walking and dancing. There's no doubt about that."

"You see how I've thought of everything. There's only one thing I can't picture: what you'll think of me when you read this. I'm always laughing and being naughty. I made you angry this morning, but I promise you, before I even picked up my pen, I prayed before the Image of the Mother of God, and I'm praying now, and I'm almost crying."

"My secret's in your hands now. When you come tomorrow, I don't know how I'll be able to look at you. Ah, Alexey Fyodorovitch, what if I can't hold myself back, like a silly thing, and laugh when I look at you, the way I did today? You'll think I'm a nasty girl making fun of you, and you won't believe my letter at all. And so I beg you, dear one, if you have any pity for me at all, when you come tomorrow, don't look me straight in the face, because if I meet your eyes, it's sure to make me laugh, especially since you'll be wearing that long robe. I go cold all over just thinking about it, so when you come, don't look at me at all for a while, look at mamma, or out the window...."

"So there, I've written you a love letter. Oh dear, what have I done? Alyosha, don't despise me, and if I've done something truly awful and hurt you, forgive me. Now the secret of my reputation, ruined forever perhaps, is in your hands."
"I'm certainly going to cry today. Goodbye until we meet, our awful meeting. -- LISE.
"P.S. -- Alyosha! You must, must, must come! -- LISE."

Alyosha read the note in amazement, read it through twice, thought for a moment, and suddenly let out a soft, sweet laugh. He caught himself. That laugh struck him as sinful, somehow. But a minute later he laughed again, just as softly, just as happily. He slowly folded the note back into its envelope, crossed himself, and lay down. The turmoil in his heart passed at once. "God, have mercy on all of them, keep all these unhappy, restless souls in your care, and set them on the right path. All roads are yours. Save them according to your wisdom. You are love. You will send joy to all!" Alyosha murmured, crossing himself, and drifted into peaceful sleep.
PART II

chapters.title: I. Father Ferapont
paragraphs: Alyosha was woken early, before daybreak. Father Zossima had woken up feeling very weak, though he wanted to get out of bed and sit up in a chair. His mind was completely clear; his face looked tired but bright, almost joyful. It wore an expression of good humor, kindness, and warmth. "I may not live through the coming day," he told Alyosha. Then he asked to confess and take communion right away. He always confessed to Father Païssy. After taking communion, he received the rite of extreme unction. The monks gathered, and the cell gradually filled with people from the hermitage. By now it was daylight. People began arriving from the monastery. When the service ended, the elder wanted to kiss and say goodbye to everyone. Since the cell was so small, the earlier visitors stepped out to make room for others. Alyosha stood beside the elder, who had been settled back into his armchair. He talked as much as he could. His voice was weak but fairly steady.

"I've been teaching you for so many years, and talking out loud for so many years, that I've fallen into the habit of talking—so much so that it's harder for me to hold my tongue than to speak, even now, weak as I am, dear fathers and brothers," he joked, looking with emotion at the group around him.

Alyosha remembered parts of what he said afterward. Though he spoke clearly and his voice held fairly steady, his speech wandered. He touched on many things—he seemed anxious, before the moment of death, to say everything he hadn't managed to say in his life, and not simply to instruct them, but as if he were thirsting to share his joy and ecstasy with everyone and everything alive, and to open his whole heart once more before he died.

"Love one another, fathers," Father Zossima said, as far as Alyosha could recall afterward. "Love God's people. We are not holier than those outside these walls simply because we've come here and shut ourselves in—on the contrary, the very act of coming here means each of us has admitted to himself that he is worse than others, worse than everyone on earth.... And the longer a monk lives in seclusion, the more sharply he has to recognize that. Otherwise he'd have had no reason to come here at all. Only when he understands that he is not merely worse than others, but that he is answerable to everyone for everyone and for everything—for all human sins, of nations and of individuals alike—only then is the purpose of our seclusion fulfilled. Know this, dear ones: every one of us is unquestionably responsible for all people and everything on earth, not just through the general sinfulness of creation, but personally, each of us, for all mankind and every individual person. This knowledge is the crown of life for a monk, and for every human being. Monks aren't a special breed of people—they're simply what every person ought to be. Only through that knowledge does the heart soften into infinite, universal, inexhaustible love. Then every one of you will have the power to win over the whole world with love, and to wash away the world's sins with your tears.... Each of you, watch over your own heart, and confess your sins to yourself without ceasing. Don't be afraid of your sins, even once you recognize them, as long as there is repentance—but don't bargain with God. I say again: don't be proud. Be proud neither toward the small nor toward the great. Don't hate those who reject you, who insult you, who abuse and slander you. Don't hate the atheists, the teachers of evil, the materialists—and I don't just mean the good ones among them, though there are many good ones, especially nowadays—don't hate even the wicked ones. Remember them in your prayers, saying: Save, O Lord, all those who have no one to pray for them, and save too those who will not pray. And add: it is not out of pride that I offer this prayer, O Lord, for I am lower than everyone.... Love God's people, and don't let strangers lead the flock astray, for if you doze off in laziness and contemptuous pride, or worse, in greed, they will come from every direction and lead your flock away. Explain the Gospel to the people without ceasing... don't be greedy for money.... Don't love gold and silver, don't hoard it.... Have faith. Hold to the banner and raise it high."

But the elder's speech was more disjointed than Alyosha's later account of it. Sometimes he broke off entirely, as if to catch his breath and gather his strength, but he was in a kind of ecstasy. They listened with emotion, though many were puzzled by his words and found them obscure.... Afterward everyone remembered those words.

When Alyosha stepped out of the cell for a moment, he was struck by the general excitement and tension among the monks crowding around it. In some it showed as anxiety, in others as solemn devotion. Everyone was expecting some kind of marvel to happen the instant the elder died. The suspense was, in a way, almost frivolous, but even the sternest of the monks were caught up in it. Father Païssy's face looked the gravest of all.

Alyosha was quietly called away by a monk to see Rakitin, who had come from town with a strange letter for him from Madame Hohlakov. In it she told Alyosha about a strange and remarkably well-timed incident. Among the women who had come the previous day to receive Father Zossima's blessing, there had been an old woman from town, a sergeant's widow named Prokhorovna. She had asked whether she might pray for the soul of her son Vasenka, who had gone off to Irkutsk and hadn't written in over a year. Father Zossima had answered her sternly, forbidding it, saying that praying for the living as if they were dead was a kind of sorcery. Afterward he had forgiven her for her ignorance and added, "as if reading from the book of the future" (this was Madame Hohlakov's phrase), words of comfort: that her son Vasya was certainly alive, and would either come himself very soon or send a letter, and that she should go home and wait for him. "And would you believe it?" Madame Hohlakov exclaimed enthusiastically, "the prophecy has come true, literally—and more than that." The old woman had barely gotten home when they handed her a letter from Siberia that had been waiting for her. But that wasn't all: in the letter, written on the road from Yekaterinburg, Vasya told his mother he was returning to Russia with an official, and that three weeks after she received the letter he hoped "to embrace his mother."

Madame Hohlakov earnestly begged Alyosha to report this new "miracle of prophecy" to the Superior and the whole brotherhood. "Everyone, everyone ought to know of it!" she finished. The letter had been dashed off in a hurry, the writer's excitement showing in every line. But Alyosha didn't need to tell the monks—they already knew. Rakitin had instructed the monk carrying his message "to inform his reverence Father Païssy, most respectfully, that he, Rakitin, has a matter to discuss with him so pressing that he dares not put it off for even a moment, and humbly begs forgiveness for his presumption." Since the monk had delivered the message to Father Païssy before delivering it to Alyosha, Alyosha found, once he'd read the letter, that there was nothing left for him to do but hand it to Father Païssy to confirm the story.
And even that stern, cautious man, though he frowned as he read the news of the "miracle," couldn't entirely suppress some inner emotion. His eyes gleamed, and a grave, solemn smile touched his lips.
"We shall see greater things yet!" broke from him.
"We shall see greater things, greater things yet!" the monks around him repeated.

But Father Païssy, frowning again, asked everyone, at least for now, not to speak of the matter "until it is more fully confirmed, since there is so much credulity in this world, and indeed this might well have happened naturally," he added cautiously, as if to satisfy his own conscience, though he clearly didn't quite believe his own disclaimer—and his listeners could see it just as clearly.

Within the hour the "miracle" was, of course, known throughout the monastery, and to many of the visitors who had come for the mass. No one seemed more struck by it than the monk who had arrived the day before from St. Sylvester's, the small monastery of Obdorsk in the far north. He was the one who had been standing near Madame Hohlakov the day before and had earnestly asked Father Zossima, about the "healing" of the lady's daughter, "How can you presume to do such things?"

Now he was rather at a loss, unsure whom to believe. The evening before, he had visited Father Ferapont in his cell off by himself, behind the apiary, and had come away deeply impressed and awed by the visit. This Father Ferapont was the aged monk, mentioned earlier, so rigorous in fasting and keeping silence, who was hostile to Father Zossima and to the whole institution of "elders," which he regarded as a harmful and frivolous innovation. He was a formidable opponent, even though his habit of silence meant he barely spoke a word to anyone. What made him formidable was that a number of monks fully shared his feelings, and many visitors regarded him as a great saint and ascetic, even though they had no doubt he was mad. But it was precisely his madness that drew them to him.

Father Ferapont never visited the elder. Though he lived in the hermitage, no one pressed him to keep its rules, largely because he behaved as though he were mad. He was seventy-five or older, and lived in a corner beyond the apiary, in an old, decaying wooden cell that had been built long ago for another great ascetic, Father Iona, who had lived to a hundred and five, and about whose saintly doings many odd stories still circulated in the monastery and the surrounding area.

Father Ferapont had managed to get himself installed in this same isolated cell seven years earlier. It was really just a peasant's hut, though it looked like a chapel, since it held an extraordinary number of icons, with lamps burning before them perpetually—icons that people had brought to the monastery as offerings to God. Father Ferapont had been assigned to look after them and keep the lamps lit. It was said—and it was true—that he ate only two pounds of bread every three days. The beekeeper, who lived close to the apiary, brought him bread every three days, and even to this man who waited on him, Father Ferapont rarely said a word. The four pounds of bread, along with the sacramental bread the Father Superior regularly sent him after the late mass on Sundays, made up his weekly rations. The water in his jug was changed daily. He rarely appeared at mass. Visitors who came to pay him homage sometimes found him kneeling all day in prayer without so much as glancing around. If he spoke to them at all, it was brief, abrupt, strange, and almost always rude. On very rare occasions he would talk with visitors, but usually he would just utter some strange saying that was a complete riddle, and no amount of pleading could get him to explain it. He was not a priest, only a simple monk. There was a strange belief, mostly among the more ignorant, that Father Ferapont communed with heavenly spirits and would only speak with them, which was why he stayed silent with men.

The monk from Obdorsk, directed to the apiary by the beekeeper—himself a very silent and surly monk—went to the corner where Father Ferapont's cell stood. "He might talk to you, being a stranger, or you might get nothing out of him at all," the beekeeper had warned him. The monk, as he related afterward, approached in a state of considerable apprehension. It was fairly late in the evening. Father Ferapont was sitting on a low bench at the door of his cell. A huge old elm rustled softly overhead. There was an evening chill in the air. The monk from Obdorsk bowed low before the saint and asked for his blessing.
"You want me to bow to you, monk?" said Father Ferapont. "Get up!"
The monk got up.
"Blessing—be blessed! Sit beside me. Where have you come from?"

What struck the poor monk most was that, despite his strict fasting and great age, Father Ferapont still looked a vigorous old man. He was tall, stood erect, and had a thin but fresh, healthy face.
