"Don't trouble yourself. We'll tell you what to do," said Nikolay Parfenovitch, his voice downright peremptory, or so it seemed to Mitya.

Meanwhile a low-voiced consultation was going on between the two lawyers. It turned out there was a huge bloodstain on the coat, especially on the left side at the back — dried, and still stiff. There were bloodstains on the trousers too. Nikolay Parfenovitch, moreover, in front of the peasant witnesses, ran his fingers along the collar, the cuffs, and every seam of the coat and trousers, obviously searching for something — money, of course. He didn't even bother hiding from Mitya his suspicion that he was capable of sewing money into his clothes.

"He's treating me like a thief, not an officer," Mitya muttered to himself. The two of them shared their thoughts with astonishing candor. The secretary, for instance, also behind the curtain, fussing about and listening in, drew Nikolay Parfenovitch's attention to the cap, which they were also examining.

"You remember Gridyenko, the copying clerk," the secretary observed. "Last summer he collected the wages for the whole office, and claimed he'd lost the money while drunk. And where was it found? Why, in the piping of his cap, of all places. The hundred-rouble notes were rolled up small and sewn into the seam."
Both lawyers remembered the Gridyenko case perfectly well, and so set Mitya's cap aside, deciding that all his clothing needed a more thorough examination later.
"Excuse me," cried Nikolay Parfenovitch suddenly, noticing that the right cuff of Mitya's shirt was turned in and covered in blood, "excuse me, what's that, blood?"
"Yes," Mitya bit out.
"That is — whose blood? ... And why is the cuff turned in?"
Mitya told him how he'd gotten the sleeve stained with blood while tending to Grigory, and had turned it inward while washing his hands at Perhotin's.
"You'll need to remove your shirt too. It's important as material evidence."
Mitya flushed and flew into a rage.
"What, am I supposed to sit here naked?" he shouted.
"Don't trouble yourself. We'll arrange something. And in the meantime, take off your socks."
"You're not joking? Is that really necessary?" Mitya's eyes flashed.
"We're in no mood for joking," Nikolay Parfenovitch answered, sternly.

"Well, if I must—" Mitya muttered, and, sitting on the bed, took off his socks. He felt unbearably self-conscious. Everyone else was dressed, while he was bare, and strangely enough, being undressed made him feel somehow guilty in front of them, almost ready to believe himself genuinely inferior to them, that they now had every right to look down on him.

"When everyone's undressed, somehow it's not shameful, but when you're the only one, and everyone's looking, it's degrading," he kept repeating to himself, over and over. "It's like a dream — I've sometimes dreamed of being in a humiliating position like this." Taking off his socks was misery. They were filthy, and so was his underwear, and now everyone could see it. And worse still, he hated his own feet. All his life he'd thought his big toes hideous. He particularly loathed the coarse, flat, crooked nail on the right one, and now they'd all see it. The unbearable shame of it made him, at once and deliberately, rougher. He pulled off his shirt himself.
"Would you care to look anywhere else, if you're not too ashamed?"
"No, there's no need for that, at present."
"Well, am I supposed to just stand here naked, then?" he added, savagely.
"Yes, that can't be helped for now.... Kindly sit here for a while. You can wrap yourself in a quilt from the bed, and I ... I'll see to all this."

All the items were shown to the witnesses. A report of the search was drawn up, and at last Nikolay Parfenovitch went out, the clothes carried out behind him. Ippolit Kirillovitch went out too. Mitya was left alone with the peasants, who stood in silence, never taking their eyes off him. Mitya wrapped himself in the quilt. He felt cold. His bare feet stuck out, and he couldn't pull the quilt far enough to cover them. Nikolay Parfenovitch seemed to be gone a long time, "an unbearably long time." "He thinks of me as a puppy," thought Mitya, grinding his teeth. "That rotten prosecutor's gone too, no doubt full of contempt, disgusted at the sight of me naked!"

Mitya assumed, though, that his clothes would be examined and returned to him. So imagine his outrage when Nikolay Parfenovitch came back carrying entirely different clothes, brought in behind him by a peasant.

"Here's something for you to wear," he remarked, breezily, looking rather pleased with how his errand had gone. "Mr. Kalganov has kindly provided these for this unusual situation, along with a clean shirt. Fortunately he had them all in his trunk. You may keep your own socks and underclothes."
Mitya flew into a rage.
"I won't wear other people's clothes!" he shouted, menacingly. "Give me my own!"
"That's not possible!"
"Give me my own. Damn Kalganov and his clothes too!"

It took a long while before they could talk him round. But somehow they managed to calm him down. They impressed on him that his clothes, being stained with blood, had to be "included among the other material evidence," and that they "didn't even have the right to let him keep them now ... given the possible outcome of the case." Mitya finally understood this. He sank into gloomy silence and hurriedly got dressed. As he put them on, he only remarked that the clothes were much better than his old ones, and that he disliked "coming out ahead" from the exchange. The coat, besides, was "ridiculously tight. Am I meant to be dressed up like a fool ... for your amusement?"

They assured him again that he was exaggerating, that Kalganov was only slightly taller, so it would only be the trousers that might run a little long. But the coat did, in fact, turn out to be tight across the shoulders.
"Damn it all! I can barely button it," Mitya grumbled. "Be so good as to tell Mr. Kalganov, from me, that I didn't ask for his clothes, and it's not my doing that they've dressed me up like a clown."
"He understands that, and he's sorry ... I mean, not sorry to lend you the clothes, but sorry about this whole business," Nikolay Parfenovitch mumbled.
"To hell with his sorry! Well, where now? Am I to keep sitting here?"

He was asked to go back into the "other room." Mitya went in, scowling with anger, trying to avoid anyone's eyes. Dressed in someone else's clothes, he felt disgraced, even in front of the peasants, and of Trifon Borissovitch, whose face appeared for some reason in the doorway, then vanished at once. "He's come to look at me all dressed up," thought Mitya. He sat back down in the same chair as before. He had an absurd, nightmarish feeling, as though he'd lost his mind.

"Well, what now? Are you going to flog me? That's all that's left," he said, clenching his teeth, addressing the prosecutor. He wouldn't turn to Nikolay Parfenovitch, as though he scorned to speak to him.
"He examined my socks a little too closely, and turned them inside out on purpose, so everyone could see how filthy they were — the scoundrel!"
"Well, now we must move on to the questioning of witnesses," Nikolay Parfenovitch observed, as though replying to Mitya's outburst.
"Yes," said the prosecutor, thoughtfully, as though turning something over in his mind.

"We've done everything we could in your interest, Dmitri Fyodorovitch," Nikolay Parfenovitch went on, "but given your uncompromising refusal to explain to us the source of the money found on you, we find ourselves, at this moment—"
"What's that stone in your ring?" Mitya cut in suddenly, as though waking from a daydream. He pointed to one of the three large rings on Nikolay Parfenovitch's right hand.
"Ring?" Nikolay Parfenovitch repeated, surprised.
"Yes, that one ... on your middle finger, with the little veins running through it — what stone is that?" Mitya persisted, like a fretful child.
"That's a smoky topaz," said Nikolay Parfenovitch, smiling. "Would you like to see it? I'll take it off ..."

"No, don't take it off," Mitya cried furiously, suddenly snapping back to himself, angry at his own distraction. "Don't take it off ... there's no need.... Damn it!... Gentlemen, you've sullied my heart! Do you really think I'd hide it from you, if I'd actually killed my father — that I'd dodge, lie, hide myself away? No, that's not Dmitri Karamazov, he couldn't do that, and if I were guilty, I swear to you I wouldn't have waited for you to get here, or for the sunrise as I first planned — I'd have killed myself before now, without waiting for dawn! I know that about myself now. I've learned more about myself in this cursed night than in twenty years!... And would I be like this tonight, at this very moment, sitting here with you — could I talk like this, move like this, look at you, look at the world, like this, if I'd really been my father's murderer, when the mere thought of having accidentally killed Grigory gave me no peace all night — not out of fear, oh, not simply fear of your punishment! The disgrace of it! And you expect me to be open with mockers like you, who see nothing, believe in nothing, blind moles and scoffers, and confess to you some other filthy thing I've done, some other disgrace, even if it would save me from your accusation? No — better Siberia! Whoever opened that door to my father, whoever walked through it — he killed him, he robbed him. Who was it? I'm racking my brains and I can't think who. But I can tell you it wasn't Dmitri Karamazov, and that's all I can tell you, and that's enough, enough — leave me alone.... Send me into exile, punish me, but stop tormenting me. I'll say no more. Call your witnesses!"

Mitya delivered this sudden monologue as though he'd resolved to fall completely silent from here on out. The prosecutor watched him the whole time, and only once he'd stopped speaking did he remark, as though it were the most ordinary thing in the world, in the coldest, most composed tone:

"Oh, speaking of that open door you mentioned just now, we might as well tell you, in passing, about a very interesting piece of testimony, of great importance to both of us, given by Grigory, the old man you wounded. On regaining consciousness, he stated clearly and emphatically, in answer to our questions, that when, having come out onto the steps and heard a noise in the garden, he decided to go in through the little gate that stood open — before he noticed you running, as you've already told us, in the dark from the open window where you saw your father — he, Grigory, glanced to the left, and, while noticing the open window, also noticed, much closer to him, the door standing wide open — that same door you've claimed was shut the entire time you were in the garden. I won't hide from you that Grigory himself states, confidently, and testifies, that you must have run from that door, though, of course, he didn't see you do it with his own eyes, since he first spotted you some distance off in the garden, running toward the fence."
Mitya had leapt from his chair halfway through this speech.
"Nonsense!" he yelled, in a sudden frenzy. "It's a bald-faced lie. He couldn't have seen the door open, because it was shut. He's lying!"
"I consider it my duty to repeat that he's firm in his statement. He doesn't waver. He sticks to it. We've cross-examined him several times."
"Precisely. I have cross-examined him several times myself," Nikolay Parfenovitch confirmed, warmly.

"It's false, false! Either it's an attempt to slander me, or the ravings of a madman," Mitya kept shouting. "He's simply delirious, from loss of blood, from the wound. He must have imagined it, once he came to.... He's delirious."
"Yes, but he noticed the open door not once he'd come to after his injuries, but before that, as soon as he went out into the garden from the lodge."
"But it's false, it's false! It can't be! He's slandering me out of spite.... He couldn't have seen it ... I didn't come from that door," Mitya gasped.
The prosecutor turned to Nikolay Parfenovitch and said, with weight:
"Confront him with it."
"Do you recognize this object?"
Nikolay Parfenovitch laid a large, thick official envelope on the table, its three seals still unbroken. The envelope was empty, slit open at one end. Mitya stared at it, eyes wide.

"It ... it must be that envelope of my father's, the one that held the three thousand roubles ... and if it's inscribed, let me see, 'For my little chick' ... yes — three thousand!" he shouted. "You see, three thousand, do you see?"
"Of course we see. But we didn't find the money inside it. It was empty, lying on the floor by the bed, behind the screen."
For a few seconds Mitya stood as though struck by lightning.

"Gentlemen, it's Smerdyakov!" he shouted suddenly, at the top of his voice. "He's the one who murdered him! He's robbed him! No one else knew where the old man hid the envelope. It's Smerdyakov, it's obvious now!"
"But you knew about the envelope too — that it was under the pillow."

"I never knew that. I've never seen it. This is the first time I've laid eyes on it. I'd only heard of it from Smerdyakov.... He was the only one who knew where the old man kept it hidden, I didn't know ..." Mitya was completely out of breath.
"But you told us yourself that the envelope was under your late father's pillow. You specifically stated it was under the pillow — so you must have known."
"We have it written down," Nikolay Parfenovitch confirmed.

"Nonsense! It's absurd! I had no idea it was under the pillow. And maybe it wasn't under the pillow at all.... It was just a guess, that it might be under the pillow. What does Smerdyakov say? Have you asked him where it was? What does Smerdyakov say — that's the main point.... And I went out of my way to tell lies against myself.... I told you, without thinking, that it was under the pillow, and now you— Oh, you know how a man says the wrong thing without meaning to. No one knew but Smerdyakov, only Smerdyakov, no one else.... He didn't even tell me where it was! But it's his doing, his doing, there's no doubt about it, he murdered him, it's as clear as daylight now," Mitya exclaimed, more and more frantic, repeating himself incoherently, growing more exasperated and worked up by the moment. "You have to understand that, and arrest him at once.... He must have killed him while I was running away and Grigory lay unconscious, that's clear now.... He gave the signal, and father opened the door for him ... because no one but he knew the signal, and without the signal father would never have opened that door...."

"But you're forgetting the circumstance again," the prosecutor observed, still speaking with the same restraint, though with a note of triumph now, "that there was no need to give the signal at all, if the door already stood open while you were there, while you were in the garden...."
"The door, the door," Mitya muttered, and stared speechlessly at the prosecutor. He sank back into his chair, helpless. Everyone fell silent.
"Yes, the door!... It's a nightmare! God is against me!" he exclaimed, staring straight ahead, in complete stupefaction.

"Come now, you see," the prosecutor went on, with dignity, "you can judge for yourself, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. On the one hand, we have the testimony about the open door you ran out through — a fact that overwhelms you, and us. On the other hand, your baffling, persistent, one might say stubborn silence about the source of the money that appeared so suddenly in your hands, when only three hours earlier, by your own account, you were pawning your pistols for the sake of ten roubles! Given all these facts, judge for yourself. What are we to believe, and what can we rely on? And don't accuse us of being 'cold, cynical, mocking men,' incapable of believing in the generous impulses of your heart.... Try to see it from our position ..."
Mitya was agitated beyond description. He turned pale.
"Very well!" he exclaimed, suddenly. "I'll tell you my secret. I'll tell you where I got the money!... I'll expose my own shame, so I don't have to reproach myself, or you, afterward."

"And believe me, Dmitri Fyodorovitch," Nikolay Parfenovitch put in, in a voice of almost touching delight, "that any sincere and complete confession from you at this moment may, later on, weigh enormously in your favor, and may, moreover—"
But the prosecutor gave him a slight nudge under the table, and he caught himself in time. Mitya, it's true, hadn't even heard him.

chapters.title: VII. Mitya’s Great Secret. Received With Hisses
paragraphs: "Gentlemen," he began, still just as agitated, "I want to make a full confession: that money was my own." The lawyers' faces fell. That wasn't at all what they'd expected.
"What do you mean?" Nikolay Parfenovitch faltered, "when at five o'clock that very day, by your own admission—"

"Damn five o'clock that day and my own admission! That has nothing to do with it now! That money was my own, my own — that is, stolen by me ... not mine, I mean, but stolen by me, and it was fifteen hundred roubles, and I had it on me the whole time, the whole time ..."
"But where did you get it?"

"I took it off my neck, gentlemen, off this very neck ... it was here, around my neck, sewn into a rag, and I'd had it round my neck for a long while, a month since I put it there ... to my shame and disgrace!"
"And from whom did you ... appropriate it?"
"You mean 'steal it'? Say it plainly. Yes, I consider that I effectively stole it, but if you prefer, I 'appropriated' it. I consider that I stole it. And last night I stole it once and for all."
"Last night? But you said it's been a month since you ... obtained it?..."

"Yes. But not from my father. Not from my father, don't worry. I didn't steal it from my father, but from her. Let me tell it without interruptions. It's hard enough as it is, you know. You see, a month ago, Katerina Ivanovna, formerly my betrothed, sent for me. Do you know her?"
"Yes, of course."
"I know you know her. She's a noble creature, the noblest of the noble. But she's hated me for a long time now, oh, a long time ... and hated me with good reason, good reason!"
"Katerina Ivanovna!" Nikolay Parfenovitch exclaimed, astonished. The prosecutor stared too.

"Oh, don't take her name in vain! I'm a scoundrel to drag her into this. Yes, I've seen that she's hated me ... for a long time.... From the very start, even that evening at my lodgings ... but enough, enough. You're not even worthy of knowing about that. No need for it at all.... I only need tell you that she sent for me a month ago, gave me three thousand roubles to send to her sister and another relation in Moscow (as though she couldn't have sent it herself!) and I ... it happened to be that fateful moment in my life when I ... well, in fact, when I'd just fallen in love with another woman, with her — she's sitting downstairs right now, Grushenka. I carried her off here to Mokroe then, and burned through half that cursed three thousand here in two days, but I kept the other half on me. Well, I kept that other half, that fifteen hundred, like a locket around my neck, but yesterday I undid it, and spent it. What's left of it, eight hundred roubles, is in your hands right now, Nikolay Parfenovitch. That's the change from the fifteen hundred I had yesterday."
"Excuse me. How's that? Why, when you were here a month ago you spent three thousand, not fifteen hundred — everyone knows that."
"Who knows it? Who counted the money? Did I let anyone count it?"
"Why, you told everyone yourself that you'd spent exactly three thousand."

"That's true, I did. I told the whole town so, and the whole town repeated it. And right here at Mokroe, too, everyone reckoned it was three thousand. And yet I didn't spend three thousand, only fifteen hundred. And the other fifteen hundred I sewed into a little pouch. That's how it was, gentlemen. That's where that money came from yesterday...."
"This is almost miraculous," Nikolay Parfenovitch murmured.
"Allow me to ask," the prosecutor said at last, "have you told absolutely anyone about this before now — that you had fifteen hundred left on you a month ago?"
"I told no one."
"That's strange. You mean, absolutely no one?"
"Absolutely no one. No one at all, nobody."

"What was your reason for this secrecy? What motive did you have for keeping it so hidden? To put it more precisely: you've finally told us your secret, one you yourself called so 'disgraceful,' though in reality — comparatively speaking, of course — this act, the appropriation of three thousand roubles belonging to someone else, and only temporarily, is, in my view at least, an act of great recklessness, but not so disgraceful, given your character.... Even granting it was a highly discreditable act, still, discreditable isn't 'disgraceful.'... Plenty of people have already guessed, over the past month, at Katerina Ivanovna's three thousand that you spent, and I heard the rumor myself, apart from your own confession.... Mihail Makarovitch, for instance, had heard it too, so it was scarcely even a rumor, but the talk of the whole town. There are also indications, unless I'm mistaken, that you confessed this yourself to someone — that the money was Katerina Ivanovna's — and so it strikes me as extremely surprising that until now, up to this very moment, you've made such an extraordinary secret of the fifteen hundred you claim to have set aside, apparently attaching something like sheer dread to that secret.... It's hard to believe it could have cost you such anguish, to confess a secret like that.... You just cried out, a moment ago, that Siberia would be better than confessing it ..."

The prosecutor fell silent. He was irritated. He made no attempt to hide his annoyance, which was close to anger, venting all his pent-up frustration in a disjointed, incoherent rush, without choosing his words.
"It's not the fifteen hundred that's the disgrace, it's that I set it apart from the rest of the three thousand," said Mitya, firmly.

"Why?" the prosecutor smiled, irritably. "What's disgraceful, in your view, about having set aside half the three thousand you'd discreditably — 'disgracefully,' if you prefer — appropriated? Taking the three thousand in the first place matters more than what you did with it afterward. And by the way, why did you do that — why did you set aside that half, to what purpose, for what end did you do it? Can you explain that to us?"

"Oh, gentlemen, the purpose is the whole point!" cried Mitya. "I set it aside because I was vile — that is, because I was calculating, and to be calculating in a situation like that is vile ... and that vileness has been going on a whole month."
"It's incomprehensible."

"I'm amazed at you. But let me make it clearer. Maybe it really is hard to follow. Listen closely to what I say. Suppose I appropriate three thousand entrusted to my honor, spend it on a spree — say I spend it all — and the next morning I go to her and say, 'Katya, I did wrong, I squandered your three thousand.' Well, is that right? No, it's not right — it's dishonest and cowardly, I'm an animal with no more self-control than a beast, that's so, isn't it? But even so, I'm not a thief. Not an out-and-out thief, you'll grant me that! I squandered it, but I didn't steal it. Now here's a second, somewhat better alternative: follow me carefully, or I'll get muddled again — my head's spinning — so, the second alternative: I spend only fifteen hundred of the three thousand here, that is, only half. The next day I go and bring her that other half: 'Katya, take this fifteen hundred from me, I'm a low beast, an untrustworthy scoundrel, because I've squandered half the money, and I'll squander this too, so keep it out of my reach!' Well, what about that? I'd be a beast and a scoundrel, and whatever else you like — but not a thief, not entirely a thief, or I wouldn't have brought back what was left, I'd have kept that too. She'd see at once that, since I'd brought back half, I'd pay back what I'd spent, that I'd never stop trying, that I'd work to earn it and repay it. So in that case I'd be a scoundrel, but not a thief — you can say what you like, but not a thief!"
"I grant there's a certain distinction," said the prosecutor, with a cold smile. "But it's strange that you see such a vital difference there."

"Yes, I do see a vital difference! Any man can be a scoundrel, and maybe every man is a scoundrel, but not everyone can be a thief — it takes an arch-scoundrel for that. Oh, of course, I don't know how to draw these fine distinctions properly ... but a thief is lower than a scoundrel, that's my conviction. Listen — I carry the money on me for a whole month, I may decide to give it back tomorrow, and I'm no longer a scoundrel, but I can't bring myself to do it, you see, even though I resolve to do it every single day, spurring myself on to it every day, and yet for a whole month I can't manage it, you see. Is that right, do you think — is that right?"

"Certainly, that's not right, I can understand that much, and I won't dispute it," the prosecutor answered, reservedly. "And let's drop this discussion of subtleties and distinctions, and, if you'd be so kind, get back to the point. And the point is that you still haven't told us — despite all our asking — why, in the first place, you split the money in two, squandering one half and hiding the other? What exactly did you mean to do with that hidden fifteen hundred? I press this question, Dmitri Fyodorovitch."

"Yes, of course!" cried Mitya, striking himself on the forehead. "Forgive me, I'm wearing you out and not explaining the main point, or you'd understand in a moment, because it's precisely the motive for it that's the disgrace! You see, it all came down to the old man, my late father. He was always pestering Agrafena Alexandrovna, and I was jealous; I thought at the time she was torn between him and me. So I kept thinking, every day, suppose she suddenly made up her mind, suppose she suddenly stopped tormenting me, and said to me one day, 'I love you, not him; take me to the ends of the earth.' And I'd have had only forty kopecks; how could I take her away, what could I do? Why, I'd have been ruined. You see, I didn't know her then, I didn't understand her, I thought she wanted money, and that she wouldn't forgive me my poverty. And so I fiendishly counted out half of that three thousand, and sewed it up, calculating in advance, sewed it up before I'd even gotten drunk, and once I'd sewn it up, went off to get drunk on the rest. Yes, that was low. Do you understand now?"
Both lawyers laughed out loud.
"I'd have called it sensible and even principled on your part, not to have squandered it all," Nikolay Parfenovitch chuckled. "After all, what does it amount to?"

"Why, that I stole it, that's what it amounts to! Oh, God, it horrifies me that you don't understand! Every day I had that fifteen hundred sewn up around my neck, every day, every hour, I said to myself: 'You're a thief! You're a thief!' Yes, that's why I've been so vicious this whole month, that's why I fought in the tavern, that's why I attacked my father — because I felt like a thief. I couldn't bring myself to do anything about it, I didn't even dare tell Alyosha, my own brother, about that fifteen hundred: I felt like such a scoundrel, such a common pickpocket. But, you know, while I carried it, I told myself, at the very same time, every single hour: 'No, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, you may still not be a thief.' Why? Because I might go the next day and pay Katya back that fifteen hundred. And it was only yesterday that I made up my mind to tear the amulet from my neck, on my way from Fenya's to Perhotin's. I hadn't been able to bring myself to it before that moment. And it was only once I'd torn it off that I truly became a thief, outright — a thief and a dishonest man for the rest of my life. Why? Because with that, I also destroyed my dream of going to Katya and saying, 'I'm a scoundrel, but not a thief!' Do you understand now? Do you understand?"
"What made you decide to do it yesterday?" Nikolay Parfenovitch broke in.

"Why? What a strange thing to ask. Because I'd sentenced myself to die at five o'clock this morning, right here, at dawn. I thought it made no difference whether I died a thief or a man of honor. But I see now that it's not so — it turns out it makes all the difference. Believe me, gentlemen, what tormented me most this whole night wasn't the thought that I'd killed the old servant, and was facing Siberia just when my love was finally being rewarded, when Heaven had opened up to me again. Oh, that tormented me too, but not the same way, not nearly as much as the damned awareness that I'd finally torn that cursed money off my chest and spent it, and become an outright thief! Oh, gentlemen, I tell you again, with a bleeding heart, I've learned a great deal this night. I've learned that it's not just impossible to live as a scoundrel — it's impossible to die as one either.... No, gentlemen, a man must die honest...."
Mitya was pale. His face had a haggard, exhausted look, despite his being intensely worked up.

"I'm beginning to understand you, Dmitri Fyodorovitch," the prosecutor said slowly, in a soft, almost sympathetic tone. "But all of this, if you'll forgive me saying so, is a matter of nerves, in my opinion ... your overwrought nerves, that's what it is. And why, for instance, couldn't you have spared yourself nearly a month of this torment, simply by going and returning that fifteen hundred to the lady who'd entrusted it to you? And why couldn't you have explained things to her, and, given your situation, which you describe as so dire, why couldn't you have turned to the plan that would so naturally occur to anyone — that is, after honestly confessing your errors to her, why couldn't you have asked her to lend you the sum you needed, which, with her generous heart, she surely wouldn't have refused you in your distress, especially with some guarantee, or even the same kind of security you offered the merchant Samsonov and Madame Hohlakov? I take it you still regard that security as worth something?"
Mitya suddenly flushed crimson.
"Surely you don't take me for that much of an out-and-out scoundrel? You can't be serious?" he said, indignantly, looking the prosecutor straight in the face, seeming unable to believe his own ears.
"I assure you, I'm quite serious.... Why would you think otherwise?" Now it was the prosecutor's turn to be surprised.

"Oh, how vile that would have been! Gentlemen, do you know, you're torturing me! Let me tell you everything, so be it. I'll confess all my infernal wickedness, if only to put you to shame, and you'll be amazed yourselves at just how low a tangle of human passions can sink. You should know I'd already had that very plan myself, the one you just mentioned, Prosecutor! Yes, gentlemen, I too had that thought in my mind this whole past month, so that I very nearly decided to go to Katya — I was low enough for that. But to go to her, to tell her of my betrayal, and, for the sake of that very betrayal, to carry it through, to beg her — Katya — for money to fund it (to beg, do you hear, to beg), and then walk straight from her to run off with the other woman, her rival, who'd hated and insulted her — just think of it! You must be out of your mind, Prosecutor!"

"I'm not out of my mind, but I did speak hastily, without thinking ... about that feminine jealousy ... if jealousy could enter into it, as you claim ... yes, perhaps there's something to that," said the prosecutor, smiling.

"But that would have been so vile!" Mitya slammed his fist down on the table. "That would have been filthy beyond anything! Yes, do you know, she might have given me that money — yes, she would have given it, too; she'd certainly have given it, to get her revenge on me, she'd have given it to satisfy her vengeance, to show her contempt for me, because hers is an infernal nature too, and she's a woman of great wrath. And I'd have taken the money, oh, I would have taken it; I'd have taken it, and then, for the rest of my life ... oh, God! Forgive me, gentlemen, I'm making such a scene because I had that very thought in my mind so recently — just two days ago, that night I was having all that trouble with Lyagavy, and then yesterday, all day yesterday, I remember, right up until that happened ..."
"Until what happened?" Nikolay Parfenovitch put in, curious, but Mitya didn't hear him.

"I've made you a terrible confession," Mitya said, gloomily, in conclusion. "You ought to appreciate it, and more than that, you ought to respect it, because if you don't, if it leaves your souls untouched, then you simply have no respect for me at all, gentlemen, I tell you that, and I'll die of shame at having confessed it to men like you! Oh, I'll shoot myself! Yes, I see it now, I see you don't believe me. What, you want to write that down too?" he cried, dismayed.

"Yes, what you just said," Nikolay Parfenovitch said, looking at him in surprise, "that up until the last hour you were still considering going to Katerina Ivanovna to beg that sum from her.... I assure you, that's a very significant piece of testimony for us, Dmitri Fyodorovitch — for the whole case, I mean ... and especially significant for you."

"Have mercy, gentlemen!" Mitya threw up his hands. "Don't write that down, at least — have some shame. Here I've torn my own heart open in front of you, and you seize the chance and start poking at the wounds on both halves.... Oh, my God!"
In despair, he buried his face in his hands.

"Don't distress yourself so, Dmitri Fyodorovitch," the prosecutor remarked. "Everything written down will be read back to you afterward, and whatever you don't agree with, we'll change to your satisfaction. But now let me ask you one small question a second time. Has absolutely no one, no one at all, heard from you about that money you sewed up? I have to say, that's almost impossible to believe."
"No one, no one, I told you already, or you haven't understood a word of it! Leave me be!"

"Very well, this matter is bound to come to light, and there's ample time for that, but in the meantime, consider — we have perhaps a dozen witnesses that you yourself spread the story around, even shouted it nearly everywhere, about the three thousand you spent here — three thousand, not fifteen hundred. And even now, when you got hold of the money you had yesterday, you gave plenty of people to understand you'd brought three thousand with you."
"You've got not dozens, but hundreds of witnesses, two hundred witnesses, two hundred have heard it, thousands have heard it!" cried Mitya.
"Well, you see, they all testify to it. And the word all means something."
"It means nothing. I talked rubbish, and everyone started repeating it."
"But what need did you have to 'talk rubbish,' as you put it?"

"The devil knows. Bravado, maybe ... at having wasted so much money.... To try to forget the money I had sewn away, maybe ... yes, that was it ... damn it ... how many more times are you going to ask me that? Well, I told a fib, and that was that — once I'd said it, I couldn't be bothered to correct it. What does a man tell lies for, sometimes?"

"That's a very hard thing to determine, Dmitri Fyodorovitch — what makes a man tell lies," the prosecutor observed, weightily. "Tell me, though — was that 'amulet,' as you call it, around your neck, a large thing?"
"No, not large."
"How large, for instance?"
"If you fold a hundred-rouble note in half, that would be about the size."
"You'd better show us the remains of it. You must have them somewhere."
"Damnation, what nonsense! I have no idea where they are."
"But excuse me — where and when did you take it off your neck? By your own testimony, you never went home."
"On my way from Fenya's to Perhotin's, along the way, I tore it off my neck and took out the money."
"In the dark?"
"What would I need a light for? I did it with my fingers, in a minute."
"Without scissors, in the street?"
"In the marketplace, I believe it was. Why would I need scissors? It was an old rag. It tore in a minute."
"Where did you put it afterward?"
"I dropped it there."
"Where, exactly?"
"In the marketplace, in the marketplace! The devil knows exactly where. What do you need to know for?"
"That's extremely important, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. It would be material evidence in your favor. How is it you don't grasp that? Who helped you sew it up, a month ago?"
"No one helped me. I did it myself."
"Can you sew?"
"A soldier has to know how to sew. No special skill was needed for that."
"Where did you get the material — the rag you sewed the money into?"
"Are you making fun of me?"
"Not at all. And we're in no mood for jokes, Dmitri Fyodorovitch."
"I don't know where I got the rag from — somewhere or other, I suppose."
"I'd have thought you couldn't forget a thing like that."
"Upon my word, I don't remember. I might have torn a piece off some linen of mine."
"That's very interesting. We might find, tomorrow, in your lodgings, the shirt or whatever it was you tore the rag from. What sort of rag was it — cloth, or linen?"
"Heaven only knows what it was. Wait a moment.... I don't believe I tore it off anything. It was a scrap of calico.... I think I sewed it up inside a cap belonging to my landlady."
"Your landlady's cap?"
"Yes. I took it from her."
"How did you come by it?"

"You see, I remember once taking a cap to use as a rag, maybe to wipe my pen on. I took it without asking, because it was a worthless scrap. I tore it up, and took the notes and sewed them into it. I believe it was that very rag I sewed them in. An old bit of calico, washed a thousand times."
"And you're certain of that now?"
"I don't know if I'm certain. I think it was the cap. But hang it, what does it matter?"
"In that case, your landlady will remember the thing going missing?"
"No, she won't, she never noticed it was gone. It was an old rag, I tell you, an old rag not worth a kopeck."
"And where did you get the needle and thread?"
"I'll stop now. I won't say another word. Enough of this!" said Mitya, finally losing his temper.
"It's strange that you'd have so completely forgotten where you threw the pieces, in the marketplace."

"Give orders to have the marketplace swept tomorrow, and maybe you'll find it," said Mitya, sneering. "Enough, gentlemen, enough!" he decided, in an exhausted voice. "I see you don't believe me! Not for one moment! It's my fault, not yours. I shouldn't have been so eager to talk. Why, why did I lower myself, confessing my secret to you? It's all a joke to you. I can see it in your eyes. You led me into it, Prosecutor? Sing your hymn of triumph, if you can.... Damn you, you torturers!"

He bowed his head and buried his face in his hands. The lawyers said nothing. A minute later he raised his head and looked at them, almost blankly. His face now showed complete, hopeless despair, and he sat mute and passive, as if barely aware of what was happening. Meanwhile, they had to finish what they'd set out to do. They now had to begin questioning the witnesses without delay. It was already eight in the morning. The lamps had been put out long ago. Mihail Makarovitch and Kalganov, who'd been going in and out of the room continually the whole time the questioning had gone on, had both stepped out again now. The lawyers looked worn out too. It was a wretched morning; the whole sky lay overcast, and rain poured down in sheets. Mitya stared blankly out the window.
"May I look out the window?" he asked Nikolay Parfenovitch, suddenly.
"Oh, as much as you like," the man replied.

Mitya got up and went to the window.... The rain lashed against its small, greenish panes. He could see the muddy road just below the house, and farther off, through the rain and mist, a row of poor, black, dismal huts, looking even blacker and poorer in the downpour. Mitya thought of "Phoebus the golden-haired," and how he'd planned to shoot himself at the first ray of light. "Maybe it would be even better on a morning like this," he thought, with a smile, and suddenly, flinging his hand down, he turned back to his "torturers."

"Gentlemen," he cried, "I see that I'm lost! But her — tell me about her, I beg you. Surely she doesn't have to be ruined along with me? She's innocent, you know, she was out of her mind when she cried out last night, 'It's all my fault!' She's done nothing, nothing! I've been grieving over her all night, the whole time I've been sitting here with you.... Can't you, won't you, tell me what you intend to do with her now?"

"You can set your mind entirely at ease on that score, Dmitri Fyodorovitch," the prosecutor answered at once, with evident readiness. "So far, we have no grounds for taking any action against the lady you're so concerned about. I trust that will remain true as the case develops further.... On the contrary, we'll do everything in our power in that regard. Set your mind entirely at ease."
"Gentlemen, I thank you. I knew you were honest, straightforward people, in spite of everything. You've taken a weight off my heart.... Well, what do we do now? I'm ready."
"Well, we ought to hurry. We need to move on to questioning the witnesses without delay. That must happen in your presence, and so—"
"Shouldn't we have some tea first?" Nikolay Parfenovitch put in. "I think we've earned it!"

They decided that if tea was ready downstairs (Mihail Makarovitch had no doubt gone down to arrange some), they'd have a glass and then "press on and on," putting off a proper breakfast for a more convenient moment. Tea really was ready below, and was soon brought up. Mitya at first refused the glass Nikolay Parfenovitch politely offered him, but then asked for it himself and drank it down greedily. He looked strikingly worn out. Given his herculean strength, one might have assumed that a single night of carousing, even one wrapped in such violent emotion, could hardly touch him. But he felt he could barely hold his head up, and every so often everything around him seemed to heave and swim before his eyes. "A little more and I'll start raving," he told himself.

chapters.title: VIII. The Evidence Of The Witnesses. The Babe
paragraphs: The questioning of the witnesses began. But we won't keep telling the story in the same detail as before. So we won't dwell on how Nikolay Parfenovitch reminded every witness that he had to testify truthfully and in good conscience, and that he would later have to repeat his testimony under oath, or on how each witness had to sign the transcript of his evidence, and so on. We'll only note that the questioning centered mainly on the matter of the three thousand roubles — that is, whether the sum Mitya spent here at Mokroe the first time, a month earlier, had been three thousand or fifteen hundred. And again, had he spent three thousand or fifteen hundred yesterday? Unfortunately, everyone's testimony turned out to be against Mitya. Not one witness spoke in his favor, and some introduced new, almost devastating facts that contradicted Mitya's own account.

The first witness questioned was Trifon Borissovitch. He wasn't in the least intimidated standing before the lawyers. On the contrary, he had an air of stern, severe indignation toward the accused, which gave him a look of honesty and personal dignity. He spoke little, and cautiously, waited to be asked, and answered precisely and deliberately. Firmly and without hesitation he testified that the sum spent a month before could not have been less than three thousand — that every peasant around here would confirm hearing that figure from Dmitri Fyodorovitch's own mouth. "What a pile of money he threw away on the gypsy girls alone! I'd guess he wasted a thousand on them alone."
"I don't believe I gave them five hundred," was Mitya's gloomy comment on this. "It's a pity I didn't count the money at the time, but I was drunk...."
Mitya sat sideways, his back to the curtains. He listened gloomily, with a weary, melancholy air, as though he wanted to say:
"Say whatever you like. It makes no difference now."

"More than a thousand went on them, Dmitri Fyodorovitch," Trifon Borissovitch retorted firmly. "You scattered it around at random and they snatched it up. A thieving, rascally lot they were, horse-stealers — they've been chased out of here since, or maybe they'd testify themselves how much they got out of you. I saw the sum in your hands myself — I didn't count it, you wouldn't let me, that's true enough — but by the look of it I'd say it was far more than fifteen hundred ... fifteen hundred, indeed! We've handled money too. We know how to judge amounts...."
As for the sum spent yesterday, he insisted that Dmitri Fyodorovitch had told him, the moment he arrived, that he'd brought three thousand with him.
"Come now, is that really so, Trifon Borissovitch?" Mitya replied. "Surely I didn't say so flatly that I'd brought three thousand?"

"You did say so, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. You said it in front of Andrey. Andrey's still here — send for him. And in the hall, when you were treating the chorus, you shouted outright that you'd leave your sixth thousand here — meaning, we're to understand, on top of what you spent before. Stepan and Semyon heard it, and Pyotr Fomitch Kalganov was standing right beside you at the time. Maybe he remembers it too...."

This evidence about the "sixth" thousand made an extraordinary impression on the two lawyers. They were delighted with this new way of reckoning: three and three made six — three thousand back then and three thousand now made six. That was clear enough.

They questioned all the peasants Trifon Borissovitch had named — Stepan, Semyon, the driver Andrey, and Kalganov. The peasants and the driver confirmed Trifon Borissovitch's testimony without hesitation. They noted down, with particular care, Andrey's account of the conversation he'd had with Mitya on the road: "'Where,' he says, 'am I going, Dmitri Fyodorovitch — to heaven or to hell, and will I be forgiven in the next world or not?'"
The psychologically minded Ippolit Kirillovitch heard this with a subtle smile, and ended by recommending that these remarks about where Dmitri Fyodorovitch was headed be "included in the record."

Kalganov, when called, came in reluctantly, scowling and ill-tempered, and spoke to the lawyers as if he'd never met them before in his life, though they were acquaintances he'd been seeing daily for a long time. He began by saying "he knew nothing about it and didn't want to." But it turned out he had heard of the "sixth" thousand, and he admitted he'd been standing close by at the time. As far as he could tell, he "didn't know" how much money Mitya had had in his hands. He confirmed that the Poles had cheated at cards. Under repeated questioning he stated that after the Poles had been turned out, Mitya's standing with Agrafena Alexandrovna had definitely improved, and that she'd said she loved him. He spoke of Agrafena Alexandrovna with reserve and respect, as though she were a lady of the finest society, and never once let himself call her Grushenka. Despite the young man's obvious distaste for giving evidence, Ippolit Kirillovitch questioned him at great length, and it was only from him that he learned the full details of what made up Mitya's "romance," so to speak, that night. Mitya never once interrupted Kalganov. At last they let the young man go, and he left the room with undisguised indignation.

The Poles were questioned too. Though they had gone to bed in their room, they hadn't slept at all that night, and when the police officers arrived they hastily dressed and made themselves ready, realizing they'd certainly be sent for. They gave their evidence with dignity, though not without some unease. The smaller Pole turned out to be a retired official of the twelfth class who had served as a veterinary surgeon in Siberia. His name was Mussyalovitch. Pan Vrublevsky turned out to be an uncertified dentist. Although Nikolay Parfenovitch directed his questions at them, they both addressed their answers to Mihail Makarovitch, who was standing off to one side, mistaking him in their ignorance for the most important person in charge, and calling him "Pan Colonel" at every turn. Only after several corrections from Mihail Makarovitch himself did they grasp that they were to address Nikolay Parfenovitch alone. It turned out they could speak quite correct Russian, apart from their accent on certain words. Of his relations with Grushenka, past and present, Pan Mussyalovitch spoke proudly and warmly, so that Mitya flared up at once and declared he wouldn't allow the "scoundrel" to talk like that in his presence! Pan Mussyalovitch immediately drew attention to the word "scoundrel" and asked that it be entered in the record. Mitya seethed with rage.
"He's a scoundrel! A scoundrel! You can write that down. And write down too that, record or no record, I still say he's a scoundrel!" he cried.

Though Nikolay Parfenovitch did enter this in the record, he showed remarkably good tact and judgment in handling it. After sternly reprimanding Mitya, he cut off all further inquiry into the romantic side of the case and hurried on to what mattered. One piece of evidence given by the Poles caught the lawyers' particular interest: how, in that very room, Mitya had tried to buy off Pan Mussyalovitch, offering him three thousand roubles to give up his claims — seven hundred roubles down, and the remaining two thousand three hundred "to be paid the next day in town." He'd sworn at the time that he didn't have the whole sum with him at Mokroe, but that his money was in town. Mitya protested hotly that he hadn't said he'd definitely pay him the rest the next day in town. But Pan Vrublevsky backed up the claim, and Mitya, after thinking a moment, admitted, frowning, that it must have happened the way the Poles described — that he'd been worked up at the time and might well have said so.

The prosecutor seized on this piece of evidence at once. It seemed to establish for the prosecution (and in fact they built this very conclusion on it) that half, or a part, of the three thousand that had come into Mitya's hands might really have been left hidden somewhere in town — or even, perhaps, somewhere here at Mokroe. This would explain the fact that had so puzzled the prosecution, that only eight hundred roubles had been found on Mitya. That fact, small as it was, had until now been the one piece of evidence that told, to some degree, in Mitya's favor. Now that one piece of evidence in his favor had collapsed. When the prosecutor pressed him on where he'd have gotten the remaining two thousand three hundred roubles, since he himself had denied having more than fifteen hundred, Mitya confidently replied that he'd meant to offer the "little fellow" not money, but a formal deed transferring his rights to the village of Tchermashnya — the same rights he'd already offered Samsonov and Madame Hohlakov. The prosecutor all but smiled at the "innocence of this dodge."
"And you imagine he would have accepted such a deed as a substitute for two thousand three hundred roubles in cash?"

"He certainly would have accepted it," Mitya declared warmly. "Why, look here — he might have squeezed out not two thousand but four or six for it. He'd have set his lawyers on it, Poles and Jews, and could have gotten not three thousand but the whole property out of the old man."

Pan Mussyalovitch's testimony was, of course, entered into the record in the fullest detail. Then they let the Poles go. The matter of the card-cheating was barely touched on. Nikolay Parfenovitch was too pleased with them as it was and didn't want to bother them over trifles — besides, it was nothing but a foolish, drunken quarrel over cards. There had been plenty of drinking and disorder that night.... So the two hundred roubles stayed in the Poles' pockets.

Then old Maximov was summoned. He came in timidly, with small steps, looking disheveled and downcast. All this time he'd been taking shelter downstairs with Grushenka, sitting mutely beside her, and "now and then he'd start blubbering over her and wiping his eyes with a blue checked handkerchief," as Mihail Makarovitch described it afterward. So much so that she herself had started trying to calm and comfort him. The old man confessed right away that he'd done wrong, that he'd borrowed "ten roubles in my poverty" from Dmitri Fyodorovitch, and that he was ready to pay it back. To Nikolay Parfenovitch's direct question — whether he'd noticed how much money Dmitri Fyodorovitch was holding, since he must have been able to see the sum better than anyone when he took the note from him — Maximov declared, quite positively, that there had been twenty thousand.
"Have you ever seen as much as twenty thousand before, then?" Nikolay Parfenovitch asked, with a smile.

"To be sure I have — not twenty, but seven, when my wife mortgaged my little property. She only let me look at it from a distance, boasting of it to me. It was a very thick bundle, all rainbow-colored notes. And Dmitri Fyodorovitch's were all rainbow-colored too...."

He wasn't kept long. At last it was Grushenka's turn. Nikolay Parfenovitch was visibly worried about the effect her appearance might have on Mitya, and he murmured a few words of caution to him, but Mitya bowed his head in silence, letting him understand "that he wouldn't make a scene." Mihail Makarovitch himself led Grushenka in. She came in with a stern, gloomy face that looked almost composed, and sat quietly in the chair Nikolay Parfenovitch offered her. She was very pale, seemed to be cold, and wrapped herself tightly in her magnificent black shawl. She was running a slight fever — the first symptom of the long illness that followed that night. Her grave manner, her direct, earnest gaze and quiet bearing made a very favorable impression on everyone. Nikolay Parfenovitch was even a little "charmed." He admitted afterward, talking about it, that only then had he seen "how handsome the woman was," for though he'd seen her several times before, he'd always thought of her as something of a "provincial hetaira." "She has the manners of the best society," he said enthusiastically, gossiping about her in a circle of ladies. But this was met with real indignation from the ladies, who at once called him a "naughty man," to his great satisfaction.

As she entered the room, Grushenka only glanced at Mitya for an instant; he looked at her uneasily. But her face reassured him at once. After the usual preliminary inquiries and warnings, Nikolay Parfenovitch asked her, hesitating slightly but keeping his most courteous manner, what her relations were with the retired lieutenant Dmitri Fyodorovitch Karamazov. To this Grushenka replied firmly and quietly:

"He was an acquaintance. He came to see me as an acquaintance over the last month." To further probing questions she answered plainly and with complete frankness that, though "at times" she'd found him attractive, she hadn't loved him, but had won his heart, as well as his old father's, "out of my own nasty spite" — that she'd seen Mitya was very jealous of Fyodor Pavlovitch and everyone else, but that had only amused her. She'd never meant to go to Fyodor Pavlovitch — she'd simply been laughing at him. "I had no thoughts for either of them this whole last month. I was waiting for another man, one who'd wronged me. But I don't think," she said in conclusion, "that there's any need for you to ask about that, or for me to answer, because that's my own affair."

Nikolay Parfenovitch immediately took the hint. He again set aside the "romantic" side of the case and moved to the serious one — that is, to the question that mattered most, the three thousand roubles. Grushenka confirmed that three thousand roubles had certainly been spent on the first spree at Mokroe, and, though she hadn't counted the money herself, she'd heard it was three thousand from Dmitri Fyodorovitch's own lips.
"Did he tell you that alone, or in front of someone else, or did you only hear him mention it to others in your presence?" the prosecutor asked at once.
To which Grushenka answered that she'd heard him say so in front of other people, and had heard him say so when they were alone together.
"Did he say it to you alone once, or several times?" the prosecutor asked, and learned that he'd told Grushenka so several times.

Ippolit Kirillovitch was very pleased with this piece of evidence. Further questioning brought out that Grushenka also knew where the money had come from — that Dmitri Fyodorovitch had gotten it from Katerina Ivanovna.
"And did you never, not once, hear that the money spent a month ago wasn't three thousand but less, and that Dmitri Fyodorovitch had kept back half that sum for himself?"
"No, I never heard that," answered Grushenka.
It came out further that Mitya had, on the contrary, often told her he didn't have a farthing.
"He was always expecting to get some from his father," Grushenka said in conclusion.
"Did he ever say in front of you ... offhandedly, or in a fit of temper," Nikolay Parfenovitch put in suddenly, "that he meant to make an attempt on his father's life?"
"Ah, he did say that," Grushenka sighed.
"Once, or several times?"
"He mentioned it several times, always in anger."
"And did you believe he'd do it?"
"No, I never believed it," she answered firmly. "I had faith in his noble heart."
"Gentlemen, allow me," Mitya suddenly cried, "allow me to say one word to Agrafena Alexandrovna, in front of you all."
"You may speak," Nikolay Parfenovitch agreed.
"Agrafena Alexandrovna!" Mitya got up from his chair. "Have faith in God and in me. I am not guilty of my father's murder!"

Having said these words, Mitya sat back down on his chair. Grushenka stood up and crossed herself devoutly before the icon. "Thanks be to Thee, O Lord," she said, her voice thrilled with emotion, and, still standing, she turned to Nikolay Parfenovitch and added:

"Since he's said that now, believe it! I know him. He'll say anything as a joke, or out of stubbornness, but he'll never deceive you against his conscience. He's telling the whole truth — you can believe it."
"Thank you, Agrafena Alexandrovna, you've given me fresh courage," Mitya answered in a trembling voice.

As for the money spent the day before, she said she didn't know what sum it was, but had heard him tell several people that he had three thousand on him. Asked where he'd gotten the money, she said he'd told her he'd "stolen" it from Katerina Ivanovna, and that she'd replied that he hadn't stolen it, and that he must pay the money back the next day. When the prosecutor pressed her on whether the money he'd said he'd stolen from Katerina Ivanovna was what he'd spent yesterday, or what he'd squandered here a month before, she declared he'd meant the money spent a month before, and that that was how she'd understood him.

Grushenka was finally released, and Nikolay Parfenovitch told her impulsively that she could return to town at once, and that if he could be of any help to her — with horses, say, or if she wanted an escort — he ... would be—

"I thank you sincerely," said Grushenka, bowing to him, "I'm going with this old gentleman, I'm driving him back to town with me, and in the meantime, if you'll allow me, I'll wait downstairs to hear what you decide about Dmitri Fyodorovitch."

She went out. Mitya was calm, even looking somewhat more cheerful — but only for a moment. He felt more and more weighed down by a strange physical weakness. His eyes kept closing with fatigue. The questioning of the witnesses was finally over. They moved on to a final review of the record. Mitya got up, moved from his chair to the corner by the curtain, lay down on a large chest covered with a rug, and instantly fell asleep.
He had a strange dream, entirely out of keeping with the place and the moment.

He was driving somewhere across the steppe, where he'd once been stationed long ago, and a peasant was driving him in a cart pulled by a pair of horses, through snow and sleet. He was cold — it was early November, and the snow was falling in big wet flakes that melted as soon as they touched the ground. The peasant drove him briskly; he had a fair, long beard. He wasn't an old man, somewhere around fifty, and wore a gray peasant's smock. Not far off was a village — he could see the black huts, and half of them were burned down, only the charred beams still sticking up. And as they drove in, there were peasant women lined up along the road, a great many of them, a whole row, all thin and gaunt, their faces a sort of brownish color — especially one at the edge, a tall, bony woman who looked forty but might have been only twenty, with a long, thin face. In her arms was a little baby, crying. Her breasts seemed so dried up there wasn't a drop of milk in them. And the child cried and cried, holding out its little bare arms, its little fists blue with cold.
"Why are they crying? Why are they crying?" Mitya asked, as they dashed cheerfully past.
"It's the babe," the driver answered, "the babe weeping."
And Mitya was struck by the way he said it, in his peasant fashion — "the babe" — and he liked the peasant calling it a "babe." There seemed to be more pity in it.
"But why is it weeping?" Mitya persisted stupidly. "Why are its little arms bare? Why don't they wrap it up?"
"The babe's cold, its little clothes are frozen and don't warm it."
"But why is that? Why?" foolish Mitya persisted still.
"Well, they're poor folk, burned out. They've got no bread. They're begging because they've been burned out."

"No, no," Mitya still seemed not to understand. "Tell me why those poor mothers are standing there. Why are people poor? Why is the babe poor? Why is the steppe so bare? Why don't they hug each other and kiss? Why don't they sing songs of joy? Why are they so dark with black misery? Why don't they feed the babe?"

And he felt that, senseless and unreasonable as his questions were, he still wanted to ask exactly that, and had to ask it in just that way. And he felt a passion of pity rising in his heart such as he'd never known before — that he wanted to cry, that he wanted to do something for all of them, so that the babe would weep no more, so that the dark-faced, dried-up mother wouldn't weep, so that no one would shed another tear from that moment on — and he wanted to do it at once, right away, regardless of every obstacle, with all the Karamazov recklessness.

"And I'm coming with you. I won't leave you now for the rest of my life, I'm coming with you," he heard close beside him, Grushenka's tender voice, thrilling with feeling. And his heart glowed, and he pushed forward toward the light, longing to live, to live, to go on and on, toward the new, beckoning light, and to hurry, hurry, now, at once!

"What! Where?" he exclaimed, opening his eyes and sitting up on the chest, as if he'd come back to life from a faint, smiling brightly. Nikolay Parfenovitch was standing over him, suggesting he listen to the record read aloud and sign it. Mitya guessed he'd been asleep an hour or more, but he wasn't listening to Nikolay Parfenovitch. He was suddenly struck by the fact that there was a pillow under his head — one that hadn't been there when he'd slumped back, exhausted, on the chest.
"Who put this pillow under my head? Who was so kind?" he cried, with a sort of ecstatic gratitude and tears in his voice, as though some great kindness had been shown him.

He never found out who this kind soul had been — maybe one of the peasant witnesses, or Nikolay Parfenovitch's little secretary, had thought, out of compassion, to put a pillow under his head — but his whole soul was trembling with tears. He went to the table and said he'd sign whatever they liked.
"I've had a good dream, gentlemen," he said in a strange voice, a new light, like joy, on his face.

chapters.title: IX. They Carry Mitya Away
paragraphs: Once the record had been signed, Nikolay Parfenovitch turned solemnly to the prisoner and read him the "Committal," stating that in such-and-such a year, on such-and-such a day, in such-and-such a place, the investigating lawyer of such-and-such a district court, having examined so-and-so (namely, Mitya), accused of this and that (all the charges were carefully spelled out), and having found that the accused, not pleading guilty to the charges against him, had offered nothing in his defense, while the witnesses so-and-so and so-and-so, and the circumstances such-and-such, testified against him — acting in accordance with such-and-such articles of the Statute Book, and so on — had ruled that, in order to prevent so-and-so (Mitya) from evading pursuit and judgment by any means, he be held in such-and-such a prison, which he hereby notifies to the accused and of which he sends a copy to the deputy prosecutor, and so on, and so on.

In short, Mitya was informed that from that moment he was a prisoner, and that he'd be driven to town at once and locked up somewhere thoroughly unpleasant. Mitya listened attentively, and only shrugged his shoulders.
"Well, gentlemen, I don't blame you. I'm ready.... I understand there's nothing else for you to do."
Nikolay Parfenovitch informed him gently that he'd be escorted at once by the rural police officer, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch, who happened to be on hand....
"Wait," Mitya interrupted suddenly, and, driven by an uncontrollable urge, he addressed everyone in the room:

"Gentlemen, we're all cruel, we're all monsters, we all make people weep — mothers, and babies at the breast — but of all of us, let it be settled here, now, that I'm the lowest reptile of them all! I've sworn to reform, and every day I've done the same filthy things. I understand now that men like me need a blow — a blow of fate to catch them like a noose and bind them by force from outside. I would never, never have risen on my own! But the thunderbolt has fallen. I accept the torment of the accusation, my public shame — I want to suffer, and through suffering I'll be purified. Maybe I'll be purified, gentlemen? But listen, for the last time: I am not guilty of my father's blood. I accept my punishment, not because I killed him, but because I meant to kill him, and might really have killed him. Still, I intend to fight this out with you. I warn you of that. I'll fight it out with you to the end, and then God will decide. Goodbye, gentlemen, don't hold it against me for shouting at you during the questioning. Oh, I was such a fool then.... In another minute I'll be a prisoner, but now, for the last time, as a free man, Dmitri Karamazov offers you his hand. In saying goodbye to you, I say it to all men."

His voice shook and he stretched out his hand, but Nikolay Parfenovitch, who happened to be standing nearest him, with a sudden, almost nervous movement, hid his hands behind his back. Mitya noticed this at once and started. He let his outstretched hand drop instantly.

"The preliminary inquiry isn't over yet," Nikolay Parfenovitch faltered, somewhat embarrassed. "We'll continue it in town, and I, for my part, of course, am ready to wish you every success ... in your defense.... As a matter of fact, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, I've always been inclined to see you as, so to speak, more unfortunate than guilty. All of us here, if I may speak for everyone, are ready to recognize that you are, at bottom, a young man of honor, but one who has been carried away, alas, by certain passions to a rather excessive degree...."

By the time he finished speaking, Nikolay Parfenovitch's little figure had become positively majestic. It struck Mitya that in another minute this "boy" would take his arm, lead him to another corner, and pick up their conversation about "girls" again. But all sorts of irrelevant, inappropriate thoughts can occur even to a prisoner being led out to execution.
"Gentlemen, you're kind, you're humane — may I see her, to say goodbye for the last time?" Mitya asked.
"Certainly, but considering ... in fact, right now it's not possible except in the presence of—"
"Oh, well, if it has to be, it has to be!"
Grushenka was brought in, but the farewell was brief, said in few words, and didn't at all satisfy Nikolay Parfenovitch. Grushenka bowed low to Mitya.
"I've told you I am yours, and I will be yours. I'll follow you forever, wherever they send you. Farewell — you are innocent, though you've been your own ruin."
Her lips trembled, tears streamed from her eyes.
"Forgive me, Grusha, for my love — for ruining you too with my love."

Mitya would have said more, but he broke off and went out. He was at once surrounded by men keeping constant watch over him. At the bottom of the steps up which he'd driven with such a dash the day before, behind Andrey's three horses, two carts now stood ready. Mavriky Mavrikyevitch, a sturdy, thickset man with a lined face, was annoyed about something — some sudden mix-up. He was shouting angrily. He told Mitya to get into the cart with rather excessive gruffness.

"When I was standing him drinks in the tavern, the man had quite a different face," Mitya thought, as he climbed in. At the gates a crowd had gathered — peasants, women, drivers. Trifon Borissovitch came down the steps too. Everyone stared at Mitya.
"Forgive me as I go, good people!" Mitya shouted suddenly from the cart.
"Forgive us too!" two or three voices called back.
"Goodbye to you too, Trifon Borissovitch!"

But Trifon Borissovitch didn't even turn around. He was, perhaps, too busy. He too was shouting and fussing about something. It turned out that not everything was ready yet in the second cart, in which two constables were to accompany Mavriky Mavrikyevitch. The peasant ordered to drive the second cart was pulling on his smock, stubbornly insisting it wasn't his turn to go, but Akim's. But Akim was nowhere to be seen. They ran off to find him. The peasant kept insisting and begging them to wait.

"You see what our peasants are like, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch. No shame at all!" exclaimed Trifon Borissovitch. "Akim gave you twenty-five kopecks the day before yesterday. You've drunk it all up and now you're making a fuss. I'm simply amazed at your patience with our low peasants, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch, that's all I have to say."
"But what do we need a second cart for?" Mitya put in. "Let's just go with the one, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch. I won't misbehave, I won't run off from you, old fellow. What do we need an escort for?"

"I'll trouble you, sir, to learn how to address me, if no one's taught you yet. I'm not 'old fellow' to you, and you can keep your advice to yourself!" Mavriky Mavrikyevitch snapped out savagely, as if glad of the chance to vent his temper.

Mitya fell silent. He flushed all over. A moment later he suddenly felt very cold. The rain had stopped, but the dull sky was still overcast with clouds, and a sharp wind was blowing straight into his face.
"I've caught a chill," Mitya thought, twitching his shoulders.

At last Mavriky Mavrikyevitch too climbed into the cart, sat down heavily, and, as if without noticing, squeezed Mitya into the corner. True, he was out of sorts and thoroughly disliked the task that had been dumped on him.
"Goodbye, Trifon Borissovitch!" Mitya shouted again, and felt, himself, that this time it hadn't come from good nature but involuntarily, out of resentment.
But Trifon Borissovitch stood there proudly, both hands behind his back, staring straight at Mitya with a stern, angry face, and made no reply.
"Goodbye, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, goodbye!" he suddenly heard Kalganov's voice, who'd darted out unexpectedly. Running up to the cart, he held out his hand to Mitya. He had no cap on.
Mitya just managed to seize and press his hand.
"Goodbye, dear fellow! I won't forget your generosity," he cried warmly.
But the cart moved and their hands came apart. The bell began ringing and Mitya was driven off.

Kalganov ran back, sat down in a corner, bent his head, buried his face in his hands, and burst into tears. He sat like that for a long while, crying like a little boy rather than a young man of twenty. Oh, he believed, almost without a doubt, in Mitya's guilt.
"What are these people? What can men be, after this?" he exclaimed incoherently, in bitter despondency, nearly despair. At that moment he had no desire to live at all.
"Is it worth it? Is it worth it?" the boy exclaimed in his grief.
PART IV

chapters.title: I. Kolya Krassotkin
paragraphs: It was the beginning of November. There had been a hard frost — eleven degrees Réaumur — without snow, but a little dry snow had fallen on the frozen ground overnight, and a sharp, dry wind was lifting it and blowing it along the dreary streets of our town, especially around the market square. It was a dull morning, but the snow had stopped.

Not far from the market square, close to Plotnikov's shop, stood a small house, very clean both inside and out. It belonged to Madame Krassotkin, the widow of a former provincial secretary who had been dead for fourteen years. His widow, still a nice-looking woman of thirty-two, was living in her tidy little house on her own private means. She lived in respectable seclusion; she had a gentle but fairly cheerful temperament. She'd been about eighteen when her husband died — married only a year, and had just given birth to a son. From the day of his death she had devoted herself heart and soul to raising her precious treasure, her boy Kolya. Though she'd loved him passionately for those fourteen years, he'd caused her far more suffering than happiness. She trembled and nearly fainted with terror almost every day, afraid he'd fall ill, catch cold, do something reckless, climb on a chair and fall off it, and so on and so forth. When Kolya started school, his mother threw herself into studying every subject alongside him, so she could help him and go through his lessons with him. She hurried to make friends with the teachers and their wives, even courted Kolya's schoolmates, fawning over them in hopes of sparing Kolya from being teased, laughed at, or beaten. She went so far that the boys actually started mocking him for it, taunting him as a "mama's boy."

But the boy could hold his own. He was a determined boy, "tremendously strong," as the rumor went in his class, and it soon proved true; he was agile, strong-willed, bold and enterprising by temperament. He did well at his lessons, and there was a rumor around school that he could beat the teacher, Dardanelov, at arithmetic and world history. Though he looked down on everyone, he was a good companion, not stuck-up. He accepted his schoolmates' respect as his due, but stayed friendly with them. Above all, he knew where to draw the line. He could restrain himself when he chose, and in his dealings with the teachers he never crossed that last invisible boundary past which a prank becomes an unforgivable breach of discipline. But he was as fond of mischief on every possible occasion as the smallest boy in the school — and not so much for the sake of mischief as for making a splash, inventing something striking and conspicuous. He was extremely vain. He knew how to make even his mother give in to him; he ruled her almost like a little despot. She gave in to him — oh, she'd been giving in to him for years. The one thought she couldn't bear was that her boy had no great love for her. She was always imagining Kolya was "cold" toward her, and at times, dissolving into hysterical tears, she'd reproach him for his coldness. The boy disliked this, and the more he was pressed for shows of feeling, the more he seemed to deliberately avoid them. Yet it wasn't deliberate on his part but instinctive — it was simply his nature. His mother was wrong; he was very fond of her. He only disliked "soppy sentimentality," as he put it in his schoolboy way.

There was a bookcase in the house holding a few of his father's old books. Kolya loved to read, and had gotten through several of them on his own. His mother didn't mind, and only sometimes wondered, seeing the boy stand for hours at the bookcase poring over a book instead of going out to play. And that was how Kolya came to read a few things unsuitable for his age.

Though the boy generally knew where to draw the line in his mischief, he'd lately begun playing pranks that seriously alarmed his mother. It's true there was nothing vicious in what he did, only a wild, reckless streak.

It happened that in July, during summer break, mother and son went to another district, forty-five miles away, to spend a week with a distant relation whose husband worked as an official at the railway station — the very station, nearest to our town, from which Ivan Fyodorovitch Karamazov would set off for Moscow a month later. There Kolya began by thoroughly investigating every detail connected with the railway, knowing he could impress his schoolmates back home with his newly gained knowledge. But it happened there were some other boys in the area, and he soon made friends with them. Some lived at the station, others nearby; there were six or seven of them, all between twelve and fifteen, and two came from our own town. The boys played together, and on the fourth or fifth day of Kolya's stay at the station, the foolish boys made a mad bet. Kolya, who was almost the youngest of the group and rather looked down on by the others because of it, was moved by vanity, or reckless bravado, to bet them two roubles that he'd lie down between the rails at night when the eleven o'clock train was due, and lie there without moving while the train rolled over him at full speed. True, they'd made a preliminary check beforehand, which showed it was possible to lie flat enough between the rails that the train would pass over without touching — but lying there was no joke! Kolya stoutly maintained he'd do it. At first they laughed at him, called him a little liar, a braggart, but that only spurred him on. What stung him most was that these fifteen-year-olds turned up their noses at him too, and were at first inclined to treat him as "a little kid," not fit company for them — an insult he couldn't bear.

So it was decided to go out that evening, half a mile from the station, so the train would have time to reach full speed after leaving. The boys gathered. It was a pitch-black night with no moon. At the appointed time, Kolya lay down between the rails. The five others who'd taken the bet waited in the bushes below the embankment, hearts pounding with suspense, which soon gave way to alarm and remorse. At last they heard, in the distance, the rumble of the train leaving the station. Two red lights gleamed out of the darkness; the monster roared as it approached.

"Run, run away from the rails," the boys cried to Kolya from the bushes, breathless with terror. But it was too late: the train rushed up and flew past. The boys ran to Kolya. He lay there without moving. They pulled at him, lifted him up. He suddenly got up and walked off without a word. He later explained that he'd lain there as though senseless just to frighten them, but the truth was he'd really lost consciousness, as he confessed long afterward to his mother. That's how his reputation as "a desperate character" was sealed for good. He came back to the station white as a sheet. The next day he ran a slight nervous fever, but he was in high spirits and thoroughly pleased with himself. The incident didn't become known right away, but once they returned to town it reached the school and even the teachers' ears. But then Kolya's mother rushed to plead with the teachers on her boy's behalf, and in the end Dardanelov, a respected and influential teacher, exerted himself on his behalf, and the matter was let drop.
