Dardanelov was a middle-aged bachelor who had been passionately in love with Madame Krassotkin for years, and had once already, about a year before, ventured — trembling with fear and the delicacy of his feelings — to offer her, most respectfully, his hand in marriage. But she'd refused him flatly, feeling that accepting would be a betrayal of her son, though Dardanelov had, judging by certain mysterious signs, reason to believe he wasn't unwelcome to the charming but overly cautious and tender-hearted widow. Kolya's mad prank seemed to have broken the ice, and Dardanelov was rewarded for his intervention with a hint of hope. That hint, true, was a faint one, but Dardanelov was such a paragon of purity and delicacy that it was enough, for the time being, to make him perfectly happy. He was fond of the boy, though he'd have considered it beneath him to try to win him over, and he was strict and severe with him in class. Kolya, for his part, kept him at a respectful distance. He learned his lessons perfectly; he stood second in his class, was reserved with Dardanelov, and the whole class firmly believed that Kolya was so good at world history he could "beat" even Dardanelov. Kolya had indeed once asked him, "Who founded Troy?" — to which Dardanelov had given a very vague answer, gesturing toward the movements and migrations of peoples, the remoteness of the period, the mythical legends involved. But the question of who, specifically, had founded Troy, he couldn't answer, and even seemed to regard the question as idle and frivolous. But the boys stayed convinced that Dardanelov didn't know who founded Troy. Kolya had read about the founders of Troy in Smaragdov, whose history was among the books in his father's bookcase. Eventually all the boys grew curious about who had founded Troy, but Krassotkin wouldn't give away his secret, and his reputation for knowledge remained intact.

After the incident on the railway, a certain change came over Kolya's attitude toward his mother. When Anna Fyodorovna (Madame Krassotkin) learned of her son's exploit, she nearly lost her mind with horror. She suffered such terrible fits of hysterics, on and off for several days, that Kolya, genuinely alarmed at last, promised on his honor never to repeat such pranks. He swore it on his knees before the holy icon, and swore by his father's memory, at Madame Krassotkin's insistence, and the "manly" Kolya burst into tears like a boy of six. And all that day mother and son kept flinging themselves into each other's arms, sobbing. The next day Kolya woke up just as "cold" as before, but he'd grown more silent, more modest, sterner, more thoughtful.

Six weeks later, true, he got into another scrape, which even reached the ears of our Justice of the Peace — but it was a scrape of quite another sort, foolish and amusing, and he turned out not to have taken the lead in it, only to have been dragged into it. But more of that later. His mother still fretted and trembled, but the more anxious she grew, the higher Dardanelov's hopes rose. It should be noted that Kolya understood and guessed what was in Dardanelov's heart, and, of course, despised him thoroughly for his "feelings"; he'd once even been tactless enough to show this contempt in front of his mother, hinting vaguely that he knew what Dardanelov was after. But since the railway incident his behavior on this point had also changed; he never allowed himself the faintest allusion to it anymore, and began speaking more respectfully of Dardanelov in front of his mother, which the sensitive woman noticed at once with boundless gratitude. But at the slightest mention of Dardanelov by a visitor in Kolya's presence, she'd flush as pink as a rose. At such moments Kolya would either stare out the window scowling, or examine the state of his boots, or shout angrily for "Perezvon," the big, shaggy, mangy dog he'd picked up a month before, brought home, and kept indoors for some reason in secret, never showing him to any of his schoolmates. He bullied him mercilessly, teaching him all kinds of tricks, so that the poor dog howled whenever he was away at school, and whined with delight when he came in, ran about as if crazed, begged, lay down pretending to be dead, and so on — going through all the tricks he'd been taught, not at any command, but simply out of the zeal of his excited, grateful heart.

I've forgotten to mention, by the way, that Kolya Krassotkin was the boy stabbed with a penknife by the boy the reader already knows as the son of Captain Snegiryov. Ilusha had been defending his father when the schoolboys jeered at him, shouting the nickname "wisp of tow."

chapters.title: II. Children
paragraphs: So on that frosty, snowy, windy day in November, Kolya Krassotkin was sitting at home. It was Sunday, no school. It had just struck eleven, and he badly wanted to go out "on very urgent business," but he'd been left alone in charge of the house, because all its adult residents happened to be out on account of a sudden, singular event. Madame Krassotkin had let two small rooms, separated from the rest of the house by a passage, to a doctor's wife with her two small children. This lady was the same age as Anna Fyodorovna and a close friend of hers. Her husband, the doctor, had left twelve months earlier, first for Orenburg and then for Tashkent, and for the last six months she hadn't heard a word from him. If not for her friendship with Madame Krassotkin, which gave her some comfort, the abandoned lady would surely have dissolved entirely into tears. And now, to top off her troubles, Katerina, her one servant, had suddenly announced the evening before, to her mistress's amazement, that she meant to bring a child into the world before morning. It struck everyone as almost miraculous that no one had noticed it coming sooner. The astonished doctor's wife decided to move Katerina, while there was still time, to a place in town kept by a midwife for such emergencies. Since she set great store by her servant, she carried out the plan at once and stayed there looking after her. By morning, all of Madame Krassotkin's friendly sympathy and energy had been called on to help and to appeal to someone for assistance with the whole matter.

So both ladies were away from home, the Krassotkins' servant Agafya had gone off to market, and Kolya was left for the time being to protect and look after "the kids" — that is, the son and daughter of the doctor's wife, who'd been left alone. Kolya wasn't afraid to look after the house; besides, he had Perezvon, who'd been told to lie flat, without moving, under the bench in the hall. Every time Kolya, pacing back and forth through the rooms, came into the hall, the dog shook his head and gave two loud, coaxing thumps of his tail on the floor — but alas, the whistle that would release him never sounded. Kolya looked sternly at the unlucky dog, who sank back into obedient stillness. The one thing that troubled Kolya was "the kids." He looked, of course, with total scorn on Katerina's unexpected turn of events, but he was very fond of the orphaned little "kiddies," and had already brought them a picture-book. Nastya, the elder, an eight-year-old girl, could read, and Kostya, the boy, seven, loved being read to by her. Krassotkin could, of course, have come up with livelier entertainment for them. He could have lined them up and played soldiers, or sent them off hiding around the house. He'd done that more than once before, and wasn't above doing it again, so much so that a rumor had gone around school that Krassotkin played horses with the little lodgers at home, prancing along with his head cocked to one side like a trace-horse. But Krassotkin haughtily deflected this jab, pointing out that playing horses with boys his own age, boys of thirteen, would certainly be beneath him "at this stage," but that he did it for "the kids'" sake because he liked them, and no one had any right to call him to account over his feelings. The two "kids" adored him.

But this time he was in no mood for games. He had important business of his own ahead of him, something almost mysterious. Meanwhile time was passing, and Agafya, with whom he could have left the children, wouldn't come back from market. He'd already crossed the passage several times, opened the door to the lodgers' room, and looked anxiously in at "the kids," who sat over the book as he'd told them. Every time he opened the door they grinned at him, hoping he'd come in and do something delightful and amusing. But Kolya was preoccupied and didn't go in.

At last it struck eleven, and he made up his mind, once and for all, that if that "cursed" Agafya didn't get back within ten minutes he'd go out without waiting for her, making "the kids" promise, of course, to be brave while he was gone, not to misbehave, not to cry out of fright. With that settled, he put on his padded winter overcoat with its catskin collar, slung his satchel over his shoulder, and — ignoring his mother's constantly repeated pleas that he always wear galoshes in such cold weather — looked at them with contempt as he crossed the hall and went out wearing only his boots. Perezvon, seeing him dressed to go out, began tapping his tail on the floor nervously, but eagerly. Twitching all over, he even let out a plaintive whine. But Kolya, seeing his dog's passionate excitement, decided it was a breach of discipline, kept him under the bench a moment longer, and only whistled for him once he'd opened the door into the passage. The dog sprang up like a wild thing and rushed bounding ahead of him in ecstasy.

Kolya opened the door to look in on "the kids." They were both sitting as before at the table, not reading but arguing hotly about something. The children often argued together about various pressing questions of life, and Nastya, being the elder, usually won. If Kostya didn't agree with her, he almost always appealed to Kolya Krassotkin, and his verdict was treated as infallible by both. This time the "kids'" argument rather interested Krassotkin, and he stood still in the passage to listen. The children saw he was listening, which only made them argue with even greater energy.

"I will never, never believe," Nastya was chattering, "that old women find babies among the cabbages in the vegetable garden. It's winter now, there aren't any cabbages, so the old woman couldn't have brought Katerina a daughter."
Kolya whistled quietly to himself.
"Or maybe they do bring babies from somewhere, but only to people who are married."
Kostya stared at Nastya and listened, pondering it deeply.
"Nastya, how silly you are!" he said finally, firmly and calmly. "How can Katerina have a baby when she isn't married?"
Nastya was exasperated.
"You don't know anything about it," she snapped irritably. "Maybe she has a husband, only he's in prison, so now she's got a baby."
"But is her husband really in prison?" the matter-of-fact Kostya asked gravely.

"Or, I'll tell you what," Nastya interrupted impulsively, entirely dropping and forgetting her first theory. "She doesn't have a husband, you're right about that, but she wants to be married, and so she's been thinking about getting married, and thinking and thinking about it until now she's got it — that is, not a husband, but a baby."
"Well, maybe so," Kostya agreed, thoroughly won over. "But you didn't say that before. So how was I supposed to know?"
"Come, kiddies," said Kolya, stepping into the room. "You're a couple of terrors, I see."
"And Perezvon's with you!" Kostya grinned, and started snapping his fingers and calling Perezvon.

"I'm in a difficulty, kids," Krassotkin began solemnly, "and you have to help me. Agafya must have broken her leg, since she still hasn't shown up — that's certain. I have to go out. Will you let me go?"
The children looked at each other anxiously. Their smiling faces showed a flicker of unease, but they didn't yet fully grasp what was being asked of them.
"You won't be naughty while I'm gone? You won't climb on the cupboard and break your legs? You won't get scared alone and cry?"
A look of deep despondency crossed the children's faces.
"And I could show you something as a reward — a little copper cannon that can be fired with real gunpowder."
The children's faces brightened instantly. "Show us the cannon," said Kostya, beaming all over.
Krassotkin reached into his satchel, pulled out a little bronze cannon, and stood it on the table.
"Ah, of course you'd ask that! Look, it's on wheels." He rolled the toy along the table. "And it can be fired off, too. You can load it with shot and fire it."
"And could it kill someone?"

"It can kill anyone — you just have to aim it at somebody," and Krassotkin explained where the powder went, where the shot rolled in, showing them a tiny hole like a touch-hole, and told them it kicked when it was fired.
The children listened with intense interest. What especially struck their imagination was that the cannon kicked.
"And do you have any powder?" Nastya asked.
"Yes."
"Show us the powder too," she drawled, with a pleading smile.

Krassotkin dove back into his satchel and pulled out a small flask holding a little real gunpowder. He had some shot too, wrapped in a twist of paper. He even uncorked the flask and shook a little powder into his palm.
"You have to be careful there's no fire around, or it would blow up and kill us all," Krassotkin warned them dramatically.
The children stared at the powder with an awestruck alarm that only sharpened their delight. But Kostya liked the shot better.
"And does the shot burn?" he asked.
"No, it doesn't."
"Give me a little shot," he begged.
"I'll give you a little shot — here, take it, but don't show it to your mother until I get back, or she'll be sure to think it's gunpowder, and die of fright, and give you a thrashing."
"Mother never whips us," Nastya remarked at once.

"I know, I just said that to finish the sentence. And don't you ever deceive your mother, except just this once, until I get back. So, kiddies — can I go out? You won't cry and get scared while I'm gone?"
"We sha—all cry," Kostya drawled, already on the verge of tears.
"We shall cry, we're sure to cry," Nastya chimed in, with timid haste.
"Oh, children, children, what a dangerous age you're at! There's no help for it, chicks, I'll have to stay with you, I don't know how long. And time's passing, time's passing, oogh!"
"Tell Perezvon to play dead!" Kostya begged.
"There's no help for it, we'll have to fall back on Perezvon. _Ici_, Perezvon." And Kolya began giving the dog orders, and he ran through all his tricks.

He was a rough-coated dog of medium size, with a sort of lilac-gray coat. He was blind in his right eye, and his left ear was torn. He whined and jumped, stood and walked on his hind legs, lay on his back with his paws in the air, stiff as though dead. While this last trick was going on, the door opened and Agafya, Madame Krassotkin's servant, a stout, pockmarked woman of forty, appeared in the doorway. She'd come back from market with a bag full of provisions in her hand. Holding the bag up in her left hand, she stood still to watch the dog. Though Kolya had been so anxious for her to get back, he didn't cut the performance short, and after keeping Perezvon dead the usual length of time, he finally whistled to him. The dog jumped up and bounded about joyfully at having done his duty.
"Just fancy, a dog!" Agafya observed sententiously.
"Why are you late, woman?" Krassotkin asked sternly.
"Woman, indeed! Go on with you, you brat."
"Brat?"

"Yes, a brat. What's it to you if I'm late? If I'm late, you can be sure I had a good reason," Agafya muttered, busying herself about the stove, without a trace of anger or irritation in her voice. She actually seemed pleased to enjoy a little skirmish with her merry young master.

"Listen, you frivolous woman," Krassotkin began, getting up from the sofa, "can you swear on everything you hold sacred in the world, and something more besides, that you'll keep a close watch on the kids while I'm away? I'm going out."
"And what would I swear for?" laughed Agafya. "I'll watch them without that."
"No, you have to swear on your eternal salvation. Otherwise I won't go."
"Well, then don't. What does it matter to me? It's cold out — stay home."

"Kids," Kolya turned to the children, "this woman will stay with you until I get back, or until your mother comes home, since she really ought to have been back long ago. She'll give you lunch too. You'll feed them, Agafya, won't you?"
"I can do that."

"Goodbye, chickens, I'm going with my mind at ease. And you, granny," he added gravely, in an undertone, as he passed Agafya, "I hope you'll spare their tender years and not tell them any of your old woman's nonsense about Katerina. _Ici_, Perezvon!"
"Get along with you!" Agafya retorted, genuinely angry now. "Ridiculous boy! You need a whipping, talking like that!"

chapters.title: III. The Schoolboy
paragraphs: But Kolya didn't hear her. At last he could go out. As he stepped out at the gate he looked around, hunched his shoulders, said "It's freezing," and went straight down the street, turning off to the right toward the market square. When he reached the second-to-last house before the market square, he stopped at the gate, pulled a whistle from his pocket, and blew it with all his might, like a signal. He didn't have to wait more than a minute before a rosy-cheeked boy of about eleven, wearing a warm, neat, even stylish coat, darted out to meet him. This was Smurov, a boy in the preparatory class (two years below Kolya Krassotkin), the son of a well-to-do official. He was apparently forbidden by his parents to associate with Krassotkin, who was well known as a hopelessly naughty boy, so Smurov was clearly slipping out on the sly. He was — if the reader hasn't forgotten — one of the group of boys who, two months before, had thrown stones at Ilusha. He was the one who told Alyosha Karamazov about Ilusha.
"I've been waiting for you for the last hour, Krassotkin," said Smurov flatly, and the boys strode toward the market square.
"I'm late," answered Krassotkin. "I was held up by circumstances. You won't get thrashed for being seen with me?"
"Come on, I'm never thrashed! And you've got Perezvon with you?"
"Yes."
"You're taking him too?"
"Yes."
"Ah! If only it were Zhutchka!"
"Impossible. Zhutchka doesn't exist. Zhutchka is lost in the mists of obscurity."

"Ah! Couldn't we do this?" Smurov suddenly stopped. "You see, Ilusha says Zhutchka was a shaggy, grayish, smoky-looking dog, like Perezvon. Couldn't you tell him this is Zhutchka, and maybe he'd believe you?"
"Boy, shun a lie — that's one thing; even for a good purpose — that's another. Above all, I hope you haven't told anyone that I'm coming."

"Heaven forbid! I know what I'm doing. But you won't comfort him with Perezvon," said Smurov, with a sigh. "You know his father, the captain, the 'wisp of tow,' told us he was going to bring him a real mastiff pup, with a black nose, today. He thinks that would comfort Ilusha, but I doubt it."
"And how is Ilusha?"

"Ah, he's bad, very bad! I think he's got consumption: he's fully conscious, but his breathing's off. It's gone wrong. The other day he asked to have his boots put on so he could be walked around the room. He tried to walk, but couldn't stand. 'Ah, I told you before, father,' he said, 'that those boots were no good. I could never walk properly in them.' He imagined it was his boots making him stagger, but really it was just weakness. He won't live another week. Herzenstube's looking after him. Now they're rich again — they've got heaps of money."
"They're rogues."
"Who's rogues?"

"Doctors, and the whole tribe of quacks, collectively — and individually too, of course. I don't believe in medicine. It's a useless institution. I mean to look into all that someday. But what's this sentimentality you've all got going up there? The whole class seems to be there every day."
"Not the whole class — only about ten of us go to see him every day. There's nothing in that."

"What I don't understand in all this is what part Alexey Karamazov is playing. His brother's going to be tried tomorrow or the day after for a crime like that, and yet he has so much time to spend on sentimentality with schoolboys."
"There's no sentimentality about it. You're going yourself right now to make peace with Ilusha."
"Make peace with him? What an absurd way to put it! But I won't have anyone analyzing my actions."
"And how pleased Ilusha will be to see you! He has no idea you're coming. Why was it, why was it you wouldn't come all this time?" Smurov cried, with sudden warmth.

"My dear boy, that's my business, not yours. I'm going because I choose to; but all of you were hauled there by Alexey Karamazov — there's a difference, you know. And how do you know? Maybe I'm not going to make peace with him at all. It's a stupid expression."

"It's not Karamazov at all — it's not his doing. Our fellows started going there on their own. Of course, at first they went with Karamazov. And there was nothing of that sort about it — no silliness. First one went, then another. His father was terribly pleased to see us. You know he'll simply go out of his mind if Ilusha dies. He can see Ilusha is dying. And he seems so glad we made peace with Ilusha. Ilusha just asked after you, that was all. He just asks, and says nothing more. His father will go out of his mind or hang himself. He acted like a madman before. You know he's a very decent man. We made a mistake back then. It's all the fault of that murderer who beat him."

"Karamazov's a riddle to me, all the same. I could have made his acquaintance long ago, but I like to have a proper pride in some matters. Besides, I have a theory about him I still need to work out and confirm."

Kolya lapsed into dignified silence. Smurov, too, was quiet. Smurov, of course, worshipped Krassotkin and never dreamed of putting himself on his level. Now he was tremendously intrigued by Kolya's saying he was "going of his own accord" to see Ilusha. He sensed there must be some mystery in Kolya's suddenly deciding to go see him that day. They crossed the market square, which at that hour held many loaded wagons in from the country and a great number of live fowls. The market women sold rolls, cottons, threads and so on from their stalls. These Sunday markets were naively called "fairs" in the town, and there were many such fairs through the year.
Perezvon ran about in the highest spirits, sniffing first one way, then the other. When he met other dogs they zealously sniffed each other over, following the rules of canine etiquette.
"I like watching realistic little scenes like that, Smurov," said Kolya suddenly. "Have you noticed how dogs sniff each other when they meet? It seems to be a law of their nature."
"Yes; it's a funny habit."

"No, it's not funny; you're wrong there. There's nothing funny in nature, no matter how funny it may look to man with his prejudices. If dogs could reason and criticize us, they'd be sure to find just as much that struck them as funny — if not more — in the social habits of men, their masters. Far more, in fact. I say that because I'm convinced there's far more foolishness among us. That's Rakitin's idea — a remarkable idea. I'm a Socialist, Smurov."
"And what's a Socialist?" asked Smurov.

"It's when everyone's equal, and all property is held in common, there are no marriages, and everyone can have whatever religion and laws they like best, and all the rest of it. You're not old enough to understand that yet. It's cold, though."
"Yes, twelve degrees of frost. Father just looked at the thermometer."

"Have you noticed, Smurov, that in the middle of winter we don't feel the cold as much, even at fifteen or eighteen degrees of frost, as we do now, at the start of winter, when there's a sudden frost of twelve degrees, especially when there isn't much snow yet? It's because people aren't used to it. Everything is habit with human beings, everything, even in their social and political relations. Habit is the great driving force. What a funny-looking peasant!"

Kolya pointed to a tall peasant with a good-natured face, in a long sheepskin coat, standing by his wagon, clapping his hands together in their shapeless leather gloves to warm them. His long fair beard was white with frost.
"That peasant's beard is frozen," Kolya called out in a loud, provoking voice as he passed him.
"Plenty of people's beards are frozen," the peasant replied, calm and matter-of-fact.
"Don't provoke him," Smurov said.
"It's all right, he won't get cross — he's a nice fellow. Goodbye, Matvey."
"Goodbye."
"Is your name Matvey?"
"Yes. Didn't you know?"
"No, I didn't. It was a guess."
"You don't say! You're a schoolboy, I take it?"
"Yes."
"You get whipped, I expect?"
"Nothing much — sometimes."
"Does it hurt?"
"Well, yes, it does."
"Eh, what a life!" The peasant heaved a sigh from the bottom of his heart.
"Goodbye, Matvey."
"Goodbye. You're a nice lad, that you are."
The boys walked on.
"That was a nice peasant," Kolya remarked to Smurov. "I like talking to peasants, and I'm always glad to give them their due."
"Why did you lie, pretending we get whipped?" asked Smurov.
"I had to say that to please him."
"How do you mean?"

"You know, Smurov, I don't like being asked the same thing twice. I like people to catch on at the first word. Some things can't be explained. In a peasant's view, schoolboys are whipped, and ought to be whipped. What would a schoolboy even be if he weren't whipped? And if I told him we weren't, he'd be disappointed. But you don't understand that. You have to know how to talk to peasants."
"Only don't tease them, please, or you'll get into another scrape like the one with the goose."
"So you're scared?"
"Don't laugh, Kolya. Of course I'm scared. My father would be awfully cross. I'm strictly forbidden to go out with you."
"Don't worry, nothing will happen this time. Hallo, Natasha!" he shouted to a market woman at one of the stalls.
"Call me Natasha! What next! My name's Marya," the middle-aged market woman shouted back.
"I'm glad it's Marya. Goodbye!"
"Ah, you young rascal! A brat like you, carrying on like that!"
"I'm in a hurry. Can't stay now. You can tell me next Sunday." Kolya waved his hand at her, as if she'd attacked him and not the other way around.
"I've nothing to tell you next Sunday. You went after me, you impudent young monkey, I didn't say a thing," Marya bawled. "You need a whipping, that's what you need, you saucy jackanapes!"

There was a roar of laughter among the other market women around her. Suddenly a man in a furious temper darted out from the arcade of shops nearby. He was a young man, not a local, with dark curly hair and a long, pale, pockmarked face. He wore a long blue coat and a peaked cap, and looked like a merchant's clerk. He was in a state of stupid excitement and shook his fist at Kolya.
"I know you!" he cried angrily. "I know you!"
Kolya stared at him. He couldn't recall when he might have had a run-in with the man. But he'd been in so many street scrapes he could hardly remember them all.
"Do you?" he asked sarcastically.
"I know you! I know you!" the man repeated idiotically.
"So much the better for you. Well, it's time I was going. Goodbye!"
"Up to your saucy pranks again, are you?" the man cried. "Up to your saucy pranks again? I know it, you're at it again!"
"It's none of your business, brother, if I'm up to my saucy pranks again," said Kolya, standing still and looking him over.
"Not my business?"
"No; it's not your business."
"Whose, then? Whose, then? Whose, then?"
"It's Trifon Nikititch's business, not yours."
"What Trifon Nikititch?" the youth asked, staring at Kolya with loutish astonishment, still as furious as ever.
Kolya looked him over gravely.
"Have you been to the Church of the Ascension?" he suddenly asked, with stern emphasis.
"What Church of the Ascension? What for? No, I haven't," said the young man, somewhat thrown off.
"Do you know Sabaneyev?" Kolya went on, even more emphatically, even more sternly.
"What Sabaneyev? I don't know him."

"Well then, you can go to the devil," said Kolya, cutting the conversation short, and, turning sharply right, he strode off quickly, as though he disdained to say another word to a blockhead who didn't even know Sabaneyev.
"Stop, hey! What Sabaneyev?" the young man, shaking off his momentary stupor, was as worked up as before. "What did he mean?" He turned to the market women with a blank stare.
The women laughed.
"You never can tell what he's after," one of them said.
"What Sabaneyev is he talking about?" the young man repeated, still furious and waving his right arm.
"Must be a Sabaneyev who worked for the Kuzmitchovs, that's who it must be," one of the women suggested.
The young man stared at her wildly.
"For the Kuzmitchovs?" another woman repeated. "But his name wasn't Trifon. His name's Kuzma, not Trifon; but the boy said Trifon Nikititch, so it can't be the same one."
"His name isn't Trifon and it isn't Sabaneyev, it's Tchizhov," a third woman put in suddenly, who'd been silent until now, listening gravely. "Alexey Ivanitch is his name. Tchizhov, Alexey Ivanitch."
"No doubt about it, it's Tchizhov," a fourth woman confirmed emphatically.
The bewildered youth stared from one to another.
"But what did he ask for, what did he ask for, good people?" he cried, almost in despair. "'Do you know Sabaneyev?' he says. And who the devil's supposed to know who Sabaneyev is?"
"You're a hopeless fellow. I'm telling you it's not Sabaneyev, it's Tchizhov, Alexey Ivanitch Tchizhov, that's who it is!" one of the women shouted at him, impressed with herself.
"What Tchizhov? Who is he? Tell me, if you know."
"That tall, sniveling fellow who used to sit in the market in the summer."
"And what's your Tchizhov to do with me, good people, eh?"

"How should I know what he's got to do with you?" put in another. "You ought to know that yourself, if you're making such a fuss about him. He spoke to you, not to us, you fool. Don't you really know him?"
"Know who?"
"Tchizhov."
"The devil take Tchizhov, and you along with him. I'll give him a hiding, that I will. He was laughing at me!"
"Give Tchizhov a hiding! More likely he'll give you one. You're a fool, that's what you are!"
"Not Tchizhov, not Tchizhov, you spiteful, mischief-making woman. I'll give the boy a hiding. Catch him, catch him, he was laughing at me!"

The woman burst out laughing. But by now Kolya was a long way off, marching along with a triumphant air. Smurov walked beside him, glancing back at the shouting group behind them. He too was in high spirits, though still a little afraid of landing in some scrape with Kolya.
"What Sabaneyev did you mean?" he asked Kolya, already guessing what the answer would be.

"How should I know? Now there'll be an uproar among them all day long. I like stirring up fools in every walk of life. There's another blockhead — that peasant over there. You know how they say 'there's no one stupider than a stupid Frenchman,' but a stupid Russian shows it right on his face too. Can't you see it all over that peasant's face that he's a fool, eh?"
"Leave him alone, Kolya. Let's go on."
"Nothing's going to stop me now that I'm started. Hey there, good morning, peasant!"
A sturdy-looking peasant with a round, simple face and a grizzled beard, walking by, raised his head and looked at the boy. He seemed not quite sober.
"Good morning, if you're not laughing at me," he said deliberately.
"And if I am?" Kolya laughed.
"Well, a joke's a joke. Laugh away, I don't mind. There's no harm in a joke."
"I beg your pardon, brother, it was a joke."
"Well, God forgive you!"
"Do you forgive me too?"
"I forgive you entirely. Go along."
"I say, you seem a clever peasant."
"Cleverer than you," the peasant answered unexpectedly, with the same gravity.
"I doubt it," said Kolya, somewhat thrown off.
"It's true, though."
"Perhaps it is."
"It is, brother."
"Goodbye, peasant!"
"Goodbye!"
"There are all sorts of peasants," Kolya remarked to Smurov after a brief silence. "How was I supposed to know I'd run into a clever one? I'm always ready to recognize intelligence in a peasant."

In the distance the cathedral clock struck half past eleven. The boys hurried, and walked the considerable distance to Captain Snegiryov's lodgings quickly and almost in silence. Twenty paces from the house Kolya stopped and told Smurov to go on ahead and ask Karamazov to come out to him.
"One has to sniff around a bit first," he remarked to Smurov.
"Why ask him to come outside?" Smurov protested. "Just go in, they'll be delighted to see you. What's the point of making friends out here in the frost?"
"I know why I want to see him out here in the frost," Kolya cut him off, in the imperious tone he liked to take with "small boys," and Smurov ran off to do as he was told.

chapters.title: IV. The Lost Dog
paragraphs: Kolya leaned against the fence with an air of dignity, waiting for Alyosha to appear. Yes, he'd long wanted to meet him. He'd heard a great deal about him from the other boys, but until now he'd always kept up an air of disdainful indifference whenever Alyosha was mentioned, and had even "criticized" what he'd heard about him. But secretly he was dying to make his acquaintance; there was something appealing and attractive in everything he'd been told about Alyosha. So this moment mattered: first of all, he had to show himself at his best, to show his independence. "Or he'll take me for thirteen and treat me like the rest of them. And what are these boys to him anyway? I'll ask him once I know him. It's a pity I'm so short, though. Tuzikov's younger than me, and yet he's half a head taller. But I have a clever face. I'm not good-looking, I know I'm ugly, but I have a clever face. I mustn't talk too freely — if I throw myself at him all at once, he might think — ugh! how awful if he thought—!"

Such were the thoughts racing through Kolya's mind while he did his utmost to look as independent as possible. What distressed him most wasn't so much his "ugly" face as his being so short. On the wall in a corner at home he'd made a pencil mark the year before to record his height, and every two months since then he'd anxiously measured himself against it to see how much he'd grown. But alas, he grew very slowly, and this sometimes drove him nearly to despair. His face, in fact, was by no means "ugly"; on the contrary, it was rather appealing — fair, pale skin, freckled. His small, lively gray eyes had a fearless look and often lit up with feeling. He had rather high cheekbones, small, very red, but not very full lips; his nose was small and unmistakably turned up. "I've got a real pug nose, a real pug nose," Kolya used to mutter to himself when he looked in the mirror, and always walked away indignant. "But maybe I don't even have a clever face?" he'd sometimes think, doubtful even of that. But it shouldn't be assumed his mind dwelled on his face and height. On the contrary, however bitter those moments before the mirror, he forgot them quickly, and for a long time, "giving himself over entirely to ideas and to real life," as he put it to himself.

Alyosha came out quickly and hurried up to Kolya. Before he even reached him, Kolya could see he looked delighted. "Can he really be that glad to see me?" Kolya wondered, pleased. We might note here, in passing, that Alyosha's appearance had completely changed since we last saw him. He'd given up the cassock and now wore a well-cut coat, a soft round hat, and had his hair cropped short. All of it suited him very well, and he looked quite handsome. His charming face always had a good-humored look; but there was gentleness and calm in his good humor. To Kolya's surprise, Alyosha came out to him just as he was, without an overcoat — clearly he'd hurried out. He held out his hand to Kolya at once.
"Here you are at last! How anxiously we've been waiting for you!"

"There were reasons, which you'll learn shortly. Anyway, I'm glad to make your acquaintance. I've been hoping for the chance a long time, and have heard a great deal about you," Kolya muttered, a little breathless.
"We'd have met anyway. I've heard a great deal about you too — but you've taken a long time getting here."
"Tell me, how are things?"
"Ilusha is very ill. He's certainly dying."
"How awful! You must admit medicine is a fraud, Karamazov," Kolya cried warmly.

"Ilusha has mentioned you often, very often, even in his sleep, in his delirium, you know. One can see you used to mean a great deal to him ... before the incident ... with the knife.... There's another reason too.... Tell me, is that your dog?"
"Yes, Perezvon."
"Not Zhutchka?" Alyosha looked at Kolya with eyes full of pity. "Is she lost for good?"

"I know you'd all like it to be Zhutchka. I've heard all about it." Kolya smiled mysteriously. "Listen, Karamazov, I'll tell you the whole thing. That's what I came for — that's why I asked you to come out here, to explain the whole episode before we go in," he began animatedly. "You see, Karamazov, Ilusha came into the preparatory class last spring. Well, you know what our preparatory class is like — a pack of little boys. They started teasing Ilusha right away. I'm two classes above, so of course I only watch from a distance. I saw the boy was weak and small, but he wouldn't give in to them; he fought back. I saw he was proud, and his eyes were full of fire. I like children like that. And they only teased him more for it. Worst of all, he was dressed horribly at the time — his trousers were too small for him, and his boots had holes in them. They gave him grief over it, jeered at him. That I can't stand. I stood up for him right away and gave it to them hot. I beat them, but they adore me, you know, Karamazov?" Kolya boasted impulsively. "But I've always had a soft spot for children. I've got two chicks at home in my hands right now — that's what kept me today. So they left off beating Ilusha, and I took him under my wing. I saw the boy was proud, I tell you, the boy was proud — but in the end he became devoted to me like a slave: did my every bidding, obeyed me as if I were God, tried to copy me. Between classes he'd run straight to me, and I'd go around with him. Sundays too. People always laugh when an older boy makes friends with a younger one like that, but that's just prejudice. If it's my own choice, that's enough. I'm teaching him, developing him. Why shouldn't I develop him if I like him? You, Karamazov, have taken up with all these fledglings yourself. I can see you want to influence the younger generation — to develop them, to be useful to them — and I assure you, this trait of your character, which I knew about by hearsay, drew me to you more than anything. But let's get to the point. I noticed a kind of softness, a sentimentality, creeping over the boy, and you know I have an absolute hatred of this soppy sentimentality, I've had it since I was a baby. There were contradictions in him too: he was proud, yet slavishly devoted to me, and then suddenly his eyes would flash and he'd refuse to agree with me, argue, fly into a rage. I'd sometimes put forward certain ideas; I could see it wasn't so much that he disagreed with the ideas as that he was simply rebelling against me, because I was cool in the face of his affection. So, in order to train him properly, the tenderer he got, the colder I became. I did it on purpose — that was my plan. My goal was to shape his character, to lick him into form, to make a man of him ... and besides ... no doubt you follow me without my spelling it out. Suddenly I noticed that for three days running he was gloomy and downcast, not because of my coldness, but over something else, something more serious. I wondered what the trouble was. I pressed him and found out he'd somehow gotten to know Smerdyakov, who was footman to your late father — this was before his death, of course — and Smerdyakov had taught the poor fool a stupid trick, that is, a brutal, nasty trick. He told him to take a piece of bread, stick a pin in it, and throw it to one of those hungry dogs that snap up anything without chewing it, and then watch what happened. So they prepared a piece of bread like that and threw it to Zhutchka, that shaggy dog there's been all this fuss about. The people who owned it never fed it at all, though it barked all day. (Do you like that stupid barking, Karamazov? I can't stand it.) So it lunged at the bread, swallowed it, and started to squeal — it turned round and round and ran off, squealing as it went, out of sight. That was Ilusha's own account of it. He confessed it to me, crying bitterly. He hugged me, shaking all over. He kept repeating, 'He ran off squealing' — the sight of it haunted him. I could see he was tormented by remorse. I took it seriously. I decided to teach him a lesson about other things too, while I was at it. So I'll admit I wasn't entirely straight with him — I pretended to be more outraged than I really was. 'You've done a rotten thing,' I said, 'you're a scoundrel. I won't tell on you, of course, but I'll have nothing more to do with you for a while. I'll think it over and let you know through Smurov' — that's the boy who just came with me, he's always ready to do anything for me — 'whether I'll have anything more to do with you in the future, or whether I write you off for good as a scoundrel.' He was tremendously upset. I'll admit I felt I'd gone too far as I was saying it, but there was no helping it — I did what I thought was right at the time. A day or two later, I sent Smurov to tell him I wouldn't speak to him again. That's what we call it when two schoolfellows cut each other off entirely. Privately, I only meant to send him to Coventry for a few days, and then, if I saw signs of repentance, hold out my hand to him again. That was my plan. But do you know what happened? He heard Smurov's message, and his eyes flashed. 'Tell Krassotkin from me,' he cried, 'that I'll throw bread with pins in it to every dog there is — every last one!' 'So he's got a bit of a temper on him. We'll have to smoke that out of him.' And I started treating him with contempt; whenever I ran into him I'd turn away or smile sarcastically. And right about then, that business with his father happened. You remember? You have to understand he was already worked up to a fever pitch over what had already happened. The boys, seeing I'd given him up, went after him and taunted him, shouting, 'Wisp of tow, wisp of tow!' And soon there were regular skirmishes with them, which I'm very sorry about now. They seem to have given him one particularly bad beating. One day he flew at all of them as they came out of school. I was standing a few yards off, watching. And I swear, I don't remember laughing — quite the opposite, I felt terribly sorry for him, and in another minute I'd have run over to take his side. But he suddenly met my eyes. I don't know what he imagined, but he pulled out a penknife, rushed at me, and struck at my thigh, here, in my right leg. I didn't move. I don't mind admitting I have my nerve sometimes, Karamazov. I simply looked at him with contempt, as if to say, 'This is how you repay all my kindness! Do it again if you like, I'm at your service.' But he didn't stab me again; he broke down, terrified of what he'd done, threw away the knife, burst into tears, and ran off. I didn't rat on him, of course, and I made everyone keep quiet, so it wouldn't reach the masters. I didn't even tell my mother until it had healed. And the wound was barely a scratch. And then I heard that the same day he'd been throwing stones and had bitten your finger — but you understand now what state he was in! Well, it can't be helped: it was stupid of me not to come and forgive him — that is, make peace with him — once he fell ill. I regret it now. But I had a particular reason. So now I've told you the whole thing ... though I'm afraid it was stupid of me."

"Oh, what a shame," Alyosha exclaimed, with feeling, "that I didn't know before what things stood between you two, or I'd have come to you long ago to beg you to come with me to see him. Would you believe it, when he was feverish he talked about you in his delirium. I had no idea how much you meant to him! And you really haven't managed to find that dog? His father and the boys have been hunting all over town for it. Would you believe it, since he's been ill I've heard him say, three times, with tears, 'It's because I killed Zhutchka, father, that I'm sick now. God is punishing me for it.' He can't get the idea out of his head. And if the dog were found and turned out to be alive, one might almost imagine the joy of it would cure him. We've all pinned our hopes on you."
"Tell me, what made you hope I'd be the one to find him?" Kolya asked, intensely curious. "Why did you count on me rather than anyone else?"

"There was a rumor going around that you were looking for the dog, and that you'd bring it once you found it. Smurov said something of the sort. We've all been trying to convince Ilusha the dog is alive, that it's been seen. The boys brought him a live hare; he just looked at it with a faint smile and asked them to let it go in the fields. So we did. His father just this minute got back, bringing him a mastiff pup, hoping to comfort him with that — but I think it only makes things worse."
"Tell me, Karamazov, what sort of man is the father? I know him, but what do you make of him — a mountebank, a buffoon?"

"Oh, no; there are people of deep feeling who've somehow been crushed. Buffoonery in people like that is a kind of resentful irony against those they don't dare tell the truth to, from years of being humiliated and intimidated by them. Believe me, Krassotkin, that sort of buffoonery is sometimes tragic in the extreme. His whole life now centers on Ilusha, and if Ilusha dies, he'll either go mad with grief or kill himself. I feel almost certain of that when I look at him now."
"I understand you, Karamazov. I can see you understand human nature," Kolya added, with feeling.
"And the moment I saw you with a dog, I thought you were bringing Zhutchka."

"Wait a bit, Karamazov, maybe we'll still find him yet; but this is Perezvon. I'll let him in now, and maybe it'll cheer Ilusha up more than the mastiff pup did. Wait a bit, Karamazov, you'll see something in a minute. But, I say, I'm keeping you standing here!" Kolya cried suddenly. "You've got no overcoat on in this bitter cold. You see what an egoist I am. Oh, we're all egoists, Karamazov!"
"Don't worry about it — it's cold, but I don't catch cold easily. Let's go in, though, and, by the way, what's your name? I know you're called Kolya, but what else?"
"Nikolay — Nikolay Ivanovitch Krassotkin, or, as they say in official documents, 'son of Krassotkin.'" Kolya laughed for some reason, but then added suddenly, "Of course I hate my name, Nikolay."
"Why is that?"
"It's so trivial, so ordinary."
"You're thirteen?" Alyosha asked.

"No, fourteen — that is, I'll be fourteen very soon, in a fortnight. I'll confess one weakness of mine to you, Karamazov, just to you, since this is our first meeting, so you can understand my character right away. I hate being asked my age — more than that ... and actually ... there's a slanderous story going around about me, that last week I was playing robbers with the preparatory boys. It's true I played with them, but it's a complete slander to say I did it for my own amusement. I have reason to believe you've heard the story; but I wasn't playing for my own amusement, it was for the children's sake, because they couldn't think up anything to do on their own. But they always have some silly tale going around. This is an awful town for gossip, I can tell you."
"But what if you had been playing for your own amusement — what's the harm in that?"
"Come now, my own amusement! You don't play horses, do you?"

"But you have to look at it this way," Alyosha said, smiling. "Grown-ups go to the theater, and there the adventures of all sorts of heroes are acted out — sometimes there are robbers and battles too — and isn't that just the same thing, in a different form, of course? And young people's games of soldiers or robbers in their free time are also art in its earliest stage. You know, they spring from the same growing artistic instincts in the young. And sometimes these games are much better than performances at the theater — the only difference is that people go there to watch actors, while in these games the young people are the actors themselves. But that's only natural."

"You think so? Is that your idea?" Kolya looked at him intently. "Oh, you know, that's actually a rather interesting way of looking at it. When I get home, I'll think it over. I'll admit I thought I might learn something from you. I've come to learn from you, Karamazov," Kolya concluded, in a voice full of unguarded feeling.
"And I from you," said Alyosha, smiling and pressing his hand.
Kolya was very pleased with Alyosha. What struck him most was that Alyosha treated him exactly as an equal, talking to him just as though he were "fully grown up."
"I'll show you something in a minute, Karamazov — it's a bit of theater, too," he said, laughing nervously. "That's why I came."
"Let's go first to the landlord's, on the left. All the boys leave their coats there, since the room's small and hot."

"Oh, I'm only coming in for a minute. I'll keep my overcoat on. Perezvon will stay here in the hallway and play dead. _Ici_, Perezvon, lie down and be dead! You see how dead he is. I'll go in first and scout around, then I'll whistle for him when I think it's time, and you'll see, he'll dash in like mad. Only Smurov mustn't forget to open the door at the right moment. I'll arrange it all — you'll see something."

chapters.title: V. By Ilusha’s Bedside
paragraphs: The room occupied by the family of the retired captain Snegiryov is already familiar to the reader. It was close and crowded just then with a number of visitors. Several boys were sitting with Ilusha, and though all of them, like Smurov, would have denied that it was Alyosha who'd brought them there and reconciled them with Ilusha, that was in fact the truth. All the skill he'd used had been to bring them, one by one, to see Ilusha, without any "soppy sentimentality," making it look casual and unplanned. It was a great comfort to Ilusha in his suffering. He was deeply touched by the almost tender affection and sympathy these boys — his former enemies — showed him. Krassotkin was the only one missing, and his absence weighed heavily on Ilusha's heart. Perhaps the bitterest of all his bitter memories was stabbing Krassotkin, who had been his one friend and protector. Clever little Smurov, the first to make peace with Ilusha, thought that was the reason. But when Smurov hinted to Krassotkin that Alyosha wanted to come see him about something, Krassotkin cut him off, telling Smurov to tell "Karamazov" right away that he knew perfectly well what to do, that he wanted no one's advice, and that if he went to see Ilusha he'd choose his own time, since he had "his own reasons."

That was a fortnight before this Sunday. That was why Alyosha hadn't gone to see him, as he'd meant to. But though he waited, he sent Smurov to him twice more. Both times Krassotkin met him with a curt, impatient refusal, sending word back to Alyosha not to bother him anymore, and that if he came himself, he, Krassotkin, wouldn't go to Ilusha's at all. Right up until the last day, Smurov had no idea Kolya meant to go to Ilusha's that morning, and only the evening before, as he parted from Smurov, Kolya abruptly told him to wait at home for him the next morning, since he'd go with him to the Snegiryovs' — but warned him not to breathe a word that he was coming, since he wanted to drop in casually. Smurov obeyed. Smurov's guess that Kolya would bring back the lost dog was based on something Kolya had let slip — that "they must be asses not to find the dog, if it's alive." When Smurov, waiting for the right moment, timidly hinted at his guess about the dog, Krassotkin flew into a violent rage. "I'm not such an ass as to go hunting all over town for other people's dogs when I've got a dog of my own! And how can you imagine a dog could stay alive after swallowing a pin? Soppy sentimentality, that's all it is!"

For the last fortnight Ilusha hadn't left his little bed under the icons in the corner. He hadn't been to school since the day he met Alyosha and bit his finger. He fell ill that very same day, though for a month afterward he could sometimes still get up and walk around the room and hallway. But lately he'd grown so weak he couldn't move without his father's help. His father was terribly worried about him. He'd even given up drinking and was nearly out of his mind with fear that his boy would die. And often, especially after leading him around the room on his arm and putting him back to bed, he'd rush off to a dark corner in the hallway, lean his head against the wall, and break into fits of violent weeping, stifling his sobs so Ilusha wouldn't hear them.

Coming back into the room, he'd usually start doing something to amuse and comfort his precious boy — telling him stories, funny anecdotes, or mimicking comic people he'd happened to meet, even imitating the howls and cries of animals. But Ilusha couldn't bear watching his father clown and play the buffoon. Though the boy tried not to show how much he disliked it, he saw, with an aching heart, that his father was an object of ridicule, and he was continually haunted by the memory of the "wisp of tow" and that "terrible day."

Nina, Ilusha's gentle, crippled sister, didn't care for her father's buffoonery either (Varvara had gone off some time before to Petersburg to study at the university). But the half-witted mother found it hugely entertaining, and laughed heartily whenever her husband started capering about or performing something. It was the only way she could be amused; the rest of the time she grumbled and complained that everyone had forgotten her now, that no one treated her with respect, that she was slighted, and so on. But over the last few days she'd changed completely. She'd started staring constantly at Ilusha's bed in the corner, seeming lost in thought. She was quieter, more subdued, and, if she cried, she cried softly so as not to be heard. The captain noticed the change in her with mournful bewilderment. The boys' visits had at first only irritated her, but later their cheerful shouting and stories began to entertain her, and eventually she grew so fond of them that, if the boys had stopped coming, she'd have felt lonely without them. When the children told a story or played a game, she laughed and clapped her hands. She called some of them over and kissed them. She was especially fond of Smurov.

As for the captain, having the children in his room, coming to cheer up Ilusha, filled his heart from the start with ecstatic joy. He even hoped Ilusha would now shake off his depression, and that it would speed his recovery. Despite his fear for Ilusha, he hadn't, until lately, doubted for a moment that his boy would ultimately recover.

He greeted his young visitors with deference, waited on them hand and foot, and was ready to be their horse — even let them ride on his back — but Ilusha didn't like the game, so it was dropped. He started buying little treats for them, gingerbread and nuts, gave them tea, cut them sandwiches. It should be noted that all this time he had plenty of money. He'd taken the two hundred roubles from Katerina Ivanovna, just as Alyosha had predicted he would. And afterward Katerina Ivanovna, learning more about their circumstances and about Ilusha's illness, visited them herself, got to know the family, and managed to charm the half-witted mother. Since then she'd been generous in helping them, and the captain, terrified at the thought his boy might be dying, set aside his pride and humbly accepted her help.

All this time Doctor Herzenstube, called in by Katerina Ivanovna, came punctually every other day, but little came of his visits, and he dosed the poor invalid mercilessly. But that Sunday morning a new doctor was expected, one who'd come from Moscow with a great reputation. Katerina Ivanovna had sent for him from Moscow at considerable expense, not specifically for Ilusha, but for another purpose, of which more will be said in its place further on. But, since he'd come, she'd asked him to see Ilusha as well, and the captain had been told to expect him. He had no idea whatsoever that Kolya Krassotkin was coming, though he'd long hoped for a visit from the boy Ilusha was pining for.

At the moment Krassotkin opened the door and came into the room, the captain and all the boys were gathered around Ilusha's bed, looking at a tiny mastiff pup, only born the day before, though the captain had ordered it a week earlier to comfort and amuse Ilusha, still grieving over the lost and probably dead Zhutchka. Ilusha, who'd heard three days before that he was to be given a puppy — not just any puppy, but a pedigree mastiff, a very important point, of course — tried, out of delicacy, to pretend he was pleased. But his father and the boys couldn't help seeing that the puppy only served to remind his little heart of the poor dog he'd killed. The puppy lay beside him, feebly stirring, and he, smiling sadly, stroked it with his thin, pale, wasted hand. He clearly liked the puppy, but ... it wasn't Zhutchka; if he could have had both Zhutchka and the puppy, then he'd have been completely happy.
"Krassotkin!" one of the boys suddenly cried. He was the first to see him come in.
Krassotkin's entrance caused a general stir; the boys stepped back and lined up on either side of the bed, so he could see Ilusha clearly. The captain rushed eagerly to meet Kolya.
"Please, come in ... you're most welcome!" he said hurriedly. "Ilusha, Mr. Krassotkin has come to see you!"

But Krassotkin, shaking his hand hastily, immediately demonstrated his complete grasp of proper manners. He turned first to the captain's wife, sitting in her armchair, who was in a rather sour mood just then, grumbling that the boys were standing between her and Ilusha's bed and blocking her view of the new puppy. With the greatest courtesy he bowed to her, scraping his foot, and, turning to Nina, gave her, as the only other lady present, a similar bow. This polite behavior made an extremely favorable impression on the deranged lady.
"There, you can tell at once he's a young man who's been well brought up," she remarked aloud, throwing up her hands; "but as for our other visitors, they come piling in one on top of another."
"What do you mean, mamma, one on top of another? How's that?" the captain muttered affectionately, though with a hint of anxiety on her account.
"That's how they come riding in. They climb on each other's shoulders out in the passage and go prancing in like that, into a respectable family's home. Strange sort of visitors!"
"But who came in like that, mamma?"
"Why, that boy came riding in on that one's back, and this one on that one's."

Kolya was already at Ilusha's bedside. The sick boy went visibly pale. He raised himself in the bed and stared intently at Kolya. Kolya hadn't seen his little friend in two months, and he was stunned at the sight of him. He'd never imagined he'd see such a wasted, yellow face, such huge, feverishly glowing eyes, such thin little hands. He saw, with grieved surprise, Ilusha's quick, labored breathing and his dry lips. He stepped close, held out his hand, and, nearly overcome, said:

"Well, old man ... how are you?" But his voice failed him; he couldn't manage an easy tone; his face suddenly twitched and the corners of his mouth trembled. Ilusha smiled a pitiful little smile, still unable to say a word. Something made Kolya raise his hand and run it over Ilusha's hair.
"Never mind!" he murmured softly, to cheer him up, or maybe without even knowing why he said it. For a minute they were silent again.
"Hey, so you've got a new puppy?" Kolya said suddenly, in a thoroughly offhand voice.
"Ye—es," Ilusha answered in a long whisper, gasping for breath.

"A black nose — that means he'll be fierce, a good watchdog," Kolya observed gravely and stolidly, as though the puppy and its black nose were the only thing on his mind. But in truth he was still struggling with all his might not to burst into tears like a child, and try as he might, he couldn't quite manage it. "When he's grown, you'll have to keep him on a chain, I'm sure."
"He'll be a huge dog!" one of the boys cried.
"Of course he will," "a mastiff," "big," "like this," "big as a calf," several voices shouted.

"Big as a calf, a real calf," the captain chimed in. "I got one like that on purpose, one of the fiercest breeds, and his parents are huge and very fierce — they stand this high off the floor.... Sit down here, on Ilusha's bed, or here on the bench. You're welcome, we've been hoping to see you a long time.... You were kind enough to come with Alexey Fyodorovitch?"
Krassotkin sat on the edge of the bed, at Ilusha's feet. Though he'd perhaps prepared some easy, casual opening for the conversation on the way over, he now completely lost the thread of it.

"No ... I came with Perezvon. I've got a dog now, called Perezvon. A Slavonic name. He's out there ... if I whistle, he'll come running in. I brought a dog too," he said, suddenly addressing Ilusha. "Do you remember Zhutchka, old man?" he fired the question at him abruptly.

Ilusha's little face quivered. He looked at Kolya with an anguished expression. Alyosha, standing by the door, frowned and signaled to Kolya not to mention Zhutchka, but Kolya either didn't notice or wouldn't.
"Where ... is Zhutchka?" Ilusha asked in a broken voice.
"Oh, well, my boy, your Zhutchka's lost and gone for good!"
Ilusha said nothing, but fixed an intent gaze on Kolya once more. Alyosha, catching Kolya's eye, signaled to him again, more urgently, but Kolya looked away, pretending not to notice.

"He must have run off and died somewhere. Must have died after a meal like that," Kolya pronounced pitilessly, though he seemed a little out of breath himself. "But I've got a dog, Perezvon ... a Slavonic name.... I brought him to show you."
"I don't want him!" Ilusha said suddenly.

"No, no, you really must see him ... it'll cheer you up. I brought him on purpose.... He's the same kind of shaggy dog.... Will you let me call my dog in, madam?" he suddenly asked Madame Snegiryov, with an inexplicable excitement in his manner.
"I don't want him, I don't want him!" Ilusha cried, a mournful break in his voice. There was a reproachful light in his eyes.

"You'd better," the captain started up from the chest by the wall, where he'd just sat down, "you'd better ... another time," he muttered, but Kolya couldn't be held back. He hurriedly shouted to Smurov, "Open the door," and as soon as it opened, he blew his whistle. Perezvon dashed headlong into the room.

"Jump, Perezvon, beg! Beg!" Kolya shouted, jumping up, and the dog rose on its hind legs at Ilusha's bedside. What followed took everyone by surprise: Ilusha started, lurched violently forward, bent over Perezvon, and stared at him, faint with suspense.
"It's ... Zhutchka!" he suddenly cried, in a voice breaking with joy and anguish.
"And who did you think it was?" Krassotkin shouted with all his might, in a ringing, joyful voice, and, bending down, he seized the dog and lifted him up to Ilusha.

"Look, old man, you see — blind in one eye, left ear torn, exactly the marks you described to me. That's how I found him. I found him right away. He didn't belong to anyone!" he explained, turning quickly to the captain, to his wife, to Alyosha, and then back to Ilusha. "He'd been living in the Fedotovs' back yard. He made his home there, but they never fed him. He was a stray that had run off from the village ... I found him.... You see, old man, he couldn't have swallowed what you gave him. If he had, he'd have died, he'd have had to! So he must have spat it out, since he's alive. You didn't see him do it. But the pin pricked his tongue, that's why he squealed. He ran off squealing and you thought he'd swallowed it. He might well squeal — the skin inside a dog's mouth is so tender ... much more tender than in people!" Kolya cried impetuously, his face glowing, radiant with delight. Ilusha couldn't speak. White as a sheet, he stared open-mouthed at Kolya, his huge eyes almost starting out of his head. And if Krassotkin, who had no idea of it, had known what a devastating, even fatal effect a moment like this might have on the sick boy's health, nothing would have induced him to play such a trick on him. But Alyosha was perhaps the only person in the room who understood that. As for the captain, he behaved like a small child.
"Zhutchka! It's Zhutchka!" he cried in a voice full of bliss. "Ilusha, this is Zhutchka, your Zhutchka! Mamma, this is Zhutchka!" He was nearly weeping.
"And I never guessed!" Smurov cried regretfully. "Bravo, Krassotkin! I said he'd find the dog, and here he's found him."
"Here he's found him!" another boy echoed gleefully.
"Krassotkin's a brick!" a third voice cried.
"He's a brick, he's a brick!" the other boys cried, and started clapping.

"Wait, wait," Krassotkin did his utmost to shout over them all. "I'll tell you how it happened, that's the whole point. I found him, took him home, and hid him right away. I kept him locked up at home and didn't show him to anyone until today. Only Smurov's known for the last fortnight, but I told him this dog was called Perezvon, and he never guessed. And meanwhile I taught the dog all sorts of tricks. You should see everything he can do! I trained him so I could bring you a well-trained dog, in good condition, old man, so I could say to you, 'See, old man, what a fine dog your Zhutchka is now!' Have you got a bit of meat? He'll show you a trick that'll make you die laughing. A bit of meat, have you got any?"

The captain dashed across the passage to the landlady's, where their cooking was done. Not wanting to lose precious time, Kolya, in desperate haste, shouted to Perezvon, "Dead!" And the dog immediately turned around and lay on his back with all four paws in the air. The boys laughed. Ilusha watched with the same suffering smile, but the one most delighted by the dog's performance was "mamma." She laughed at the dog and began snapping her fingers and calling him, "Perezvon, Perezvon!"

"Nothing will make him get up, nothing!" Kolya cried triumphantly, proud of his success. "He won't budge for all the shouting in the world, but if I call him, he'll jump up in a second. Ici, Perezvon!" The dog leapt up and bounded about, whining with delight. The captain ran back with a piece of cooked beef.

"Is it hot?" Kolya asked briskly, businesslike, taking the meat. "Dogs don't like hot things. No, it's fine. Look, everyone, look, Ilusha, look, old man — why aren't you looking? He's not looking, now that I've brought him."

The new trick was to make the dog stand motionless, nose out, with a tempting bit of meat balanced right on his nose. The luckless dog had to stand without moving, meat balanced on his nose, for as long as his master chose to keep him there — sometimes as long as half an hour. But this time he kept Perezvon waiting only a moment.
"Paid for!" Kolya cried, and the meat flashed from the dog's nose straight into his mouth. The audience, of course, burst into applause and exclamations of amazement.
"Can you really have put off coming all this time simply to train the dog?" Alyosha exclaimed, an unintended note of reproach in his voice.
"Simply for that!" Kolya answered, with perfect simplicity. "I wanted to show him off in all his glory."
"Perezvon! Perezvon," Ilusha called suddenly, snapping his thin fingers and beckoning to the dog.

"What is it? Let him jump up on the bed! _Ici_, Perezvon!" Kolya slapped the bed, and Perezvon sprang up beside Ilusha. The boy threw both arms around his head, and Perezvon instantly licked his cheek. Ilusha pressed close to him, stretched out in bed, and hid his face in the dog's shaggy coat.
"Dear, dear!" the captain kept exclaiming. Kolya sat back down on the edge of the bed.
"Ilusha, I can show you another trick. I've brought you a little cannon. Remember, I told you about it before, and you said how much you'd like to see it. Well, here, I brought it for you."

And Kolya hurriedly pulled the little bronze cannon out of his satchel. He hurried because he was happy himself. Another time he'd have waited for the excitement over Perezvon to die down first, but now he pressed ahead, heedless of any such consideration. "You're all happy now," he felt, "so here's something to make you happier still!" He was utterly delighted himself.

"I've been coveting this thing for a long while — it's for you, old man, it's for you. It belonged to Morozov, it was no use to him, he had it from his brother. I traded him a book from father's bookcase for it — _A Kinsman of Mahomet, or Salutary Folly_, a scandalous book published in Moscow a hundred years ago, before there was any censorship. And Morozov has a taste for that sort of thing. He was grateful to me for it, too...."

Kolya held the cannon in his hand so everyone could see and admire it. Ilusha raised himself, and, still with his right arm around the dog, gazed at the toy in delight. The excitement grew even greater when Kolya announced he had gunpowder too, and that it could be fired off right there "if it won't alarm the ladies." "Mamma" immediately asked to look at the toy up close, and her request was granted. She was thoroughly pleased with the little bronze cannon on wheels, and began rolling it back and forth on her lap. She readily gave permission for the cannon to be fired, without the slightest idea what she was agreeing to. Kolya showed the powder and the shot. The captain, being a military man, took charge of loading it, putting in a tiny amount of powder. He asked that the shot be saved for another time. The cannon was set on the floor, aimed at an empty part of the room, three grains of powder were pushed into the touch-hole, and a match was struck. A magnificent bang followed. Mamma was startled, but immediately laughed with delight. The boys stared in speechless triumph. But the captain, watching Ilusha, was more delighted than any of them. Kolya picked up the cannon and at once presented it to Ilusha, along with the powder and shot.
"I got it for you, for you! I've been saving it for you a long time," he repeated once more, delighted.
"Oh, give it to me! No, give me the cannon!" mamma began begging like a little child. Her face showed a pitiful fear that she wouldn't get it. Kolya was thrown off. The captain fidgeted uneasily.

"Mamma, mamma," he ran to her, "the cannon's yours, of course, but let Ilusha have it, since it's a present to him — but it's just as much yours. Ilusha will always let you play with it; it'll belong to both of you, both of you."
"No, I don't want it to belong to both of us, I want it to be mine, entirely, not Ilusha's," mamma insisted, on the point of tears.

"Take it, mother, here, keep it!" Ilusha cried. "Krassotkin, may I give it to my mother?" he turned to Krassotkin with a pleading face, as though afraid he might be offended at his giving the present away to someone else.
"Of course you may," Krassotkin agreed warmly, and, taking the cannon from Ilusha, handed it himself to mamma with a polite bow. She was so touched she burst into tears.
"Ilusha, darling, he's the one who loves his mamma!" she said tenderly, and immediately began wheeling the cannon back and forth on her lap again.
"Mamma, let me kiss your hand." The captain darted up to her at once and did so.
"And I've never seen such a charming fellow as this nice boy," said the grateful lady, pointing at Krassotkin.

"And I'll bring you as much powder as you like, Ilusha. We make our own powder now. Borovikov figured out how it's done — twenty-four parts saltpeter, ten of sulphur, and six of birchwood charcoal. It's all ground together, mixed into a paste with water, and rubbed through a fine sieve — that's how it's done."
"Smurov told me about your powder, only father says it's not real gunpowder," Ilusha said.
"Not real?" Kolya flushed. "It burns. I don't know, of course."
"No, I didn't mean that," the captain put in, looking guilty. "I only said real powder isn't made that way, but it doesn't matter — it can be made that way."

"I don't know, you'd know best. We lit some in a pomade jar, it burned beautifully, all burned away leaving just a tiny bit of ash. But that was only the paste, and if you rub it through ... well, you know best, I don't know.... And Bulkin's father thrashed him over our powder, did you hear?" he turned to Ilusha.
"Yes," Ilusha answered. He was listening to Kolya with intense interest and enjoyment.

"We'd made up a whole bottle of it and he kept it under his bed. His father found it. Said it might explode, and thrashed him on the spot. He was going to complain about me to the masters. He's not allowed to go around with me now — no one's allowed to go around with me now. Smurov isn't allowed to either — I've got a bad name with everyone. They say I'm a 'desperate character,'" Kolya smiled scornfully. "It all started with that business on the railway."

"Ah, we've heard about that exploit of yours, too," the captain cried. "How could you lie still on the track? Is it possible you weren't the least bit afraid, lying there under the train? Weren't you scared?"
The captain was abject in his flattery of Kolya.

"N—not especially," Kolya answered carelessly. "What's damaged my reputation around here more than anything was that cursed goose," he said, turning back to Ilusha. But though he kept up a careless air as he talked, he still couldn't help himself and kept losing the tone he was trying to hold.
"Ah! I heard about the goose!" Ilusha laughed, beaming all over. "They told me, but I didn't understand it. Did they really take you to court?"

"The most stupid, trivial business — they made a mountain out of a molehill, as they always do," Kolya began carelessly. "I was walking through the market square here one day, just as they'd driven in the geese. I stopped and looked at them. All at once a fellow — he's an errand boy at Plotnikov's now — looked at me and said, 'What are you looking at the geese for?' I looked at him; he was a stupid, moon-faced fellow of twenty. I'm always on the side of the peasantry, you know. I like talking to peasants.... We've fallen behind the peasants — that's an axiom. I believe you're laughing, Karamazov?"
"No, heaven forbid, I'm listening," said Alyosha, with such a good-natured air that the sensitive Kolya was reassured at once.

"My theory, Karamazov, is clear and simple," he hurried on, pleased with himself. "I believe in the common people and I'm always glad to give them their due, but I'm not for spoiling them — that's a _sine qua non_.... But I was telling you about the goose. So I turned to the fool and answered, 'I'm wondering what the goose is thinking about.' He looked at me quite blankly. 'And what is the goose thinking about?' he asked. 'You see that cart full of oats?' I said. 'The oats are spilling out of the sack, and the goose has stuck its neck right under the wheel to gobble them up — you see?' 'I see that well enough,' he said. 'Well,' I said, 'if that cart were to move on a little, would it break the goose's neck or not?' 'It'd break it for sure,' and he grinned all over his face, thoroughly delighted. 'Come on then,' I said, 'let's try it.' 'Let's,' he said. And it didn't take us long to arrange: he took hold of the bridle without being noticed, and I stood to one side to direct the goose. And the owner wasn't watching, he was talking to someone, so I had nothing to do — the goose stuck its head in after the oats on its own, under the cart, right under the wheel. I winked at the lad, he tugged the bridle, and crack. The goose's neck snapped clean in half. And, as luck would have it, all the peasants saw us right at that moment, and they raised a ruckus at once. 'You did that on purpose!' 'No, not on purpose.' 'Yes, you did, on purpose!' Well, they shouted, 'Take him to the justice of the peace!' They took me too. 'You were in on it too,' they said, 'you helped, everyone in the market knows you!' And, for some reason, I really am known all over the market," Kolya added, with some pride. "We all trooped off to the justice's, and they brought the goose along too. The fellow was crying, in a great panic, blubbering just like a woman. And the farmer kept shouting you could kill any number of geese that way. Well, of course, there were witnesses. The justice settled it in a minute: the farmer was to be paid a rouble for the goose, and the fellow got to keep the goose. And he was warned not to play tricks like that again. And the fellow kept blubbering like a woman. 'It wasn't me,' he said, 'he put me up to it,' and pointed at me. I answered, perfectly composed, that I hadn't put him up to anything, that I'd simply stated a general proposition, spoken hypothetically. The justice of the peace smiled, and then got annoyed at himself for smiling. 'I'll complain to your teachers about you, so that in future you won't waste your time on general propositions instead of sitting over your books and learning your lessons.' He never actually complained to the teachers — that was a joke — but the story got around and reached the teachers' ears anyway. They've got long ears, you know! The classical master, Kolbasnikov, was particularly scandalized by it, but Dardanelov got me off again. But Kolbasnikov's furious with everyone these days, like a green donkey. Did you know, Ilusha, he just got married, got a dowry of a thousand roubles, and his bride's an absolute fright, first-class, bottom of the barrel. The third-year fellows wrote an epigram about it:
Astounding news has reached the class, Kolbasnikov has been an ass.

And so on — it's awfully funny, I'll bring it to you later. I've got nothing against Dardanelov, he's a learned man, no doubt about that. I respect men like that, and it's not because he stood up for me."
"But you took him down over who founded Troy!" Smurov put in suddenly, plainly proud of Krassotkin at that moment. He'd especially loved the story of the goose.
"Did you really take him down?" the captain asked, in a flattering tone. "On the question of who founded Troy? We heard about it — Ilusha told me at the time."
"He knows everything, father, he knows more than any of us!" Ilusha put in. "He just pretends to be ordinary, but really he's top of the class in every subject...."
Ilusha looked at Kolya with boundless happiness.

"Oh, that's all nonsense about Troy, a trivial matter. I consider it an unimportant question," Kolya said, with haughty humility. He'd fully recovered his dignity by now, though he was still a little uneasy. He sensed he'd gotten quite worked up, and had talked about the goose, for instance, with too little restraint, while Alyosha had looked serious and hadn't said a word the whole time. And the vain boy was gradually starting to be gnawed by a fear that Alyosha's silence meant he despised him, thought he was showing off in front of him. If Alyosha dared think anything like that, Kolya would—
"I consider the question a perfectly trivial one," he said again, sharply, with pride.
