"I can't help believing my brother. I know he wouldn't lie to me. I could see from his face that he wasn't lying."
"Only from his face? Is that the whole of your proof?"
"I have no other proof."
"And of Smerdyakov's guilt, you have no proof whatsoever, beyond your brother's word and the look on his face?"
"No, I have no other proof."

The prosecutor dropped the questioning there. The impression Alyosha's testimony left on the public was thoroughly disappointing. There'd been talk about Smerdyakov before the trial; someone had heard something, someone else had pointed out something else, and it was said Alyosha had assembled some extraordinary proof of his brother's innocence and Smerdyakov's guilt—and in the end there was nothing, no evidence at all beyond certain moral convictions, natural enough in a brother.

But then Fetyukovitch began his cross-examination. When he asked Alyosha exactly when the prisoner had told him of his hatred for their father and that he might kill him—whether he'd heard it, say, at their last meeting before the catastrophe—Alyosha started as he answered, as though only just now recollecting and grasping something.
"I remember one detail now that I'd completely forgotten myself. It wasn't clear to me at the time, but now—"

And, evidently struck by the thought for the very first time, he recounted eagerly how, at his last meeting with Mitya that evening under the tree, on the road to the monastery, Mitya had struck himself on the chest—"the upper part of the chest"—and had repeated several times that he had a way to restore his honor, that the way lay right here, here on his chest. "I thought, when he struck his chest, he meant it was in his heart," Alyosha went on, "that he might find in his heart the strength to save himself from some terrible disgrace hanging over him, one he didn't even dare confess to me. I'll admit that at the time I thought he was talking about our father, that the disgrace he shuddered at was the thought of going to our father and doing him some violence. And yet it was right then that he pointed to something on his chest, so I remember the thought striking me at the time that the heart isn't located in that part of the chest, but lower, and that he was striking himself much too high, just below the neck, and kept pointing to that same spot. My idea seemed foolish to me at the time, but perhaps he was pointing to that little pouch where he kept the fifteen hundred roubles!"
"Exactly right," Mitya cried from his seat. "That's right, Alyosha, it was the little pouch I struck with my fist."

Fetyukovitch rushed over to him in a hurry, pleading with him to stay quiet, and in the same instant pounced on Alyosha. Alyosha, swept up himself in the memory, warmly laid out his theory that this disgrace was most likely that very fifteen hundred roubles on him, money he could have returned to Katerina Ivanovna as half of what he owed her, but which he'd nonetheless decided not to repay, meaning instead to use it for another purpose—namely, to run off with Grushenka, if she agreed.

"That's it, it has to be that," Alyosha exclaimed, suddenly excited. "My brother cried out several times that half of the disgrace—half of it (he said 'half' several times)—he could free himself from right away, but that he was so wretched in his weakness of will that he wouldn't do it... that he knew beforehand he was incapable of doing it!"
"And you clearly, confidently remember that he struck himself right in this part of the chest?" Fetyukovitch asked, eagerly.

"Clearly and confidently, because I thought at the time, 'Why is he striking himself up there, when the heart is lower down?' and the thought seemed silly to me right then... I remember it seeming silly... it flashed through my mind. That's what brought it all back to me just now. How could I have forgotten it until now? That's the pouch he meant when he said he had the means but wouldn't give back that fifteen hundred. And when he was arrested at Mokroe he cried out—I know, I was told about it—that he considered it the most shameful act of his life that when he had the means to repay Katerina Ivanovna half—half, mind you—of what he owed her, he still couldn't bring himself to give the money back, and chose instead to remain a thief in her eyes rather than part with it. And what torment, what torment that debt has been to him!" Alyosha finished, exclaiming.

The prosecutor, of course, stepped in. He asked Alyosha to describe once more exactly how it had happened, and pressed the question several times: "Did the prisoner appear to be pointing at something specific? Or might he simply have struck himself on the chest with his fist?"
"But it wasn't with his fist," Alyosha cried; "he pointed with his fingers, and pointed right here, very high up.... How could I have so completely forgotten it until this very moment?"

The President asked Mitya what he had to say about the last witness's testimony. Mitya confirmed it, saying he'd been pointing to the fifteen hundred roubles he kept on his chest, just below the neck, and that this, of course, was the disgrace. "A disgrace I can't deny, the most shameful act of my entire life," Mitya cried. "I could have paid it back and didn't pay it back. I chose to remain a thief in her eyes rather than give it back. And the most shameful part of it was that I knew beforehand I wouldn't give it back! You're right, Alyosha! Thank you, Alyosha!"

With that, Alyosha's cross-examination came to an end. What mattered, what stood out about it, was that at least one fact had come to light, and even if it was only a small scrap of evidence, a mere hint at evidence, it did go some way toward proving the pouch had really existed and had really held fifteen hundred roubles, and that the prisoner hadn't been lying at the preliminary inquiry when he'd claimed, at Mokroe, that the fifteen hundred roubles were "his own." Alyosha was glad. Flushed, he made his way back to the seat set aside for him. He kept repeating to himself: "How did I forget? How could I have forgotten it? And what made it come back to me just now?"

Katerina Ivanovna was called to the witness box. As she entered, something extraordinary happened in the courtroom. The ladies clutched their lorgnettes and opera glasses. A stir passed through the men; some stood up for a better view. Everyone said afterward that Mitya had gone "white as a sheet" the moment she entered. Dressed entirely in black, she came forward modestly, almost timidly. Nothing in her face betrayed her agitation; but there was a resolute glint in her dark, brooding eyes. I should note that many people remarked afterward how especially beautiful she looked at that moment. She spoke softly but clearly, so that she could be heard throughout the whole courtroom. She expressed herself with composure, or at least made every effort to appear composed. The President began questioning her discreetly, with great respect, as though afraid to touch on "certain chords," showing consideration for her great unhappiness. But in answer to one of his first questions, Katerina Ivanovna stated firmly that she had once been engaged to the prisoner, "until he left me, of his own accord..." she added, quietly. When they asked her about the three thousand roubles she'd entrusted to Mitya to post to her relatives, she said firmly, "I didn't give him the money simply to have it mailed off. I could tell at the time that he was in great need of money.... I gave him the three thousand on the understanding that he'd mail it within the month, if he chose to. There was no need for him to worry himself over that debt afterward."
I won't repeat every question put to her and every answer she gave, in full detail. I'll only give the substance of her testimony.

"I was firmly convinced he'd send that sum off the moment he got money from his father," she went on. "I've never doubted his disinterestedness, or his honesty... his scrupulous honesty... in money matters. He felt quite certain he'd receive the money from his father, and spoke to me about it several times. I knew he was at odds with his father, and I always believed his father had treated him unfairly. I don't recall his ever making any threat against his father. He certainly never made any such threat in front of me. If he'd come to see me around that time, I'd have set his mind at rest at once about that unlucky three thousand roubles, but he'd stopped coming to see me... and I myself was placed in a position... where I couldn't invite him to.... And I really had no right, in any case, to be exacting about that money," she added suddenly, a note of resolve ringing in her voice. "I was once indebted to him myself, for a sum of assistance greater than three thousand, and I accepted it, even though at the time I couldn't have foreseen I'd ever be in a position to repay that debt."
There was a note of defiance in her voice. It was at this point that Fetyukovitch began his cross-examination.

"Did that take place not here, but at the very beginning of your acquaintance?" Fetyukovitch suggested, cautiously, feeling his way, catching the scent of something favorable at once. I should mention, in passing, that although Fetyukovitch had been brought from Petersburg partly at Katerina Ivanovna's own urging, he knew nothing at all about the episode of the four thousand roubles Mitya had given her, and of her "bowing to the ground before him." She'd concealed this from him, said not a word about it, and that was strange. One can fairly safely assume she herself hadn't known, until the very last minute, whether she'd speak of that episode in court, and had simply waited for the inspiration of the moment.

No, I can never forget those moments. She began telling her story. She told everything—the whole episode Mitya had told Alyosha, her bowing to the ground, and her reasons for it. She spoke of her father, and of going to see Mitya, and never once, not by a single word or hint, suggested that Mitya himself, through her sister, had proposed that they "send Katerina Ivanovna to him" to fetch the money. She generously kept that hidden, and wasn't ashamed to let it appear as though she'd run to the young officer entirely on her own impulse, trusting to something... to beg him for the money. It was something tremendous! I went cold and trembled as I listened. The courtroom fell silent, straining to catch every word. It was something unheard of. Even from a woman as strong-willed and contemptuously proud as she was, such a completely frank confession, such a sacrifice, such self-immolation, seemed almost unbelievable. And for what, for whom? To save the man who'd deceived and insulted her, and to help, in however small a way, secure his rescue, by building up a strong impression in his favor. And indeed, the figure of the young officer who, bowing respectfully to the innocent girl, handed over his last four thousand roubles—everything he had in the world—was cast in a very sympathetic, appealing light, but... I had an uneasy foreboding in my heart! I sensed that slander might come of this later (and it did, in fact, it did). Afterward, it went round the whole town, repeated with spiteful laughter, that the story might not be entirely complete—that is, that the claim the officer had let the young lady leave "with nothing but a respectful bow" left something out. There were hints that something had been left unsaid.

"And even if nothing had been left out, even if that were the whole story," the most highly respected of our ladies insisted, "it's still very doubtful whether it was proper for a young woman to behave that way, even to save her father."

And could Katerina Ivanovna, with her intelligence, her morbid sensitivity, have failed to understand that people would talk that way? She must have understood it—and yet she made up her mind to tell everything anyway. Of course, all these nasty little suspicions about the truth of her story only surfaced afterward, and in the first moment everyone was deeply moved by it. As for the judges and lawyers, they listened to Katerina Ivanovna in a reverent, almost shame-faced silence. The prosecutor didn't dare risk even a single question on the subject. Fetyukovitch bowed low to her. Oh, he was nearly triumphant! A great deal of ground had been won. For a man to hand over his last four thousand roubles on a generous impulse, and then for that same man to murder his father just to rob him of three thousand—the idea seemed simply too incongruous. Fetyukovitch felt that the charge of theft, at least, was now as good as disproved. "The case" had been thrown into an entirely different light. A wave of sympathy for Mitya swept through the room. As for him... I was told that once or twice, while Katerina Ivanovna was giving her testimony, he jumped up from his seat, sank back down again, and buried his face in his hands. But once she'd finished, he suddenly cried out, in a sobbing voice:
"Katya, why have you ruined me?"—and his sobs could be heard throughout the whole courtroom. But he checked himself instantly, and cried out again:
"Now I'm condemned!"

Then he sat rigid in his place, teeth clenched, arms crossed over his chest. Katerina Ivanovna remained in the courtroom, taking her seat. She was pale, and sat with her eyes cast down. Those sitting near her said afterward that for a long time she shivered all over, as if in the grip of a fever. Grushenka was called.

I'm coming now to the sudden catastrophe that was, perhaps, the final blow that sealed Mitya's ruin. For I'm convinced, as is everyone—every lawyer said the same thing afterward—that if this episode hadn't happened, the prisoner would at the very least have been recommended for mercy. But more on that later. First, a few words about Grushenka.

She too was dressed entirely in black, her magnificent black shawl draped over her shoulders. She walked to the witness box with her smooth, silent step, that slightly swaying gait common to women of a full figure. She looked steadily at the President, her eyes turning neither right nor left. To my mind she looked quite beautiful at that moment, not at all pale, as the ladies claimed afterward. They also insisted she wore a tight, spiteful expression. I believe she was simply irritated, painfully conscious of the contemptuous, curious eyes of our scandal-hungry public fixed on her. She was proud, and couldn't stand being looked down on. She was one of those people who flare up in anger, eager to strike back, at the mere hint of contempt. There was an element of timidity in her too, of course, and inward shame at her own timidity, so it wasn't strange that her tone kept shifting. At one moment it was angry, contemptuous, harsh; the next, there was a genuine note of self-reproach. At times she spoke as though taking a desperate plunge, as though thinking, 'I don't care what happens, I'll say it....' Speaking of her acquaintance with Fyodor Pavlovitch, she remarked curtly, "That's all nonsense—was it my fault he wouldn't leave me alone?" But a minute later she added, "It was all my fault. I was laughing at both of them—at the old man, and at him too—and I brought them both to this. It all happened on account of me."

Samsonov's name came up somehow. "That's nobody's business," she snapped at once, with a kind of insolent defiance. "He was my benefactor; he took me in when I didn't have a shoe to my name, when my own family had thrown me out." The President reminded her, politely but firmly, that she must answer the questions directly, without wandering off into irrelevant details. Grushenka flushed crimson, her eyes flashing.

The envelope with the money in it, she hadn't seen herself—she'd only heard from "that wicked wretch" that Fyodor Pavlovitch had an envelope with three thousand in notes inside it. "But that was all foolishness. I was only laughing. I'd never have gone to him for anything."
"Who are you referring to as 'that wicked wretch'?" the prosecutor asked.
"The lackey, Smerdyakov, who murdered his master and hanged himself last night."
She was, of course, immediately asked what grounds she had for such a definite accusation; but it turned out she had no grounds for it either.

"Dmitri Fyodorovitch told me so himself; you can believe him. The woman who came between us ruined him—she's the cause of all of it, I'll tell you that," Grushenka added. She seemed to be quivering with hatred, a vindictive edge in her voice.
She was asked again whom she meant.
"That young lady there, Katerina Ivanovna. She sent for me, offered me chocolate, tried to win me over. There's not much real shame in her, I can tell you that...."
At this point the President cut her off sternly, asking her to moderate her language. But the jealous woman's heart was on fire, and she no longer cared what she did.

"When the prisoner was arrested at Mokroe," the prosecutor asked, "everyone saw and heard you run out of the next room and cry out, 'It's all my fault! We'll go to Siberia together!' So you already believed, at that point, that he'd murdered his father?"

"I don't remember what I felt at the time," Grushenka answered. "Everyone was shouting that he'd killed his father, and I felt it was my fault, that it was on my account he'd murdered him. But when he said he wasn't guilty, I believed him at once, and I believe him now, and I always will believe him. He's not the kind of man to lie."

Fetyukovitch began his cross-examination. I remember that, among other things, he asked her about Rakitin and the twenty-five roubles "you paid him for bringing Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov to see you."

"There was nothing strange about him taking the money," Grushenka sneered, with angry contempt. "He was always coming to me for money—he used to get at least thirty roubles a month out of me, mostly for little luxuries; he had plenty to live on without my help."
"What made you so generous toward Mr. Rakitin?" Fetyukovitch asked, despite an uneasy stir from the President.
"Why, he's my cousin. His mother was my mother's sister. But he's always begged me not to tell anyone here about it—he's so dreadfully ashamed of me."

This fact came as a complete surprise to everyone; no one in town, nor at the monastery, not even Mitya, had known about it. I was told Rakitin turned purple with shame where he sat. Grushenka had somehow heard, before coming into the courtroom, that he'd testified against Mitya, and that had made her angry. Whatever effect Rakitin's speech had left on the public—his noble sentiments, his attacks on serfdom and Russia's political disorder—was now, this time, finally and thoroughly ruined. Fetyukovitch was satisfied; it was another gift from heaven. Grushenka's cross-examination didn't last long, and there was, of course, nothing particularly new in her testimony. She left a very unpleasant impression on the public; hundreds of contemptuous eyes were fixed on her as she finished testifying and took her seat again in the courtroom, at a good distance from Katerina Ivanovna. Mitya stayed silent through the whole of her testimony. He sat as though turned to stone, his eyes fixed on the floor.
Ivan was called to give evidence.

chapters.title: V. A Sudden Catastrophe
paragraphs: I should note he'd actually been called before Alyosha. But the court usher had informed the President that, owing to some kind of attack or fit, the witness couldn't appear just then, though he'd be ready to testify as soon as he recovered. But no one seemed to have caught this, and it only came out later.

For the first moment, his entrance went almost unnoticed. The main witnesses, especially the two rival women, had already been questioned. Curiosity was, for the time being, satisfied; the public felt almost worn out. A few more witnesses still had to be heard, who probably had little to add after everything already said. Time dragged on. Ivan walked up with extraordinary slowness, looking at no one, his head bowed, as if sunk in gloomy thought. He was impeccably dressed, but his face left a painful impression, on me at least—there was something earthen in it, something like the look of a dying man. His eyes were dull; he raised them and let them travel slowly around the courtroom. Alyosha jumped up from his seat and let out a groan, "Ah!" I remember that, though it went almost unnoticed.

The President began by informing him he was testifying without the oath, that he could answer or decline to answer, but that of course he must bear witness according to his conscience, and so on, and so forth. Ivan listened, staring at him blankly, but his face gradually relaxed into a smile, and the moment the President, watching him in astonishment, finished speaking, he burst out laughing.
"Well, and what else?" he asked, loudly.
A hush fell over the courtroom; there was a sense that something was wrong. The President showed signs of unease.
"You... are perhaps still unwell?" he began, glancing around for the usher.
"Don't trouble yourself, your excellency, I'm well enough, and I can tell you something interesting," Ivan answered, with sudden calm and courtesy.
"You have some particular statement to make?" the President went on, still uncertain.
Ivan looked down, waited a few seconds, and, lifting his head, answered, almost stammering:
"No... I don't. I have nothing in particular."

They began putting questions to him. He answered, as it were, reluctantly, with extreme brevity, with a kind of disgust that grew more and more visible, though his answers made sense. To a great many questions he simply said he didn't know. He knew nothing of his father's financial dealings with Dmitri. "I wasn't interested in the subject," he added. Threats to kill his father, he'd heard from the prisoner. About the money in the envelope, he'd heard from Smerdyakov.
"The same thing, over and over," he suddenly broke in, with a look of exhaustion. "I have nothing particular to tell the court."
"I can see you're unwell, and I understand your feelings," the President began.
He turned to the prosecutor and defense counsel to invite them to question the witness, if they wished, when Ivan suddenly asked, in an exhausted voice:
"Let me go, your excellency, I feel very ill."

And with those words, without waiting for permission, he turned to walk out of the courtroom. But after four steps, he stopped short, as though he'd reached some decision, smiled slowly, and turned back.

"I'm like the peasant girl, your excellency... you know how it goes? 'I'll stand up if I like, and I won't if I don't.' They were trying to dress her in her sarafan, to take her to church to be married, and she said, 'I'll stand up if I like, and I won't if I don't.'... It's in some book about the peasants."
"What do you mean by that?" the President asked, severely.

"Why, this," Ivan suddenly pulled out a roll of banknotes. "Here's the money... the notes that were in that envelope" (he nodded toward the table holding the material evidence), "the money our father was murdered for. Where should I put it? Mr. Superintendent, take it."
The court usher took the whole roll and handed it to the President.
"How did this money come into your possession, if it's the same money?" the President asked, in astonishment.

"I got it from Smerdyakov, from the murderer, yesterday.... I was with him just before he hanged himself. It was he, not my brother, who killed our father. He murdered him, and I put him up to it... Who doesn't wish for his own father's death?"
"Are you in your right mind?" burst involuntarily from the President.

"I should think I'm in my right mind... in the same nasty mind as all of you... as all these... ugly faces." He turned suddenly to the audience. "My father's been murdered, and they pretend to be horrified," he snarled, with furious contempt. "They keep up the sham with each other. Liars! Every one of them wants their fathers dead. One reptile devours another.... If there'd been no murder, they'd have gone home angry and out of sorts. It's a spectacle they want! Panem et circenses. Though who am I to talk! Is there any water? Give me a drink, for Christ's sake!" He suddenly clutched his head.

The usher hurried over to him at once. Alyosha jumped up and cried, "He's ill. Don't believe him—he has brain fever." Katerina Ivanovna rose abruptly from her seat and, frozen in horror, stared at Ivan. Mitya stood up and stared hungrily at his brother, listening to him with a wild, strange smile.
"Don't trouble yourselves. I'm not mad—I'm only a murderer," Ivan began again. "You can't expect eloquence from a murderer," he added suddenly, for no clear reason, and laughed a strange laugh.

The prosecutor bent toward the President, visibly alarmed. The two other judges exchanged agitated whispers. Fetyukovitch listened with his ears pricked up; the hall sat hushed, waiting. The President seemed to suddenly pull himself together.

"Witness, your words are incomprehensible and out of place here. Calm yourself, if you can, and tell your story... if you really have something to tell. How can you back up your statement... if you're not, in fact, delirious?"

"That's exactly it. I have no proof. That cur Smerdyakov isn't going to send you proof from the other world... in an envelope. All you people think about is envelopes—one's enough. I have no witnesses... except perhaps one," he smiled, thoughtfully.
"Who is your witness?"

"He has a tail, your excellency, and that would be irregular! Le diable n'existe point! Pay no attention to him: he's a petty, pitiful devil," he added suddenly. He'd stopped laughing now and spoke almost confidentially. "He's here somewhere, no doubt—under that table with the material evidence on it, perhaps. Where else would he sit? Listen to me. I told him I don't want to keep quiet, and he went on about the geological cataclysm... idiocy! Come, let the monster go... he's been singing a hymn. That's because his heart is light! Like a drunk man in the street bawling about how 'Vanka went to Petersburg,' and I'd give a quadrillion quadrillions for two seconds of joy. You don't know me! Oh, how stupid this whole business is! Take me instead of him! I didn't come here for nothing.... Why, why is everything so stupid?..."

And he began again, slowly, as if reflecting, looking around him once more. But by now the whole courtroom was in an uproar. Alyosha rushed toward him, but the court usher had already grabbed Ivan by the arm.

"What are you doing?" he cried, staring into the man's face, and suddenly seizing him by the shoulders, he flung him violently to the floor. But the police were right there, and he was seized. He screamed furiously. And the whole time he was being carried out, he shouted and screamed something incoherent.

The whole courtroom fell into confusion. I don't remember every detail of what happened. I was too worked up myself to follow it all. I only know that afterward, once everything had quieted down and everyone understood what had happened, the court usher was called in for a reprimand, though he explained quite reasonably that the witness had seemed perfectly well, that a doctor had examined him an hour before, when he'd had a brief spell of dizziness, but that right up until he'd entered the courtroom, he'd spoken quite coherently, so there'd been no way to foresee this—and that he had, in fact, insisted on giving evidence. But before everyone had fully regained their composure and recovered from this scene, another one followed it. Katerina Ivanovna had an attack of hysterics. She sobbed, shrieking loudly, but refused to leave the courtroom, struggling, begging them not to remove her. Suddenly she cried out to the President:

"There's more evidence I have to give right now... right now! Here's a document, a letter... take it, read it, quickly, quickly! It's a letter from that monster... that man there, there!" She pointed at Mitya. "It was he who killed his father, you'll see it in a moment. He wrote to me how he'd kill his father! But the other one is ill, he's ill, he's delirious!" she kept crying, beside herself.

The court usher took the document she was holding out and handed it to the President, and she, sinking back into her chair, burying her face in her hands, began sobbing convulsively and silently, shaking all over, stifling every sound for fear she'd be thrown out of the courtroom. The document she'd handed up was that letter Mitya had written at the Metropolis tavern, the one Ivan had called "mathematical proof." Alas, its mathematical force was borne out, and if it hadn't been for that letter, Mitya might have escaped his fate, or at least that fate might have been less terrible. It was, I repeat, hard to catch every detail. What followed is still a blur in my mind. The President must, I suppose, have passed the document at once to the judges, the jury, and the lawyers on both sides. I only remember how they began questioning the witness. Gently asked by the President whether she'd recovered enough, Katerina Ivanovna exclaimed, impetuously:

"I'm ready, I'm ready! I'm perfectly capable of answering you," she added, evidently still afraid she'd somehow be prevented from giving her testimony. She was asked to explain in detail what this letter was, and under what circumstances she'd received it.

"I received it the day before the crime was committed, but he wrote it the day before that, at the tavern—that is, two days before he committed the crime. Look, it's written on the back of some kind of bill!" she cried, breathlessly. "He hated me at that time, because he'd behaved contemptibly and was running after that creature... and because he owed me that three thousand.... Oh! He was humiliated by that three thousand, on account of his own low character! Here's how it happened, with that three thousand. I beg you, I implore you, to hear me out. Three weeks before he murdered his father, he came to see me one morning. I knew he needed money, and I knew what he needed it for. Yes, yes—to win that creature and carry her off. I already knew by then that he'd been unfaithful to me and meant to leave me, and it was I, I, who gave him that money, offered it to him under the pretext that he'd send it to my sister in Moscow. And as I handed it to him, I looked him straight in the face and told him he could send it whenever he liked—'in a month's time would do.' How, how could he have failed to understand that I was practically telling him, to his very face, 'You need money to betray me with your creature, so here's the money for you. I'm giving it to you myself. Take it, if you have so little honor left as to take it!' I wanted to prove to myself what he really was, and what happened? He took it—he took it, and squandered it on that creature in a single night.... But he knew, he knew that I knew everything about it. I assure you he understood, too, that I'd given him that money to test him, to see whether he'd sunk so low he'd take it from me. I looked into his eyes, and he looked into mine, and he understood everything, and he still took it—he carried off my money!"

"That's true, Katya," Mitya roared suddenly. "I looked into your eyes and I knew you were dishonoring me with it, and I took your money anyway. Despise me as a scoundrel, despise me, all of you! I've earned it!"
"Prisoner," the President cried, "one more word and I'll have you removed."

"That money tormented him," Katya went on, with impulsive haste. "He wanted to pay it back to me. He truly wanted to, that's true; but he needed money for that creature too. So he murdered his father, and still didn't repay me, and ran off with her to that village where he was arrested. There, once again, he squandered the money he'd stolen after murdering his father. And the day before the murder, he wrote me this letter. He was drunk when he wrote it. I saw that right away, at the time. He wrote it out of spite, absolutely certain, positively certain, that I'd never show it to anyone—even if he did kill him—or else he'd never have written it. Because he knew I wouldn't want revenge, wouldn't want to destroy him! But read it, read it carefully—more carefully, please—and you'll see he described it all, in that letter, all of it beforehand: how he'd kill his father, and where the money was kept. Look, please, don't skip over it, there's one phrase there: 'I'll kill him the moment Ivan's gone.' So he'd worked it all out beforehand, exactly how he'd kill him," Katerina Ivanovna pointed out to the court, with venomous, malicious triumph. Oh, it was plain she'd studied every line of that letter, picked apart every hidden meaning in it. "If he hadn't been drunk, he'd never have written to me; but look, it's all written there beforehand, exactly as he carried it out afterward. A complete plan of it!" she cried, frantically.

She was past caring now about any consequences to herself, though no doubt she'd foreseen them even a month before, since even then, perhaps, shaking with anger, she'd already been weighing whether to produce it at the trial or not. Now she'd taken the fatal plunge. I remember the letter was read aloud by the clerk, right afterward, I believe. It made an overwhelming impression. They asked Mitya whether he admitted to writing the letter.

"It's mine, mine!" Mitya cried. "I wouldn't have written it if I hadn't been drunk!... We've hated each other over so many things, Katya, but I swear, I swear I loved you even while I hated you, and you never loved me!"

He sank back into his seat, wringing his hands in despair. The prosecutor and the defense counsel began cross-examining her, mainly to establish what had led her to conceal such a document, and to give her testimony in such a different tone and spirit only a short while before.

"Yes, yes. I was lying just now. I was lying against my own honor, against my own conscience, but I wanted to save him, because he's hated me and despised me so!" Katya cried, wildly. "Oh, he's despised me horribly, he's always despised me, and do you know, he's despised me from the very moment I bowed down to him for that money. I saw it.... I felt it immediately, at the time, but for a long time I refused to believe it. How many times I've read it in his eyes: 'You came of your own accord, though.' Oh, he didn't understand, he had no idea why I ran to him, he can't imagine anything but baseness, he judged me by himself, he thought everyone was just like him!" Katya hissed furiously, in an absolute frenzy. "And he only wanted to marry me because I'd inherited a fortune, because of that, only because of that! I always suspected it was because of that! Oh, he's a brute! He was always convinced I'd tremble with shame in front of him my whole life, because I'd gone to him that once, and that he had the right to despise me for it forever, to hold himself above me forever—that's why he wanted to marry me! That's how it is, that's exactly how it is! I tried to win him over with my love—a love without limits. I even tried to forgive his unfaithfulness; but he understood nothing, nothing! How could he understand, really? He's a monster! I only got that letter the next evening: it was brought to me from the tavern—and only that morning, only that very morning, I wanted to forgive him everything, everything—even his betrayal!"

The President and the prosecutor, of course, tried to calm her down. I can't help thinking they felt ashamed of taking advantage of her hysteria, of listening to such confessions. I remember hearing them say to her, "We understand how difficult this is for you; believe us, we can sympathize," and so on, and so forth. And yet they went on drawing testimony out of this raving, hysterical woman. In the end she described, with an extraordinary clarity that often appears, if only for a moment, in states of overwrought emotion like this, how Ivan had very nearly been driven out of his mind over the past two months, trying to save "the monster and murderer," his brother.

"He tortured himself," she exclaimed, "he was always trying to minimize his brother's guilt, confessing to me that he too had never loved his father, and perhaps had wished for his death himself. Oh, he has such a tender, over-tender conscience! He tormented himself with it! He told me everything, everything! He came every day and talked to me as his only friend. I have the honor of being his only friend!" she suddenly cried, with a kind of defiance, her eyes flashing. "He'd been to see Smerdyakov twice. One day he came to me and said, 'If it wasn't my brother, but Smerdyakov, who committed the murder' (since the rumor was spreading everywhere that Smerdyakov had done it), 'then maybe I'm guilty too, because Smerdyakov knew I didn't love my father, and might have believed I wanted my father dead.' Then I brought out that letter and showed it to him. He became entirely convinced his brother had done it, and it crushed him. He couldn't bear the thought that his own brother was a parricide! Just a week ago, I saw it was making him ill. Over these past few days he's talked incoherently in front of me. I could see his mind was giving way. He wandered around, raving; people saw him muttering to himself in the streets. The doctor from Moscow, at my request, examined him the day before yesterday, and told me he was on the verge of brain fever—and all on his account, all because of this monster! And last night he learned Smerdyakov was dead! It was such a shock it drove him out of his mind... and all because of this monster, all for the sake of saving the monster!"

Oh, of course, an outpouring like that, a confession like that, is only possible once in a lifetime—at the hour of death, say, on the way to the scaffold! But it was entirely in keeping with Katya's character, and this was just such a moment in her life. It was the same impetuous Katya who'd once thrown herself on the mercy of a young libertine to save her father; the same Katya who, only moments before, in her pride and purity, had sacrificed herself and her maidenly modesty in front of this whole crowd, telling of Mitya's generous conduct, hoping to soften his fate just a little. And now, once again, she sacrificed herself—but this time for someone else, and perhaps only now, perhaps only in this very moment, did she feel and understand how dear that someone else truly was to her! She'd sacrificed herself in terror for him, suddenly imagining he'd destroyed himself with his confession that he, not his brother, had committed the murder; she'd sacrificed herself to save him, to save his good name, his reputation!

And yet one terrible doubt occurred to me: was she lying in her account of her earlier relationship with Mitya? That was the question. No, she hadn't slandered him on purpose when she cried out that Mitya despised her for bowing down to him! She believed it herself. She'd been firmly convinced, probably ever since that bow, that simple-hearted Mitya, who even then adored her, was laughing at her, despising her. She'd loved him with a hysterical, "lacerated" love, born only of pride, of wounded pride, and that love wasn't really love at all, but closer to revenge. Oh, perhaps that lacerated love might have grown into real love; perhaps that was all Katya had ever longed for; but Mitya's unfaithfulness had wounded her to the very bottom of her heart, and her heart couldn't forgive him for it. The moment of revenge had come upon her suddenly, and everything that had been building up, for so long and so painfully, in that wounded woman's breast burst out all at once, unexpectedly. She betrayed Mitya, but she betrayed herself too. And the instant she'd given full voice to her feelings, the tension broke, and she was overcome with shame. The hysterics started up again: she collapsed to the floor, sobbing, screaming. She was carried out. At that moment Grushenka, with a wail, rushed toward Mitya before anyone could stop her.

"Mitya," she wailed, "your serpent has destroyed you! There, she's shown you what she is!" she shouted at the judges, shaking with rage. At a signal from the President, they seized her and tried to remove her from the courtroom. She wouldn't allow it. She fought and struggled to get back to Mitya. Mitya let out a cry and struggled to reach her. He was overpowered.

Yes, I think the ladies who'd come for the spectacle must have gone home satisfied—it had certainly been a varied show. Then, I recall, the Moscow doctor appeared on the scene. I believe the President had earlier sent the court usher to arrange medical help for Ivan. The doctor announced to the court that the sick man was suffering from a dangerous attack of brain fever, and had to be removed at once. Answering questions from the prosecutor and defense counsel, he said the patient had come to see him of his own accord the day before yesterday, and that he'd warned him an attack like this was coming, though the patient had refused to be looked after. "He certainly wasn't in a normal state of mind: he told me himself that he saw visions while wide awake, that he met several people in the street who were dead, and that Satan came to visit him every evening," the doctor concluded. Having given his testimony, the celebrated doctor withdrew. The letter produced by Katerina Ivanovna was added to the material evidence. After some deliberation, the judges decided to proceed with the trial, and to enter both unexpected pieces of testimony—Ivan's and Katerina Ivanovna's—into the record.

But I won't go into detail about the testimony of the other witnesses, who only repeated and confirmed what had already been said, each in their own characteristic way. I repeat, it was all drawn together in the prosecutor's closing speech, which I'll quote shortly. Everyone was worked up, everyone was electrified by this latest catastrophe, and all were waiting for the closing speeches, for the prosecution and the defense, with intense impatience. Fetyukovitch was visibly shaken by Katerina Ivanovna's testimony. But the prosecutor was triumphant. Once all the evidence had been heard, the court adjourned for nearly an hour. I believe it was just eight o'clock when the President returned to his seat, and our prosecutor, Ippolit Kirillovitch, began his closing speech.

chapters.title: VI. The Prosecutor’s Speech. Sketches Of Character
paragraphs: Ippolit Kirillovitch began his speech trembling with nerves, cold sweat on his forehead, flashing hot and cold by turns. He said so himself afterward. He considered this speech his masterpiece — the masterpiece of his whole life, his swan song. And in fact he died nine months later of galloping consumption, so it turned out he'd had the right to compare himself to a swan singing its last song. He had put his whole heart and every ounce of brain he had into that speech. And to everyone's surprise, poor Ippolit Kirillovitch turned out to have at least some genuine feeling for the public good and for “the eternal question” hidden away in him. What really set his speech apart was its sincerity. He truly believed the prisoner was guilty; he wasn't prosecuting merely as an official duty, and when he called for retribution he trembled with real passion “for the safety of society.” Even the women in the audience, who stayed hostile to Ippolit Kirillovitch throughout, admitted he made an extraordinary impression on them. He began in a cracking voice, but it gained strength as he went and filled the courtroom by the end of his speech. Yet the moment he finished, he nearly fainted.

“Gentlemen of the jury,” the prosecutor began, “this case has caused a stir across all of Russia. But what is there to be amazed at, really — what is so uniquely horrifying about it to us? That's what's so horrifying: that we've grown so used to crimes like this. What ought to appall us is not this or that isolated crime, but the fact that we've become accustomed to it. What accounts for our indifference, our lukewarm response to acts like this, to these signs of the times, ominous as they are for an unpromising future? Is it cynicism? Is it a premature exhaustion of intellect and imagination in a society sinking into decay despite its youth? Is it that our moral principles have been shaken to their foundations, or perhaps that we have no such principles at all? I can't answer these questions, and yet they trouble me, and every citizen not only must but ought to be troubled by them. Our young and still timid press has already done the public a real service, because without it we would never have learned of the horrors of unchecked violence and moral collapse that the papers keep bringing to light — not just to those who attend the new jury courts set up under the present reign, but to everyone. And what do we read almost every day? Things next to which this case pales, seems almost ordinary. But the important point is that most of our national crimes of violence testify to a widespread evil, now so general among us that it's hard to fight.”

“One day we see a brilliant young officer from high society, at the very start of his career, coldly and treacherously, without a flicker of conscience, murdering an official who had once been his benefactor, along with the man's servant girl, in order to steal his own promissory note and whatever cash he could find on him — ‘it'll come in handy for my pleasures in fashionable society, and for my career.’ After killing them, he tucks a pillow under each victim's head, then leaves. Next, a young war hero ‘decorated for bravery’ kills the mother of his commanding officer and benefactor, like a common highwayman, and to talk his accomplices into it he insists that ‘she loves him like a son, so she'll follow all his instructions and take no precautions.’ Granted, he's a monster — but I don't dare claim these days that he's unique. Another man won't commit the murder, but will feel and think exactly as he does, and is every bit as rotten in his soul. Alone, in silence, with only his conscience for company, he may ask himself, ‘What is honor, really — and isn't condemning bloodshed just a prejudice?’”

“Perhaps people will accuse me of being morbid, hysterical, of monstrous slander, of exaggeration. Let them say so — and heaven knows, I'd be the first to rejoice if it were true! Oh, don't believe me — think of me as sick in the head if you like, but remember my words: even if only a tenth, only a twentieth, of what I say is true, it's still appalling! Look how our young people kill themselves, without so much as asking Hamlet's question about what lies beyond, without any sign that such a question has crossed their minds — as though everything to do with the soul, with what awaits us past the grave, had long ago been erased from their heads and buried in the sand. Look at our vice, our libertines. Fyodor Pavlovitch, the unlucky victim in this case, was practically an innocent babe next to many of them. And yet we all knew him — ‘he lived among us!’...”

“Yes — perhaps someday the great minds of Russia and of Europe will study the psychology of Russian crime, because the subject deserves it. But that study will come later, at leisure, once all of today's tragic upheaval lies further behind us, when it can be examined with more insight and more fairness than I can manage now. For the moment we're either horrified, or pretend to be, while actually gloating over the spectacle, drawn to strong and eccentric sensations that titillate our cynical, pampered boredom. Or else, like children, we brush the terrible ghosts away and bury our heads in the pillow, eager to get back to our games and amusements the moment they're gone. But someday we'll have to start living in sober earnest; we'll have to look at ourselves as a society; it's time we tried to understand something of our own social condition, or at least made a start in that direction.”

“A great writer of the last generation, comparing Russia to a swift troika racing toward an unknown destination, cries out, ‘Oh, troika, bird-like troika, who invented you!’ and adds, in proud ecstasy, that all the nations of the world stand respectfully aside to let the recklessly galloping troika pass. Maybe so — maybe they do stand aside, respectfully or not — but in my humble opinion the great writer ended his book that way either in a fit of childish, naïve optimism, or simply out of fear of the censors of his day. Because if the troika were being driven by his own heroes — Sobakevitch, Nozdryov, Tchitchikov — it could never reach any rational destination, no matter who held the reins. And those were the heroes of an older generation. Ours are worse specimens still....”

At this point Ippolit Kirillovitch's speech was interrupted by applause. The liberal implications of the image were not lost on anyone. The applause was brief, true, so the presiding judge didn't think it necessary to issue a warning, and only gave the offenders a stern look. But Ippolit Kirillovitch was encouraged — he had never been applauded before! All his life he had struggled to get anyone to listen to him, and now, suddenly, he had a chance to command the ear of all Russia.

“What, in the end, is this Karamazov family, which has earned such an unenviable notoriety across Russia?” he went on. “Perhaps I'm exaggerating, but it seems to me that certain fundamental traits of today's educated class are reflected in this family portrait — only, of course, in miniature, ‘like the sun in a drop of water.’ Think of that unhappy, depraved, unrestrained old man who met such a grim end — the head of a family! Born into the nobility, but in a poor, dependent position, he came into a small fortune through an unexpected marriage. A petty schemer, a toady and a buffoon, with a fairly sharp though undeveloped mind, he was above all a moneylender, growing bolder as his fortunes grew. His fawning, servile side dropped away, leaving only his malicious, sarcastic cynicism. Spiritually he never developed at all, while his appetite for life was excessive. He saw nothing in life but sensual pleasure, and he raised his children to see nothing else either. He felt no obligation to his duties as a father — he mocked them. He left his young children to the servants and was glad to be rid of them, forgot about them entirely. The old man's motto was Après moi le déluge. He stood for everything opposed to civic duty, the most complete and vicious individualism. ‘Let the world burn, so long as I'm all right’ — and he was all right; he was content, eager to keep living exactly this way for another twenty or thirty years. He cheated his own son, spending the boy's money — his inheritance from his mother — trying to steal his mistress from him. No, I don't intend to leave the prisoner's defense entirely to my talented colleague from Petersburg. I'll speak the truth myself: I understand perfectly well what resentment must have built up in the son's heart against him.”

“But enough, enough about that unhappy old man — he's paid the price. Let's remember, though, that he was a father, and one of the typical fathers of our time. Am I really being unfair in calling him typical of a great many modern fathers? Alas — plenty of them differ from him only in not openly flaunting such cynicism, because they're better educated, more cultured, but their underlying philosophy is essentially the same as his. Perhaps I'm a pessimist — but you've agreed to forgive me that. Let's agree in advance: you don't have to believe me, but let me speak. Let me say what I have to say, and hold on to a little of it.”
“Now, the children of this father, this head of a family. One of them is the prisoner before us — the rest of my speech will deal with him. Of the other two I'll speak only in passing.”

“The eldest son is one of those modern young men of brilliant education and vigorous intellect who has lost all faith in everything. He has already denied and rejected a great deal, like his father. We've all heard him speak; he was a welcome guest in local society. He never hid his views — quite the opposite, in fact — which is my justification for speaking rather openly about him now, not as an individual, of course, but as a member of the Karamazov family. Another figure closely tied to this case took his own life here just last night. I mean the afflicted, feeble-minded man who had been Fyodor Pavlovitch's servant, and possibly his illegitimate son — Smerdyakov. At the preliminary inquiry he told me, in tears, hysterically, how young Ivan Karamazov had appalled him with his spiritual daring. ‘Everything in the world is permitted, according to him, and nothing will be forbidden from now on — that's what he always taught me.’ I believe that poor, feeble-minded man was driven out of his senses by this theory, though of course the epileptic fits he suffered from, and this terrible catastrophe, no doubt helped unhinge his mind further. But he let drop one remark, quite striking, that would have done credit to a more intelligent observer, and that's exactly why I mention it: ‘If there's one of the sons who takes after Fyodor Pavlovitch in character, it's Ivan Fyodorovitch.’”

“With that remark I'll close my sketch of his character — I feel it would be indelicate to go further. Oh, I have no wish to draw further conclusions and croak over the young man's future like some raven of doom. We've seen today, in this courtroom, that there are still good impulses in his young heart, that family feeling has not been destroyed in him by his lack of faith and his cynicism — traits that came to him more by inheritance, I think, than through any exercise of his own independent thought.”

“Then the third son. Oh, he's a devout, modest young man, who doesn't share his elder brother's bleak, destructive view of life. He has tried to hold fast to ‘the ideas of the people,’ or to whatever goes by that name in certain circles of our educated class. He clung to the monastery, and came within a hair of becoming a monk. It seems to me he unconsciously betrayed, and at such an early age, that timid despair which drives so many in our unhappy society — people who dread cynicism and its corrupting influence, and mistakenly blame all our troubles on European enlightenment — to return to their ‘native soil,’ as they call it, to the bosom, so to speak, of their mother earth, like frightened children longing to fall asleep against the withered breast of their aged mother, and to sleep there forever, if only to escape the horrors that terrify them.”

“For my part, I wish the excellent, gifted young man every success. I hope his youthful idealism and his pull toward the ideas of the people never degenerate, as so often happens, into gloomy mysticism on the spiritual side and blind chauvinism on the political — two forces that pose an even greater danger to Russia than the premature decay, born of misunderstanding and the wholesale borrowing of European ideas, from which his elder brother is suffering.”

Two or three people clapped at the mention of chauvinism and mysticism. Ippolit Kirillovitch had, in truth, been swept away by his own eloquence. None of this had much to do with the case at hand — not to mention that it was rather vague — but the sickly, consumptive man was overcome by the urge to express himself, just once, in his life. People said afterward that his criticism of Ivan was driven by less than noble motives, since Ivan had gotten the better of him once or twice in argument, and Ippolit Kirillovitch, remembering it, was now taking his revenge. But I don't know whether that's true. In any case, all this was only introductory, and the speech now moved on to a more direct look at the case.

“But to return to the eldest son,” Ippolit Kirillovitch went on. “He is the prisoner before us. We have his life, and his actions too, laid out before us; the fatal day has come, and everything has risen to the surface. While his brothers seem to stand for ‘Europeanism’ and ‘the principles of the people,’ he seems to represent Russia as she actually is. Oh, not all of Russia — not all of her! God forbid it should be so! And yet here she is, our mother Russia, her very scent and sound. Oh, he is spontaneous — a marvelous jumble of good and evil, a lover of culture and of Schiller, and yet he brawls in taverns and yanks the beards of his drinking companions. Oh, he too can be good, even noble — but only when things are going well for him. What's more, he can be swept off his feet, positively carried away, by noble ideals — but only if they come to him unbidden, if they drop from heaven, if he doesn't have to pay for them. He hates paying for anything, but he loves receiving, and that's true of him in everything. Oh, give him every good thing life has to offer — he wouldn't be satisfied with less — put no obstacle in his way, and he'll show you that he too can be noble. He isn't greedy — no — but he has to have money, a great deal of money, and you'll see how generously, with what contempt for filthy lucre, he'll fling it all away in one night of reckless dissipation. But if he has no money, you'll see what he's prepared to do to get it when he needs it badly enough. But all that comes later — let's take events in their order.”

“First we have before us a poor, neglected child, running around the back yard ‘without boots on his feet,’ as our worthy and esteemed fellow citizen of foreign extraction — alas! — put it just now. I say again, I yield the defense of the accused to no one. I am here to accuse him, but to defend him too. Yes, I too am human; I too can weigh the influence of home and childhood on a man's character. But the boy grows up and becomes an officer; for a duel, and other reckless behavior, he's exiled to one of Russia's remote frontier towns. There he led the wild life of an officer. And of course he needed money — money above everything — and so, after long disputes, he came to a settlement with his father, and the last six thousand roubles were sent to him. There's a letter in existence in which he essentially waives his claim to the rest and settles his dispute with his father over the inheritance for that payment of six thousand.”

“Then came his meeting with a young woman of lofty character and brilliant education. Oh, I won't presume to repeat the details — you've only just heard them. Honor, self-sacrifice, were on display there, and I'll say no more. The figure of the young officer, frivolous and dissolute, paying homage to true nobility and a lofty ideal, appeared before us in a very sympathetic light. But the other side of the coin was unexpectedly turned toward us immediately afterward, in this very courtroom. Again I won't venture to guess why it happened that way, but there were reasons. That same lady, her eyes wet with tears of long-suppressed indignation, told us that he — he, of all men — had despised her for an act which, reckless and imprudent as it may have been, was still prompted by lofty and generous motives. He, the girl's own betrothed, looked at her with that mocking smile, more unbearable coming from him than from anyone else. And knowing already that he had deceived her — believing, as he did, that she was bound to endure anything from him, even betrayal — she deliberately offered him three thousand roubles, and let him understand, all too clearly, that she was paying him to deceive her. ‘Well — will you take it or not? Have you no shame at all?’ was the silent question in her searching eyes. He looked at her, saw plainly what was in her mind — he's admitted before you here that he understood all of it — and pocketed those three thousand roubles without a second thought, then squandered them in two days on his new love.”

“What are we to believe, then? The first version — of the young officer sacrificing his last farthing in a noble burst of generosity, doing homage to virtue — or this other, repellent picture? As a rule, when faced with two extremes, one looks for the middle ground — but in this case that won't do. It's more likely that in the first instance he was genuinely noble, and in the second, genuinely base. And why? Because he has the broad Karamazov nature — that's exactly what I'm building toward — capable of combining the most incongruous contradictions, capable of the greatest heights and the greatest depths at once. Remember the brilliant observation made by a young man who has watched the Karamazov family up close — Mr. Rakitin: ‘The sense of their own degradation is as essential to these reckless, ungoverned natures as the sense of their own lofty generosity.’ And that's true — they need this unnatural mixture continually. Two extremes at the same moment, or else they feel wretched, dissatisfied, incomplete. They are as broad as mother Russia herself; they take in everything and endure everything.”

“By the way, gentlemen of the jury, since we've just touched on those three thousand roubles, I'll venture to get a little ahead of myself. Can you really imagine a man like that — having received that sum, and in such a way, at the cost of such shame, such disgrace, such utter degradation — could have been capable, that very same day, of setting aside half the sum, sewing it into a little bag, and having the strength of character to carry it on him for a whole month afterward, in spite of every temptation and his desperate need for it! Not once, whether in drunken debauchery in taverns, or when he was racing out into the countryside trying to borrow, from God knows whom, the money he so badly needed to keep the woman he loved out of his father's clutches, did he bring himself to touch that little bag! Why, if only to keep from abandoning his mistress to the rival he was so jealous of, he'd surely have opened that bag and stayed behind to watch over her, waiting for the moment she would finally say to him, ‘I am yours,’ so that he could fly off with her, far from those fatal surroundings.”

“But no — he never touched his talisman, and what reason does he give for that? The main reason, as I've just said, was that when she said ‘I am yours, take me wherever you like,’ he wanted to have the means to take her. But that first reason, in the prisoner's own words, mattered little next to the second. As long as I have that money on me, he said, I am a scoundrel, but not a thief — because I can always go to my insulted betrothed and, laying down half the sum I fraudulently took, say to her, ‘You see, I've squandered half your money, and shown myself weak and dishonorable, a scoundrel if you like’ (I'm using the prisoner's own words) ‘— but though I'm a scoundrel, I'm not a thief, because if I were a thief, I wouldn't have brought you back this half — I'd have taken it too, the way I took the rest!’ A remarkable explanation! This frantic but weak man, who couldn't resist the temptation of taking three thousand roubles at the price of such disgrace, suddenly develops the most stoical willpower and carries around a thousand roubles without daring to touch it. Does that square at all with the character we've just examined? No — and I'll go so far as to tell you how the real Dmitri Karamazov would have behaved in such circumstances, if he had actually brought himself to set the money aside.”

“At the very first temptation — say, to treat the woman with whom he'd already squandered half the money — he would have unpicked the little bag and pulled out a hundred roubles or so. Because why, exactly, would he have kept back precisely half the money — fifteen hundred roubles? Why not fourteen hundred? He could just as easily have claimed he wasn't a thief by bringing back fourteen hundred. Then, another time, he'd have unpicked it again and taken out another hundred, and then a third time, and a fourth, and before the month was out he'd have taken the second-to-last note, reasoning that bringing back even a hundred would serve the purpose, since a thief would have stolen the whole lot. And then he'd have looked at that last note and told himself, ‘It's really not worth handing back just a hundred — let's spend that too!’ That's how the real Dmitri Karamazov, as we know him, would have behaved. Nothing could be harder to reconcile with the actual facts than this legend of the little bag. Nothing could be less conceivable. But we'll return to that later.”

After touching on what had come out at the trial concerning the financial dealings between father and son, and arguing again and again that it was utterly impossible, from the known facts, to say which of them was in the wrong, Ippolit Kirillovitch moved on to the medical experts' testimony regarding Mitya's fixed idea about the three thousand roubles owed him.

chapters.title: VII. An Historical Survey
paragraphs: “The medical experts have tried to convince us that the prisoner is out of his mind — in fact, a maniac. I maintain that he is in full possession of his senses, and that if he weren't, he would have behaved more cleverly. As for his being a maniac, I'll grant that much, but only on one point: his fixed idea about the three thousand roubles. Even so, I think one could find a far simpler explanation than any tendency toward insanity. For my part, I fully agree with the young doctor who maintained that the prisoner's mental faculties have always been normal, and that he has simply been irritable and exasperated. The object of the prisoner's continual, violent anger was never the sum of money itself — there was a special motive underneath it. That motive is jealousy!”

Here Ippolit Kirillovitch described at length the prisoner's fatal passion for Grushenka. He began with the moment the prisoner went to the ‘young woman's’ lodgings ‘to beat her’ — ‘I'm using his own words,’ the prosecutor explained — ‘but instead of beating her, he stayed there, at her feet. That was where the passion began. At the same time, the prisoner's father had fallen for the same young woman — a strange and fatal coincidence, since both of them lost their hearts to her at once, though both had known her before. And she inspired in both of them the same violent, characteristically Karamazov passion. We have her own confession: “I was laughing at both of them.” Yes — the sudden urge to make a joke of them came over her, and she conquered them both at once. The old man, who worshipped money, immediately set aside three thousand roubles as payment for a single visit from her — but soon after, he'd have been happy to lay his whole fortune and his name at her feet, if only she'd become his lawful wife. We have solid evidence of this. As for the prisoner, the tragedy of his fate is plain — it's right in front of us. But such was the young woman's “game.” The enchantress gave the unhappy young man no hope until the very last moment, when he knelt before her with hands already stained with his father's and rival's blood. That was the position he was in when he was arrested. “Send me to Siberia with him — I brought him to this, I am the one most to blame,” the woman herself cried, in genuine remorse, at the moment of his arrest.’

“The talented young man I've already mentioned, Mr. Rakitin, summed up this heroine in a few striking words: ‘She was disillusioned early in life, betrayed and ruined by a fiancé who seduced and abandoned her. She was left in poverty, cursed by her respectable family, and taken under the wing of a wealthy old man, whom to this day she still considers her benefactor. There may well have been a great deal of good in her young heart, but it was embittered too soon. She grew shrewd and started saving money. She became sarcastic and resentful toward society.’ After that sketch of her character, it's easy enough to understand how she might have laughed at both of them purely out of mischief, out of spite.”

“After a month of hopeless love and moral collapse, during which he betrayed his betrothed and misappropriated money entrusted to his honor, the prisoner was driven nearly to frenzy, nearly to madness, by relentless jealousy — of whom? His own father! And the worst part was that the crazy old man was luring and enticing the object of his son's affection with the very same three thousand roubles that the son regarded as his own, part of his inheritance from his mother, of which his father was cheating him. Yes, I admit — that was hard to bear. It might well drive a man mad. It wasn't the money itself, but the fact that this money was being used, with such revolting cynicism, to destroy his happiness!”
Then the prosecutor went on to describe how the idea of murdering his father had taken hold in the prisoner's mind, and backed up his theory with facts.

“At first he only talked about it in taverns — he talked about it all that month. Ah, he likes always having company around him, and he likes telling his companions everything, even his most diabolical and dangerous ideas; he likes sharing every thought with others, and for some reason expects the people he confides in to meet him with perfect sympathy, to enter into all his troubles and worries, to take his side and never oppose him in anything. If they don't, he flies into a rage and smashes up everything in the tavern.” (Then followed the anecdote about Captain Snegiryov.) “Those who heard the prisoner began at last to suspect he might mean more than idle threats, and that such a frenzy might turn talk into action.”
Here the prosecutor described the family's meeting at the monastery, the conversations with Alyosha, and the ugly scene of violence when the prisoner burst into his father's house just after dinner.

“I can't say for certain,” the prosecutor went on, “that the prisoner had fully made up his mind to murder his father before that incident. And yet the idea had occurred to him more than once, and he had dwelt on it — we have facts, witnesses, and his own words to prove it. I confess, gentlemen of the jury,” he added, “that until today I was uncertain whether to credit the prisoner with conscious premeditation. I was firmly convinced he had pictured that fatal moment beforehand — but only pictured it, entertained it as a possibility. He hadn't definitely worked out when or how he might commit the crime.”

“But I was uncertain only until today — until that fatal document was placed before the court just now. You yourselves heard that young lady's exclamation: ‘It's the plan — the program for the murder!’ That's how she described that wretched, drunken letter from the unfortunate prisoner. And in fact, from that letter, we can see that the murder was premeditated in its entirety. It was written two days beforehand, and so we now know, as a fact, that forty-eight hours before carrying out his terrible design, the prisoner swore that if he couldn't get money by the next day, he would murder his father to take the envelope with the notes from under his pillow, as soon as Ivan had left. ‘As soon as Ivan has gone away’ — you hear that? So he had thought it all through, weighing every circumstance, and he carried it out exactly as he had written it. The proof of premeditation is conclusive; the crime must have been committed for the sake of the money — that's stated plainly, written down, and signed. The prisoner doesn't deny his own signature.”

“I'll be told he was drunk when he wrote it. But that doesn't lessen the letter's value — quite the opposite: drunk, he wrote down what he had planned sober. If he hadn't planned it sober, he wouldn't have written it drunk. I'll be asked: then why did he talk about it in taverns? A man planning such a crime keeps quiet and holds it to himself. Yes — but he talked about it before he'd formed any plan, when he had only the desire, only the impulse toward it. Afterward he talked about it less. On the evening he wrote that letter, at the ‘Metropolis’ tavern, he was unusually silent, though he'd been drinking. He didn't play billiards; he sat in a corner and spoke to no one. True, he did turn a shopkeeper out of his seat, but that was done almost without thinking — he could never walk into a tavern without causing some kind of scene. It's true that once he'd made his final decision, he must have felt uneasy at having talked so much about his plan beforehand, worried that it might lead to his arrest and prosecution afterward. But there was nothing to be done — he couldn't take his words back. Still, his luck had served him before, and it would serve him again. He believed in his star, you understand! I should add, too, that he did a great deal to avoid the fatal catastrophe. ‘Tomorrow I'll try to borrow money from everyone,’ as he puts it in his own peculiar language, ‘and if they won't give it to me, there will be bloodshed.’”

Here Ippolit Kirillovitch went into a detailed account of all Mitya's efforts to borrow money. He described the visit to Samsonov, the trip to Lyagavy. “Harassed, mocked, hungry, having sold his watch to pay for the journey (though he tells us he had fifteen hundred roubles on him at the time — a likely story), tormented by jealousy at having left the object of his affections back in town, suspecting she'd go to Fyodor Pavlovitch while he was away, he finally returned to town, only to discover, to his joy, that she hadn't gone near his father. He even walked her home to her protector himself. (Strangely enough, he doesn't seem to have been jealous of Samsonov — which is psychologically interesting.) Then he hurries back to his hiding place in the back gardens, and there learns that Smerdyakov is having a fit, that the other servant is ill — the coast is clear, and he knows the ‘signals’ — what a temptation! And still he resists it; he goes off instead to a lady who has been living in town for some time and is highly respected among us, Madame Hohlakov. That lady, who had long watched his career with pity, gave him the most sensible advice: to give up his dissipated life, his unseemly love affair, the waste of his youth and energy in tavern debauchery, and to head off to Siberia to the gold mines — ‘that would be an outlet for your restless energy, your romantic nature, your thirst for adventure.’”

After describing the outcome of that conversation, and the moment the prisoner learned that Grushenka had not, after all, stayed at Samsonov's — the sudden frenzy of the unlucky man, worn down by jealousy and nervous exhaustion, at the thought that she had deceived him and was now with his father — Ippolit Kirillovitch closed by dwelling on the fatal role of chance. “Had the maid told him her mistress was at Mokroe with her former lover, nothing would have happened. But she lost her head; all she could do was swear and protest that she knew nothing, and if the prisoner didn't kill her on the spot, it was only because he ran off in pursuit of his faithless mistress.”

“But notice — frantic as he was, he took a brass pestle with him. Why that? Why not some other weapon? Because he'd been turning his plan over and preparing himself for it for a full month, he would have snatched up whatever looked like a weapon caught his eye. He'd realized for a month that any such object would serve, so he recognized instantly, without hesitation, that this one would do the job. So it wasn't unconscious at all, wasn't involuntary, that he grabbed that fatal pestle. And then we find him in his father's garden — the coast clear, no witnesses, darkness and jealousy all around him. The suspicion that she was there, with him, with his rival, in his arms, maybe laughing at him at that very moment — it took his breath away. And it wasn't mere suspicion; the deception was open, obvious. She had to be there, in that lit room, behind the screen — and the unhappy man would have us believe that he crept up to the window, peeked in respectfully, and discreetly withdrew, for fear something terrible and improper might happen. And he tries to persuade us of that — us, who understand his character, who know his state of mind at that moment, and know that he knew the very signals that would let him walk straight into the house.” At this point Ippolit Kirillovitch broke off to give an exhaustive discussion of the suspected connection between Smerdyakov and the murder. He went into it very thoroughly, and everyone could tell that although he claimed to dismiss the suspicion, he thought the subject mattered a great deal.

chapters.title: VIII. A Treatise On Smerdyakov
paragraphs: “To begin with, where did this suspicion come from?” (Ippolit Kirillovitch began.) “The first person to cry out that Smerdyakov had committed the murder was the prisoner himself, at the moment of his arrest — and yet from that moment to this he hasn't produced a single fact to back up the charge, not the faintest hint of one. The charge is supported by only three people: the prisoner's two brothers, and Madame Svyetlov. The elder of the two brothers voiced his suspicions only today, and while he was, without question, in the grip of brain fever. But we know that for the past two months he fully shared our conviction of his brother's guilt and made no attempt to argue against it. More on that later. The younger brother has admitted he hasn't the slightest fact to support his idea of Smerdyakov's guilt, and has been led to that conclusion purely by the prisoner's own words and the look on his face. Yes — that astonishing piece of testimony was offered twice today, by him. Madame Svyetlov was even more astonishing: ‘Whatever the prisoner tells you, you must believe — he's not a man who lies.’ That is the whole of the evidence against Smerdyakov produced by these three people, all of them deeply invested in the prisoner's fate. And yet the theory of Smerdyakov's guilt has been noised about, has been maintained, and is still being maintained. Is that credible? Is it even conceivable?”

Here Ippolit Kirillovitch thought it necessary to describe Smerdyakov's character, “a man who cut short his own life in a fit of insanity.” He portrayed him as a man of weak intellect with a smattering of education, thrown off balance by philosophical ideas above his level and by certain modern notions of duty, which he picked up in practice from the reckless life of his master — who was perhaps also his father — Fyodor Pavlovitch; and, in theory, from various odd philosophical conversations with his master's elder son, Ivan Fyodorovitch, who readily indulged in this pastime, probably out of boredom, or perhaps to amuse himself at the valet's expense. “He spoke to me himself about his state of mind during his last few days at his father's house,” Ippolit Kirillovitch explained; “but others have testified to it too — the prisoner himself, his brother, and the servant Grigory — that is, everyone who knew him well.”

“What's more, Smerdyakov, whose health had been undermined by his epileptic attacks, had no more courage than a chicken. ‘He fell at my feet and kissed them,’ the prisoner himself has told us, before he realized how damaging that statement was to his own case. ‘He's an epileptic chicken,’ was how he characteristically described him. And the prisoner chose him as his confidant — we have his own word on it — and frightened him into finally agreeing to act as his spy. In that role he betrayed his master, revealing to the prisoner the existence of the envelope full of notes, and the signals that would let him into the house. How could he help telling him, really? ‘He would have killed me — I could see he would have killed me,’ Smerdyakov said at the inquiry, trembling and shaking even in front of us, though by then his tormentor had already been arrested and could do him no harm. ‘He suspected me every single moment. In fear and trembling I hurried to tell him every secret, just to calm him down, so he'd see I hadn't deceived him and would let me live.’ Those are his own words.
